papers.title: Doyle, J. (1979). A Truth Maintenance System. Artificial Intelligence 12(3):231-272. Read via MIT AI Memo 521 (June 1979), which Doyle lists as the same paper
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified, with one caveat. Semantic Scholar resolves DOI 10.1016/0004-3702(79)90008-0 to 'A Truth Maintenance System' (1979, DBLP journals/ai/Doyle79), and Doyle's own publication page lists 'Artificial Intelligence 12 (1979), 231-272. Also MIT AI Lab Memo 521 (1979)'. I could not get the Elsevier journal PDF, which is paywalled. The DSpace copy (hdl 1721.1/5733) returned HTTP 429, so I got AIM-521.pdf from a Wayback Machine snapshot (45 scanned pages), ran OCR on it and read all of sections 1-4 and 9-10. I also read two later restatements by Doyle himself: Chapter 3 of his 1980 PhD thesis (MIT AI TR-581, 'RMS'), and 'The Ins and Outs of Reason Maintenance' (IJCAI-83), which formalizes admissible, finitely grounded extensions. Everything below that is attributed to R1 comes from the memo text. I have not checked word-for-word that it matches the journal version.
core_ideas: A node is a belief. A justification is a reason for it. A node is IN if and only if at least one of its justifications is valid, and OUT otherwise. Doyle says explicitly: 'The distinction between in and out is not that between true and false.' To reason about negation, P and not-P need separate nodes, which gives a 4-valued belief state in the style of Belnap.

An SL (support-list) justification is a pair (inlist, outlist). It is valid if and only if every inlist node is IN and every outlist node is OUT. An empty inlist and empty outlist make a premise. A nonempty inlist with an empty outlist is a monotonic deduction. A non-empty outlist makes a non-monotonic justification. An 'assumption' is a node whose current supporting justification has a non-empty outlist, so being an assumption depends on context.

The second kind is the CP (conditional-proof) justification: (CP consequent inhypotheses outhypotheses). It is converted to an SL justification by the Find Independent Support (FIS) procedure, which marks the hypotheses and their repercussions with E/S marks and collects the foundations of the consequent that do not depend on the hypotheses. In section 9 Doyle says that checking CP justifications continuously made the implementation 'considerably more complex', and suggests making FIS a facility the user calls explicitly.

Well-founded support: every IN node has exactly one designated supporting-justification, and these form a non-circular argument back to premises and assumptions. Doyle's motivating example: with G<-(F,H) and H<-(F,G) and no external support, evaluating each justification locally leaves G and H IN through circular self-support. The TMS must believe no node for circular reasons.

Doyle names three kinds of circularity. (1) All nodes in the cycle can consistently be OUT, which is the common case for equivalent or mutually constraining beliefs; the TMS makes them all OUT. (2) At least one node must be IN, e.g. F<-(SL () (G)) and G<-(SL () (F)); the TMS has to choose. (3) No IN/OUT assignment is consistent, e.g. F<-(SL () (F)). Doyle says his implementation goes into a loop on type (3) because he removed the costly check.

Dependency vocabulary, all stored or derivable per node: supporting-nodes, antecedents, foundations (transitive closure of antecedents), ancestors (transitive closure of supporting-nodes), consequences (every node whose justification mentions this node, i.e. the reverse index), affected-consequences, believed-consequences, repercussions and believed-repercussions. An OUT node's supporting-nodes are one blocking node per justification: an OUT inlist node or an IN outlist node. That way the node's status cannot change unless a recorded blocker changes or a new valid justification is added.

Retraction is reasoned rather than raw deletion. To get rid of P you justify not-P, which sits in P's outlist. In the thesis every justification is made defeasible by reifying it as a node J with (SL () (DEFEATED-J)), so justifications are defeated, never removed.

Dependency-directed backtracking: find the maximal assumptions in the foundations of the contradiction, create a NOGOOD node justified by a CP justification so that it stays IN after the culprit goes OUT, pick a culprit A_i, and justify one of the denials D_j in A_i's outlist by (SL (NG, the other assumptions) (the other denials)). Culprit and denial are chosen at random. Doyle calls this 'blind search ... inadequate for all but the simplest sorts of problems'.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Node structure in the thesis (Lisp Machine defstructure): CONTENT, SL-JUSTIFICATIONS, CP-JUSTIFICATIONS, SUPPORTING-JUSTIFICATION(S), SUPPORTING-NODES, CONSEQUENCES, SUPPORT-STATUS, CONTRADICTION-MARK, plus scratch marks (NODE-MARK, TMP-MARK, FIS-MARK, ...), signal-recalling and signal-forgetting callbacks, and CP-CONSEQUENT-LIST. An SL justification is {INLIST, OUTLIST}. A CP justification is {CONSEQUENT, INHYPOTHESES, OUTHYPOTHESES}.

Truth-maintenance procedure, steps 1-7 (memo section 3.2). (1) Add the justification and record the node in each antecedent's CONSEQUENCES. If the node is already IN, or the justification is invalid, only bookkeeping is needed (record a blocker as a supporting-node). (2) If the node has no affected-consequences, mark it IN and stop. Otherwise build L = node plus all its repercussions, saving each one's old status: 'We must collect all the repercussions of the node to avoid constructing circular arguments which use repercussions of a node in its supposedly well-founded supporting argument.' (3) Set the status of every node in L to NIL, meaning undetermined. (4) Well-founded pass: for each NIL node, try justifications oldest-first. A justification is well-founded-valid if its inlist is all IN and its outlist all OUT, where NIL counts as neither. It is well-founded-invalid if some inlist node is OUT or some outlist node is IN. Mark the node IN or OUT and recurse into its NIL consequences; otherwise defer it. (5) Relaxation pass for nodes still NIL because of circularity: treat NIL as OUT. If a node with affected-consequences becomes IN, re-mark it and those consequences NIL and loop. This does not terminate on unsatisfiable circularities, and it can need to change nodes outside L, which makes it non-incremental. (6) Re-check CP justifications and contradictions (calling DDB), restarting step 6 if truth maintenance runs again. (7) Compare final against initial status for each node in L and signal only the net OUT->IN and IN->OUT changes.

For a positive (no outlist) justification graph, step 4 alone decides everything: a NIL node with no well-founded valid justification is OUT. That is the least fixpoint, and none of the step-5 relaxation is needed.

Dependency-directed backtracking (memo section 4), steps 1-4: find the maximal assumptions S in the foundations of contradiction C. Create or reuse NOGOOD node NG for S, justified by (CP C S ()). Pick culprit A_i and a denial D_j from the outlist of A_i's supporting justification, and justify D_j with (SL (NG + S - A_i) (A_i's other denials)). Repeat while C is still IN. If C has no assumptions in its foundations, report an unanalyzable contradiction.

Formal semantics (IJCAI-83): a state S is admissible if it satisfies the interpretation of every component. An admissible extension E of a kernel S is admissible and finitely grounded, meaning every element has a finite non-circular argument from S. Fixed-point theorem: E is in AExts(S) if and only if E = sigma_omega(S,E) (stratified by shortest-argument length). Corollary: admissible extensions are minimal under set inclusion. Checking E in AExts(S) takes O(|D|^3); Doyle did not know whether constructing one can be done in polynomial time. Later work (Elkan 1990) showed that NM-TMS labeling is NP-complete.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec section 2.4: S_e(r) is exactly the positive-SL TMS. base_e(r) corresponds to premises and enabled assumptions, each justification J is an SL justification with an empty outlist, and enabled_e(j) is Doyle's defeasible reified justification (node J with (SL () (DEFEATED-J))). The spec should cite this lineage directly. Its rule that 'No support is not False' is Doyle's IN/OUT versus true/false distinction.

Spec section 3.3 (rule_by_conclusion and rules_by_premise as native indexes) duplicates Doyle's SL-JUSTIFICATIONS and CONSEQUENCES slots and the JTMS justs/consequences fields. Bidirectional dependency indexes are prior art from 1979, so the H1 novelty claim has to rest on the versioned, compact, persistent physical layout and on certified reads, not on having forward and reverse indexes.

Spec section 2.7 (V1 positive recursion): positive cycles can only be Doyle's type (1), so the correct semantics is all OUT unless some well-founded external support exists, which is the least fixpoint. That is polynomial and needs no relaxation or search. Doyle's step 2 gives a concrete V1 rule: when a node changes, collect its repercussions L, reset L to undetermined, and re-derive only from nodes outside L. That is DRed restricted to repercussions. The spec should say outright that types (2) and (3) only appear once outlists (negation or defaults) exist, which matches its rejection of negation.

Watch for a hidden non-monotonic dependency in spec section 2.3. REQUIRES_CURRENT, 'valid only while head(logical_id) = r', depends on the absence of a superseding head, which is an outlist condition in Doyle's terms. It stays safe and stratified only if head pointers are base inputs that are never derived from justifications. The spec should state this as an invariant: heads and policies are not derivable. If a later version lets heads be derived, for example 'auto-promote revision if verified', it inherits Doyle's type 2 and 3 circularities and Elkan's NP-hardness. Add a test that tries to make a head derived and expects rejection.

Spec section 4.2 batch trap: Doyle's step 7 already records statuses before maintenance and signals only net changes after it. ContextDB should do the same per transaction: snapshot the affected set's statuses, run maintenance in staging, publish only the diff with the commit epoch. Golden test: inside one transaction, A goes OUT and then back IN, and no subscriber sees a change.

The spec's WHY query (section 5) must not copy Doyle's single supporting-justification. Doyle himself lists 'multiple supporting-justifications whenever several well-founded arguments can be found' as a future improvement (section 9). Keep the active_support_count together with the list of currently valid justifications, and also designate one well-founded witness justification for explanations. Make the witness choice deterministic (for example lowest RuleId, or rank-based as in the BPS entry), because Doyle and BPS both note that justification order changes which explanation is found. Oracle equality checks should compare statuses and counts, not witness pointers, unless the witness choice is canonical.

Spec section 2.5 (CONFLICTED): use DDB as a record, not as an automatic fix. Store nogoods, meaning minimal sets of base revisions or assumptions that support a contradiction node, and show them to agents. Do not auto-retract a culprit, since Doyle reports random culprit choice as inadequate. Keep CONFLICTED orthogonal to support, as the spec already does, matching Doyle's separate contradiction mark.

Doyle section 9 names an incrementality cost: the TMS may 'examine large numbers of nodes, only to leave most of them in their original state after finding alternate non-circular arguments'. This is exactly what H2 measures. Add a benchmark metric for nodes whose status was transiently reset but whose final status is unchanged ('churn'), and compare counter-based maintenance (spec) with support-pointer and repercussion-reset maintenance (Doyle/JTMS).
papers.reported_results: No quantitative evaluation. Section 9 ('Experience and Extensions') is qualitative only: first implementation in September 1976, grown out of Stallman and Sussman's ARS 'fact garbage collector'; used in AMORD, SYN, QUAL, Steele and Sussman's constraint language, and by McAllester. Admitted limitations: loops on unsatisfiable circularities, step 5 can be non-incremental, wasted re-examination of nodes that end up unchanged, CP justification checking is complex, culprit selection is random. IJCAI-83 adds that admissibility of an extension can be checked in O(|D|^3) and leaves construction complexity open.
spec_gaps_or_errors: The spec's R1 row ('kernel natively maintains support relationships') treats native support maintenance as ContextDB's differentiator. The 1979 TMS already stores justifications natively with forward and reverse links, so this is a novelty risk, and the contribution needs to be stated more narrowly (versioning, currency, certification, physical layout, measured costs).

The spec says nothing about the well-founded explanation or witness. Doyle's main correctness concept is well-founded support, not support counts. A counter tells you that support exists, but on a graph with cycles it cannot tell you whether that support is well-founded. The spec admits this for V0 ('cannot rely on support_count alone') but should cite Doyle's type-1 circularity as the canonical counterexample and adopt his repercussion-reset idea for V1.
REQUIRES_CURRENT carries non-monotonic (outlist) semantics, and the spec presents V0 as purely positive. The spec should add the stratification invariant that heads are never derived.

UNKNOWN in the spec's StructuralState is undefined. In Doyle a node is only IN or OUT outside maintenance, and NIL appears only during maintenance. In the LTMS, UNKNOWN means neither label is derivable. The spec should define UNKNOWN, for example as 'dirty or not yet recomputed in lazy mode', and keep it distinct from OUT/UNSUPPORTED.

papers.title: de Kleer, J. (1986). An Assumption-based TMS. Artificial Intelligence 28(2):127-162
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified. I read the full scanned journal article (36 pages) from https://www.dekleer.org/Publications/An%20Assumption-Based%20TMS.pdf. The header gives 'Artificial Intelligence 28 (1986) 127-162', received April 1985 and revised September 1985, which matches the spec's citation and DOI prefix. I read all sections: 1-3 (motivation, search, Doyle TMS limitations), 4 (basic ATMS: definitions, labels, data structures, lattice, algorithm, complexity, retraction, classes), 5 (limitations removed), 6 (implementation) and 7 (summary). The companion papers 'Extending the ATMS' (pp.163-196) and 'Problem solving with the ATMS' (pp.197-224) are cited but I did not read them.
core_ideas: Instead of one global IN/OUT state, every node carries a label, which is the set of minimal environments (sets of assumptions) under which it is derivable. An environment E holds node n if and only if E is a superset of some environment in label(n), so membership is a subset test. Context switching is 'free' and many mutually inconsistent contexts can coexist.

Justifications are propositional Horn clauses (x1 and ... and xk => n). There are no outlists or negation in the basic ATMS, so it is monotone Horn. Inconsistency is handled by the distinguished node FALSE: the environments in its label are nogoods, and nogoods plus all their supersets are removed from every label.

The four label invariants are sound (n is derivable from each E), consistent (no E is nogood), complete (every consistent E that derives n is a superset of some label environment) and minimal (no label environment is a subset of another). Labels do not depend on the order in which assumptions, nodes and justifications are introduced.

An assumption (the decision to assume) is distinguished from the assumed datum. de Kleer recommends assumption/assumed-node pairs so that retracting means contradicting the assumption. Retracting a justification is done by conjoining it with an extra assumption and contradicting that assumption. Direct justification removal is 'isomorphic to LISP garbage collection' and 'a bad idea', because removing a nogood can force subsumed nogoods back and potentially touch every label.

Circular justifications cost nothing: with a=>b and b=>a both labels stay empty. If a gets an environment, the propagation round-trip adds only supersets, which minimality discards, so propagation stops. 'Checking for circular supporting justifications is unnecessary.'

Nodes fall into four sets: TRUE (label contains the empty environment; grows monotonically), IN (nonempty label), OUT (empty label) and FALSE (nogood; grows monotonically). The ATMS is meant for finding all solutions, the JTMS for finding one.

de Kleer describes 'Unouting', meaning reasserting retracted data while not missing consequents that were never derived in the old context, as an interface problem between problem solver and TMS, and defers it to the consumer protocol in 'Problem solving with the ATMS'.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Node slots: Datum, Label (set of environments), Justifications (the forward index), Consequents (justifications that use the node as an antecedent, i.e. the reverse index), and a Contradictory bit. Environment slots: Assumptions, Nodes (the nodes whose labels mention it), Contradictory bit. Justification slots: Informant, Consequent, Antecedents. With the optimizations, an assumption also has Position (bit index), Contras (bitvector of the assumptions it is binary-inconsistent with) and Nogoods (minimal nogoods of size 3 or more containing it). An environment also has Contras, a Cache (adding assumption a gives environment E'), and Count (size).

Basic label update: the complete label of n is the union over its justifications k of the cross-product unions of one environment from each antecedent's label. Remove nogood and subsumed environments. If the label is unchanged, stop. If n is FALSE, add each environment to the nogood DB and purge it and its supersets from every label. Otherwise recurse into the consequents. It terminates because assumptions are finite. The incremental version propagates only the delta label added by the new justification. When a node has one justification and only one antecedent with a nonempty label, the label is copied forward.

The incremental algorithm as given in BPS ch.12: PROPAGATE(J, a, I) computes L = WEAVE(a, I, antecedents(J)) and calls UPDATE(L, n). UPDATE: if n is FALSE, call NOGOOD on each environment in L. Otherwise drop the environments of L subsumed by n's label, drop label environments subsumed by L, add the rest, and for each consumer justification call PROPAGATE, then filter L down to what is still in the label, with early termination when it is empty. WEAVE does a cross-product union of I with each other antecedent's label, removing duplicates, nogoods and subsumed environments. NOGOOD(E) marks E and removes E and its supersets from all labels.

Implementation tricks (section 6): environments are bit-vectors (union is OR, subset test is A AND NOT B == 0). Environments are hash-consed in a table keyed by bitvector, so the nogood check runs once per environment rather than once per union. The nogood DB is kept minimal by deleting supersets when a new nogood arrives. Environments and nogoods are indexed by size: a new environment is checked only against smaller nogoods, and a new nogood only against larger environments. Size-1 nogoods kill the assumption. Size-2 nogoods are stored as a per-assumption Contras bitvector checked before creating any environment, which also makes 'oneof' disjunctions free instead of needing n^2 nogoods. Single-assumption unions get three caches (per-assumption nogoods of size 3 or more, per-environment contras, per-environment add-cache). Assumptions are garbage-collected when all their consequents are TRUE or FALSE, or their singleton is nogood (de Kleer reports about 30% are collectible), and bit positions are recycled. Things found not worth it: caching all subset/union results, and keeping a DAG of all subset relations. Untried ideas: a union-only DAG (as in ART), a discrimination net for nogoods, and lazy label update with backward 'update' messages, except that contradiction-node labels must always be eager.

Contradiction back-propagation: if all antecedents of a contradictory node but one are TRUE, the remaining one is necessarily FALSE. This uses a second, simple propagator that follows antecedent links.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec sections 2.2 and 1 (Branch/ContextView, WHAT_IF): a ContextDB branch, i.e. a selected set of heads, assumptions and enabled rules, is an ATMS environment. If each revision carried a label of minimal sets of base inputs (head choices or assumptions), 'is r supported in branch b' would be a bitset subset test, and switching branches would require no re-propagation. This is a concrete design option for the future WHAT_IF and branch milestone, and it fits the positive Horn V0 kernel without negation.

The spec's 'Not supported initially: arbitrary ATMS environment combinations' and section 4.4's grouping of 'Default / negation / inconsistent ATMS environments' are partly a misreading. The basic ATMS is monotone Horn with nogoods, the same logic class as the V0 kernel. The real reason to defer it is worst-case label size (exponential even for acyclic Horn; see McAllester 1990), not semantics. The spec should say this precisely.

Use the four label invariants (sound, consistent, complete, minimal) as oracle-checkable properties for any label or branch feature. A brute-force oracle over small assumption sets (n up to about 12) can enumerate all 2^n environments and check them, which extends the spec's section 4.1 full-recompute oracle.

Spec section 2.7 cycles: under label semantics, cycles are handled without detection, because subsumption makes propagation reach a fixpoint. For V1 positive recursion this is an alternative to SCC/DRed: if support is tracked as minimal base-input sets instead of counts, cycles are automatically well-founded. The cost is label size, so benchmark label cardinality distributions on agent workloads.

Spec section 4.2 retraction and enabled_e(j): adopt de Kleer's advice. Never physically delete a justification; give each rule an enable assumption and flip that in a new epoch. This fits the append-only arenas in section 3.4. If ContextDB ever caches nogoods or labels, deleting a nogood is the expensive path, so make rule disable go through assumption toggling.

Physical layout (spec section 3.1-3.3): use bitset environments (fixed u64/u128 words, or roaring bitmaps for large assumption universes), a hash-consed environment arena keyed by bitset, a nogood index bucketed by cardinality, and binary-nogood bitvectors per assumption. These are concrete Rust-friendly structures for a future branch or what-if layer. Take de Kleer's negative results seriously too: per-operation subset caches and a full subset DAG were not worth it.

Spec section 4.5 eager-lazy hybrid: de Kleer already suggests lazy label updates with backward 'update' messages, with contradiction labels always kept eager. That matches the spec's STRICT read requirement (dirty means PENDING), and gives prior art to cite and an invariant: conflict detection must be eager even when support is lazy.

Spec section 2.5 CONFLICTED: ATMS nogoods give all minimal conflicting base-input sets, not just those of the current derivation, which a JTMS cannot do. For agent conflict explanation, minimal nogoods are the right object to show.
papers.reported_results: No quantitative experiments or benchmarks. The claims are qualitative: practical with about 1000 assumptions (a space of 2^1000), because only greatest-lower-bound environments and minimal nogoods are stored and inconsistencies tend to sit in small subsets. Efficiency is 'directly proportional to the number of environments it is forced to consider'. Pathological cases require justifications built so that every environment becomes a minimal nogood or label environment. About 30% of assumptions are typically garbage-collectible. Bit-vectors plus hash-consing are cheap enough that caching subset or union results costs more than it saves.
spec_gaps_or_errors: The spec's R2 row says it 'avoids exhaustive environment explosion'. The ATMS paper does not guarantee that. Labels can be exponential, which the paper concedes in section 4.8 and McAllester 1990 proves even for acyclic Horn clauses. Any ContextDB WHAT_IF design needs a focus or bound mechanism (see Forbus and de Kleer, 'Focusing the ATMS', AAAI-88).
The spec treats 'ATMS environments' as belonging with negation and defaults. The basic ATMS has neither; defaults and disjunctions come from the companion 'Extending the ATMS' paper.

The spec's support_count has no ATMS counterpart. ATMS labels carry strictly more information: they say which base inputs, not how many rules. The spec's H2 baseline list (section 7, ablations) should include a label-based (minimal-support-set) variant, because it is the natural cycle-safe competitor to counters.

papers.title: Forbus, K.D. & de Kleer, J. (1993). Building Problem Solvers. MIT Press. Chapters 6 (TMS intro), 7 (JTMS), 9 (LTMS) and 12 (ATMS), plus the jtms.lsp source
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified. MIT Press allows a free searchable scan, BPS-Searchable.pdf (727 pages, 109 MB), from https://www.qrg.northwestern.edu/BPS/. I extracted the text and read chapters 6 and 7 in full, the core of chapter 9 (BCP, the counter-based LTMS algorithm, the pvs counter) and the algorithms section of chapter 12. I also read the full JTMS source, jtms.lsp (version 176, modified 2005), from https://users.cs.northwestern.edu/~forbus/c44/Code/JTRE/jtms.lsp. The spec does not cite this book.
core_ideas: JTMS specification: a node is IN if and only if it follows propositionally from (enabled assumptions plus definite clauses from justifications). Justifications are never removed, and only the enabled assumption set changes. 'It is the fact that assumptions might be retracted that introduces most of the complexity.'

Well-founded support is a sequence of justifications J1..Jk where Jk justifies n, each antecedent is justified earlier or is an enabled assumption, and no node appears twice. A node has one if and only if it is derivable. The JTMS keeps one supporting justification per IN node, and these form a DAG.

The naive retraction is incorrect: when the support of a node fails, immediately look for an alternative satisfied justification and keep the node IN if one exists. That produces circular, non-well-founded beliefs. The correct method has two phases. Phase 1 labels OUT every node whose well-founded explanation contains the retracted assumption, by following supporting justifications only. Phase 2 looks for alternative support for each node marked OUT in phase 1 and propagates IN from any node that gets it. The LTMS states the same rule: before alternative support is looked for, all consequences of the retraction must be completed in the first phase.

Taxonomy (Fig 6.10), by constraint type and label type: JTMS (Horn, simple labels), ATMS (Horn, complex labels), LTMS (arbitrary clauses, simple labels), CMS (arbitrary clauses, complex labels), and the NM-JTMS (Doyle-style), which 'are surprisingly hard to use and therefore have limited utility'. The advice is to use the simplest TMS that matches the task. Complex labels pay off when many or all solutions are needed or context switches far outnumber label queries.
A TMS hurts when re-running the inference is cheap (for example Prolog), and under OPS5-style arbitrary retraction, because all inactive justifications are kept around.

assumptions-of-node returns only the assumptions under the current well-founded explanation. There can be exponentially many explanations, so retracting one reported assumption may not remove a contradiction (section 7.7).
algorithms_or_data_structures: JTMS data structures (jtms.lsp). A tms-node has: index, datum, label (:in or :out), support (the current justification or :enabled-assumption), justs (forward index), consequences (reverse index: justifications in which the node is an antecedent), mark (for sweeps), contradictory?, assumption?, and in-rules/out-rules queued on transitions. A just has: index, informant, consequence, antecedents.

justify-node: push the justification on consequence.justs and on each antecedent's consequences. If the consequence is OUT and every antecedent is IN, call install-support, which sets the node IN with this support and then runs propagate-inness: a queue over consequences that makes each newly satisfied justification's consequence IN.

retract-assumption: make-node-out(node), then propagate-outness, which walks consequences and, for each justification j whose consequence's support is j, makes that consequence OUT, enqueues it and continues from its consequences. Then find-alternative-support(out-queue): for each node still OUT, find the first satisfied justification and install-support it (with IN propagation). Nodes in the queue can be brought back IN by propagation before their turn comes.

Exercise 7.5 is counters: 'keep a count with each justification indicating the number of antecedent nodes which are in. When the count becomes zero [of unsatisfied antecedents], the consequent node is supported. Be careful to avoid circularities.' Exercise 7.7 is blocking-node watches: record per justification one node preventing it from becoming support, and per node the justifications it blocks. Exercise 7.8 is derivation depth: each justification stores the maximum distance to an assumption or premise (infinity if invalid), and each node stores the minimum depth over its supporting justifications. The reader is asked how retraction works with circularities present.

LTMS counter-based BCP (section 9.9-9.10). Each clause keeps pvs, the number of 'potential violators' (literals that are unknown or would falsify it), and sats, the number of satisfying literals. pvs=1 forces the remaining literal and pvs=0 means a contradiction. Counts keep being maintained after the clause is satisfied, because labels might be retracted later. Each node keeps clause lists split by polarity. Retraction runs propagate-unknownness (phase 1: increment counts, and clauses that rise above one release the nodes they had forced), then a phase-2 alternative-support search over clauses with count 1. BCP is linear in total clause size, but logically incomplete for non-Horn clauses; for Horn clauses it is complete for positive literals.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec section 4.2: the counter scheme (unsatisfied_premise_count per J plus active_support_count per conclusion) is BPS Exercise 7.5 and the LTMS pvs/sats design. The spec should cite this as prior art. The research contribution is therefore not the counter algorithm. It is the versioned and currency-aware layout plus the measured costs.

Use BPS's two-phase rule for spec section 4.2's batch semantics: within one transaction, first run all OUT propagation (decrements and support loss) to completion, then run all IN propagation (alternative support and additions). This rules out transient double-counting and circular re-support, and gives the deterministic order the oracle comparison needs.

H2 and baselines (spec section 7 ablations): add 'JTMS support-pointer plus two-phase retraction' as a baseline. It is well-founded on cyclic graphs but over-retracts nodes that have alternative support and then restores them (Doyle's churn), whereas counters stop at the first node that keeps support but are only correct on DAGs. That gives three variants: counters (DAG only), support-pointer two-phase (cycle-safe), and a hybrid with counters plus a rank or derivation-depth witness (Exercise 7.8), where an alternative justification counts as safe support without a phase-1 cascade if all its premises have rank strictly lower than the node's. The hybrid is a strong candidate for the V1 positive-recursion algorithm. It is related to rank or level-based incremental Datalog methods, so cite those rather than claiming it as new.

High fan-out premises (the spec's 'multi-support' workload): Exercise 7.7's blocking-node watches (one watched unsatisfied premise per justification, comparable to watched literals in SAT solvers) avoid touching every consuming justification when a premise flips. Benchmark this against plain counters on hub-heavy graphs.

Spec section 5 'CONFLICTED' explanations: BPS warns that the assumptions under the current well-founded support are neither minimal nor complete. Either compute minimal conflict sets explicitly (BPS Exercise 7.4: drop assumptions and re-check) or keep ATMS-style nogoods. Add a test where retracting the reported culprit does not clear the conflict because an alternative derivation exists.

Spec section 6 (API) and interface design: BPS puts all node and justification creation behind the TMS and the problem solver only calls a narrow interface (justify, enable or retract assumption, why, assumptions-of). Its warning that JTMS operations 'cannot be safely aborted' or interleaved argues for ContextDB's staged-transaction design: maintenance must run on a private staged copy so that an aborted transaction never leaves half-propagated labels.
papers.reported_results: This is a textbook, so there are no benchmarks. The complexity statements are: JTMS enabling only moves labels OUT->IN, so it terminates. BCP's worst case is linear in the total number of literals ('equivalent to the circuit value problem which is P-complete'). BCP is logically incomplete on general clauses. ATMS label propagation 'is easily shown to terminate', and labels for goal nodes can grow exponentially in the sizes of the choice sets.
spec_gaps_or_errors: The spec does not cite BPS, yet its V0 maintenance algorithm, the alternative-support example (T02/T03) and the cycle pitfall all appear in BPS chapter 7 and its exercises. This is a novelty and related-work risk for the paper sketch in spec section 10.

Spec section 4.2 says to 'process scheduled nodes in topological order'. For exact counter deltas on a DAG, topological order is not required if each node's final flip is applied exactly once, but correctness with mixed adds and removes in one batch does require the two-phase discipline (OUT first, then IN). The spec should state which discipline it uses.

papers.title: McAllester, D. (1990). Truth Maintenance. Proceedings of AAAI-90, pp.1109-1116
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified, read in full from https://cdn.aaai.org/AAAI/1990/AAAI90-164.pdf. Not cited in the spec.
core_ideas: A generic monotonic TMS interface: add-constraint (constraints are never removed), follows-from?(literal, premise-set) returning yes, no or unknown, justifying-literals and justifying-constraints. Justification trees must be non-circular. Almost every implementation is 'local', meaning each derived literal is justified by one constraint.

For clausal constraints, BCP is linear time and space per query but logically incomplete. Context switching can use unrestricted incremental retraction (Doyle, McAllester 1980) or a premise stack with an undo-list. The premise stack is more efficient when most premises are static or the search is systematic.

The ATMS is described as 'universal propagation' that precomputes answers for all premise sets. After propagation, the true label of P is exactly the set of minimal BCP supports, so its interface behavior equals BCP's. But 'the ATMS implementation can require both exponential time and exponential space to answer a single query ... even in the case where the Boolean constraints are Horn clauses without implication cycles.'
algorithms_or_data_structures: Premise stack with undo-list: push a premise and run incremental BCP, logging the labels it adds; pop by undoing that log. Switching from premise set Sigma to Sigma' means popping back to a common prefix and pushing the difference, with frequently changing premises kept near the top of the stack.
ATMS label filters: drop premise sets that contain a nogood, and drop subsumed premise sets.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec section 4.2 and the staged transactions: a premise-stack undo-log is a cheap way to implement 'apply in a private staged state, then publish or abort'. Each transaction logs its label and counter deltas, and an abort replays them in reverse.

This is the formal reason to keep ATMS-style labels out of the V0 hot path. The exponential blowup happens even on acyclic Horn DAGs, which is exactly the V0 graph class, so any label or branch feature must bound or focus label sizes and be benchmarked on label cardinality.
papers.reported_results: No experiments. It is a survey with complexity results: BCP is linear, and the ATMS is exponential in the worst case even for acyclic Horn constraints.
spec_gaps_or_errors: The spec's claim that the ATMS avoids environment explosion contradicts McAllester's worst-case result.

extra_related_work: Forbus & de Kleer, Building Problem Solvers (MIT Press, 1993). Free scan at https://www.qrg.northwestern.edu/BPS/ and JTMS code at https://users.cs.northwestern.edu/~forbus/c44/Code/JTRE/jtms.lsp. It covers the canonical efficient JTMS (support pointer, two-phase retraction), the counter-based LTMS (pvs/sats) and the incremental ATMS (PROPAGATE/UPDATE/WEAVE/NOGOOD). Exercise 7.5 is the spec's counter algorithm, so it must be cited, and Exercises 7.7 (blocking watches) and 7.8 (derivation depth) are ready candidates for V1. A Scala/Haskell port exists at https://github.com/jphmrst/bps-scala.

McAllester, 'Truth Maintenance', AAAI-90 (https://cdn.aaai.org/AAAI/1990/AAAI90-164.pdf). Gives a generic TMS interface, linear-time BCP, premise-stack undo-log context switching, and a proof that the ATMS is exponential even for acyclic Horn constraints. This bounds the spec's WHAT_IF and branch ambitions.

Doyle, 'A Model for Deliberation, Action, and Introspection', MIT AI TR-581 (1980), chapter 3 (https://groups.csail.mit.edu/medg/ftp/doyle/phd80.ps.gz). Doyle's own restatement of the TMS as RMS: the node and justification defstructures, a dependency-relations table (Fig. 5-7), the 3 circularity types, an early version that used SCC decomposition plus topological sort of minimal components to resolve circularities, and defeasible reified justifications, which match ContextDB's enabled_e(j).

Doyle, 'The Ins and Outs of Reason Maintenance', IJCAI-83 (https://groups.csail.mit.edu/medg/ftp/doyle/io83.ps). Formal semantics: admissible states, finitely grounded extensions, fixed-point theorem E=sigma_omega(S,E), minimality corollary, O(|D|^3) admissibility check, and conservative (minimal-change) transitions. Useful as the formal semantics for the spec's oracle and for a minimal-change criterion in future non-monotonic versions.

Elkan, 'A rational reconstruction of nonmonotonic truth maintenance systems', Artificial Intelligence 43 (1990) 219-234, DOI 10.1016/0004-3702(90)90086-F. Only the abstract was seen, via search results; I did not read the full text. It reportedly shows that NM-TMS labelings correspond to stable models of logic programs and that NM-TMS is NP-complete. This is the formal reason to keep outlists, negation and derived heads out of the ContextDB kernel.

Forbus & de Kleer, 'Focusing the ATMS', AAAI-88 (https://cdn.aaai.org/AAAI/1988/AAAI88-035.pdf). Only the abstract was seen via search. Focus environments and implied-by consumers bound ATMS label work. It is the prior art for the spec's eager-lazy hybrid (section 4.5) and for any focused WHAT_IF over branches.

de Kleer, 'Extending the ATMS' and 'Problem solving with the ATMS', Artificial Intelligence 28 (1986) 163-196 and 197-224. Not read; cited by R2. They cover defaults and disjunctions in the ATMS and the consumer protocol that solves 'unouting', i.e. no inference done twice. They matter if ContextDB lets agents subscribe to support changes and re-run validators without redundant work.

papers.title: Maintaining Views Incrementally (Extended Abstract). Gupta, Mumick, Subrahmanian. SIGMOD 1993, pp. 157-166
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: verified. Crossref resolves the spec's DOI 10.1145/170036.170066 to the ACM SIGMOD Record 22(2) copy, pp. 157-166. The proceedings copy is 10.1145/170035.170066. Both are the same paper. The ACM PDF returned 403, but I read the full 10-page extended abstract (scanned OCR) at http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~gravano/Qual/Papers/13%20-%20Maintaining%20Views%20Incrementally.pdf. This covers Sections 1-8: counting, delta rules, Lemma 4.1 / Thm 4.1, the set-semantics optimisation, negation, aggregation and DRed (Thm 7.1). The full proofs and the details of DRed with negation and aggregation are deferred to tech report TR 921214-19-TM (AT&T 1992), which I did not access. The spec's one-line summary is accurate.
core_ideas: Counting algorithm: each materialised tuple t stores count(t), its number of alternative derivations. Change sets Delta(P) hold signed counts (+ for insert, - for delete). A combine operator adds counts and drops a tuple whose count reaches 0. A join multiplies counts.

The paper proposes Counting only for NONRECURSIVE views, including stratified negation and aggregation. In Sec 8 it says that counting for recursive views 'is expensive and furthermore counting may not terminate on some views': under duplicate semantics, derivation-tree counts can be infinite.
Counting is optimal in the sense that it computes exactly the view tuples that are inserted or deleted. It stores only the number of derivations, not the derivations themselves.

Set-semantics optimisation (boxed Statement (2) of Alg 4.1): Delta(P) := set(P_new) - set(P_old). Changes reach higher strata only if the set membership of a tuple flips. Each lower-stratum tuple is treated as having count 1, so count(t) is the number of rule instances that fire for t. Their example: 20 derivations of p(a), 10 deleted, so nothing propagates to stratum 2.
Rules are processed in increasing Rule Stratum Number. The RSN comes from a topological sort of the dependency graph after each SCC has been collapsed to a single node.

DRed (Delete and Rederive) for recursive views, set semantics only, in three steps. (1) Overdelete: semi-naive evaluation of delta-minus rules gives a superset of the deleted tuples (any tuple with at least one derivation that uses a deleted tuple). (2) Rederive: for each overdeleted tuple, check whether the rule body holds in the new state, and iterate to a fixpoint. (3) Insert: semi-naive delta-plus rules. The algorithm runs stratum by stratum, so spurious changes do not cross strata. It also handles rule insertion and deletion.
Thm 7.1: DRed's result contains t iff t has a derivation from E_new = (E - Delta-) U Delta+.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Delta rules (Def 4.1): for a rule p :- s1 & ... & sn, create n rules Delta_i: Delta(p) :- s1^new & ... & s_{i-1}^new & Delta(s_i) & s_{i+1}^old & ... & sn^old. Using new versions for j<i and old versions for j>i counts every affected rule instance exactly once, even when several body atoms change in the same batch. This is the standard fix for the 'batch trap' in spec 4.2.

Lemma 4.1 precondition: the deleted base tuples Delta- must be a subset of E. Under that condition, no intermediate count drops below -count(t) and all non-Delta subgoals have positive counts. Thm 4.1: Algorithm 4.1 derives Delta(t) with count = count_new(t) - count_old(t).

Algorithm 4.1 loop: P_new := P_old; process the unprocessed rules with the least RSN; apply each delta rule; combine the result into P_new; optionally apply Delta(P) = set(P_new) - set(P_old); mark the rule processed.
Negation (Def 6.1): Delta of a negated subgoal is +1 if the tuple was deleted from Q and is no longer in Q_new, and -1 if it was newly inserted. This is out of scope for v0.
Aggregation (Alg 6.1): incrementally recompute the group tuple, emitting (old, -1) and (new, +1) only if the value changed. Not needed for v0.

DRed rules: delta-minus(p) :- s1 & ... & delta-minus(s_i) & ... & sn, using old relations. Rederive: delta-plus(p) :- delta-minus(p) & s1^new & ... & sn^new, iterated until no change. Insert: Delta+(p) :- s1^new & ... & Delta+(s_i) & ... & sn^new, semi-naive.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec 4.2 is essentially Gupta Counting with the set-semantics Statement (2), instantiated on GROUND hyperedges. J.unsatisfied_premise_count==0 means 'the rule instance fires'. active_support_count[c] is Gupta's count(c) under the rule that each premise counts 1. 'Propagate only on status flip' is Statement (2). The spec should state explicitly that support_count is the set-semantics count (number of active justifications) and NOT the duplicate-semantics derivation-tree count. Tree counts are products along paths, can grow exponentially in deep AND/OR DAGs, and become infinite under cycles. This also enforces spec 2.6 (a count is not a confidence).

Spec 4.1 oracle and M1 property tests: Thm 4.1 gives a precise invariant to test. After every commit, every node's count must equal the oracle's count of active justifications, and every J's unsatisfied count must equal the oracle's count of unsatisfied premises. Compare the counters, not only the boolean SUPPORTED states. Counter drift can be invisible in booleans for many epochs.

Spec 4.2 batch trap and T08: normalise each transaction to a net delta before propagating (R4 line 21: E- := (E- ∩ E) \ E+, E+ := E+ \ E). This removes delete-then-reinsert pairs and deletions of non-existent facts, and satisfies Gupta's Lemma 4.1 precondition. Then process changed nodes in topological (RSN) order. Each justification's contribution to its conclusion is adjusted once, by (active_new - active_old), after all its premises are final. This is the ground-level equivalent of the j<i new / j>i old delta-rule discipline.

T09 duplicate premise: under set semantics a rule instance is a set of body atoms. Canonicalise (sort and dedup) the premise list in rule_arena at insert time. Otherwise unsatisfied_premise_count gets a double decrement or increment.

Model enabled_e(j) and currency_e(j,p) (spec 2.4) as extra base 'facts' (virtual premises) of J. A head switch L: v1 -> v2 is then a single batch with delete(head(L)=v1) and insert(head(L)=v2), and Counting maintains it unchanged. Rule insertion or deletion is the insertion or deletion of a ground instance whose enabled-fact flips. Gupta's DRed explicitly supports rule changes too.

Spec 4.3 cost bound: Counting touches exactly the rule instances whose firing status changes, plus the rules_by_premise scans of flipped nodes. This equals the spec's E_visited and is optimal in the R4 / Motik-2019 sense. A benchmark metric, 'excess rule evaluations over the optimal set', can be reported against this lower bound (spec 9.3).

V1 (spec 2.7, 4.4): Gupta explicitly does not use Counting for recursion. DRed is the recursive-case baseline. In ContextDB's ground setting, DRed's rederive step is cheap: for each overdeleted node, scan rule_by_conclusion and check whether any justification has all premises outside the overdeleted set. Its cost is overdeletion, which can sweep a whole SCC.

Process strata (SCCs of the ground dependency graph) in topological order, as Gupta does with RSN. V1 therefore needs a maintained SCC condensation and topological order, not just the v0 reachability check.
spec_gaps_or_errors: Spec lists only the 10.1145/170036.170066 DOI (SIGMOD Record copy). It is valid; the conference proceedings DOI is 10.1145/170035.170066. This is a minor issue, not an error.

Spec 2.6 / 4.2 do not say which counting semantics applies. Gupta's 'count' is defined as derivation multiplicity under duplicate semantics. The spec means the set-semantics, per-rule-instance count of Statement (2). This must be written down, or implementers may count paths or derivation trees.

Spec 4.2 suggests 'staged state + affected topological recomputation' first and exact delta counters later. Gupta's delta rules already give the exact formulation; the risk the spec names is real but has a known 1993 solution. The text should cite it rather than imply open research.

Novelty risk: the v0 kernel (AND unsatisfied counter + OR support counter + flip-only propagation in topological order) is Gupta 1993 Counting (also Blakeley 1986 / Nicolas-Yazdanian 1983 for SPJ). It is also the classic counter-based propositional Horn propagation (Dowling-Gallier 1984) and a JTMS. H2 cannot claim the algorithm as new; only the native layout, versioned currency semantics, and the transaction/certificate contract can be novel.

The paper body contains no complexity theorem beyond 'optimal: computes exactly the inserted/deleted tuples' and 'count costs little or no extra'. It contains no experimental evaluation; it is an extended abstract. Any spec claim that R3 provides measured performance would be wrong; the spec makes none.

papers.title: Optimised Maintenance of Datalog Materialisations. Pan Hu, Boris Motik, Ian Horrocks. AAAI 2018 (arXiv:1711.03987v2)
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: verified. The OJS page https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/11554 metadata matches the title, authors (Oxford) and venue. I read the full text from arXiv 1711.03987v2 (15 pages including Appendix A, the correctness proof of DRed^c). The spec's description 'Counting 与 DRed/B/F 的组合优化' is accurate. Note: the paper's main motivation is eliminating 'backward' evaluation of NON-GROUND rule bodies, which matters much less in ContextDB's ground hyperedge model (see spec_gaps).
core_ideas: DRed and B/F handle general (recursive, stratified-negation) datalog, but both evaluate rules 'backwards'. They match a rule head to a fact and evaluate the partially instantiated body as a query. This (a) re-examines rule instances that fire both before and after the update, and (b) can be asymptotically harder than forward matching. Example 1: R(x,y1) ∧ R(x,y2) -> S(y1,y2), where one-step rederivation is O(n^2) against O(n) for materialisation. Example 2: built-ins (z := z1+z2) restrict join orders, again O(n^2).

Counting avoids backward evaluation by keeping per-fact derivation counts, and is optimal (considers exactly the rule instances that stop or start firing). It is only correct for nonrecursive rules (citing Nicolas & Yazdanian 1983).

DRed^c: each fact gets TWO counters, C_nr (explicit-fact membership + instances of nonrecursive rules of its stratum) and C_r (instances of recursive rules of its stratum). A rule is recursive w.r.t. stratification λ if some positive body atom has the same stratum as the head. (i) Never overdelete a fact with C_nr > 0: it certainly survives, because lower strata are already final. (ii) After overdeletion, a fact in D survives iff C_r > 0. This replaces backward rederivation with a counter check. On nonrecursive programs DRed^c is exactly Counting.

Why (ii) is sound and kills self-support: during overdeletion C_r[F] is decremented once for every recursive instance whose body contains an overdeleted fact. After the loop, C_r[F] counts only instances whose bodies lie entirely in surviving facts (not in D), which are genuinely in the new materialisation. A cyclic group with no external support is fully overdeleted, so every C_r in it reaches 0.

B/F (Motik et al. AAAI 2015): when a fact is a deletion candidate, immediately search for an alternative proof by backward chaining (CHECK) plus forward chaining (SATURATE), with a checked set C, proved set P and delayed set Y. Delete only unproved facts. Deletion is exact, so no rederivation phase is needed. B/F^c keeps only C_nr and replaces backward evaluation of NONRECURSIVE rules with 'C_nr > 0'. Recursive rules are still evaluated backwards.

Both hybrids are 'pay-as-you-go': they become Counting on nonrecursive programs. They never perform more inferences than their unoptimised versions, apart from counter maintenance. DRed^c has the same complexity as semi-naive materialisation: ExpTime combined, PTime data complexity.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Normalisation (Alg 2 line 21): D := A := ∅; E- := (E- ∩ E) \ E+; E+ := E+ \ E.

DRed^c OVERDELETE per stratum s: for each F in (E- ∩ O_s) ⊕ Π^s_nr[I ··· D\A, A\D], do ND += F and C_nr[F] -= 1. For each F in Π^s_r[I ··· D\A, A\D], do ND += F and C_r[F] -= 1. Then loop: ΔD := {F ∈ ND \ D | C_nr[F] = 0}; break if empty; for each F in Π^s_r[I\(D\A), I∪A ··· ΔD], do ND += F and C_r[F] -= 1; D := D ∪ ΔD. ⊕ is multiset union, so each rule instance decrements exactly once (semi-naive).
DRed^c one-step rederivation: R := {F ∈ D ∩ O_s | C_r[F] > 0}. No rule evaluation is involved.

DRed^c INSERT: NA := R. For F in (E+ ∩ O_s) ⊕ Π^s_nr[(I\D)∪A ··· A\D, D\A], do C_nr[F] += 1. For F in Π^s_r[(I\D)∪A ··· A\D, D\A], do C_r[F] += 1. Then a semi-naive loop over the recursive rules with ΔA, incrementing C_r for each newly firing instance. Finally E := (E\E-) ∪ E+ and I := (I\D) ∪ A.

Counter compatibility invariant (the precondition of Thm 1): C_nr[F] = multiplicity of F in E ⊕ Π^s_nr⟦I⟧, C_r[F] = multiplicity in Π^s_r⟦I⟧, and both are 0 for F ∉ I. Thm 1: DRed^c yields mat(Π, E') and leaves the counters compatible with E'.

B/F^c DELETEUNPROVED: decrement C_nr as in DRed^c; ND ∪= Π^s_r[I ··· D\A, A\D]; loop over F ∈ ND\D: CHECK(F); if F ∉ P then ΔD ∪= {F}. CHECK(F): if F ∉ C and SATURATE(F) fails, then for each recursive instance r' with head F whose body holds in I \ ((D ∪ ΔD) \ A), CHECK each body atom G of the same stratum; return once F ∈ P. SATURATE(F): C ∪= {F}; if F ∈ Y or C_nr[F] > 0, forward-propagate P over the recursive rules, adding consequences that are in C to P and the others to Y (delayed proofs).

Worked Example 3 (ground form usable as a golden test): base A(a), A(b), A(d); edges a->c, b->c, c->d, d->e under A(x) ∧ B(x,y) -> A(y). Counters (nr, r) before: a(1,0) b(1,0) c(0,2) d(1,1) e(0,1). Delete A(a): DRed overdeletes a, c, d, e. DRed^c overdeletes only a and c, stopping at d because C_nr[d] = 1, and rederives c because C_r[c] = 1 (from b). Final: c(0,1) d(1,1) e(0,1).

Evaluation (Dell R720, 2x Xeon E5-2670, 256 GB). Small deletions of 1000 facts, avg seconds, DRed^c / DRed / B/F^c / B/F: UOBM-U 179.24 / 1185.87 / 1.18 / 31.96; Reactome-U 0.06 / 1.03 / 0.05 / 1.00; SSPE 10.53 / 1684.97 / 247.00 / 252.97; Claros-LE average 1143.55 / 1741.66 / 560.61 / 653.04, worst about 5700 / 5760 / 2803 / 3227. Counter overhead during rematerialisation: Remat-2C is at most a few percent slower than Remat. Large deletions: the hybrids are close to rematerialisation; Claros-LE (symmetric-transitive cliques) and SSPE (a small deletion removes about half of the inferred facts) remain hard.
implications_for_contextdb: V1 data structures (spec 3.2 RuntimeState, 4.4): split active_support_count into cnr (base_e(r) as +1, plus active justifications whose premises all lie in strictly earlier SCCs) and cr (active justifications with at least one premise in the conclusion's own SCC). Add a per-justification bit 'recursive' = some premise is in the same SCC as the conclusion. For DAG regions every SCC is a singleton, cr is always 0, and the algorithm is exactly the v0 counter algorithm. This is the pay-as-you-go property, so V1 does not regress v0.

Spec 2.7 self-support: R4's DRed^c overdeletion is the precise mechanism that prevents 'A->B, B->A mutually proving each other'. Golden test: base X; X->A; A->B; B->A; revoke X. Expected: A and B both UNSUPPORTED, with cr counters going 0 in the oracle. Variant: B also has base support. Expected: A survives via cr[A] = 1 after overdeletion, and B is never overdeleted because cnr[B] = 1.

Choice between DRed^c and B/F^c for V1, which spec 10 leaves open. In ContextDB rules are ground, so B/F's backward step is just a walk of rule_by_conclusion plus premise arrays. R4's headline motivation (O(n^2) non-ground backward matching) mostly vanishes. The remaining trade-off is overdeletion blast radius (DRed^c) against depth of the recursive proof search (B/F^c). Implement both behind one trait and benchmark on spec 9.1 'cycle-heavy', 'hub', and a clique workload modelled on Claros-LE (dense mutual support). Do not cite R4's speedups as expected ContextDB gains.

B/F synergy with WHY (spec 6): B/F's CHECK/SATURATE produces a well-founded alternative proof as a by-product. Recording the justification that proved F gives a WHY witness and a 'still supported because ...' explanation for agents at no extra cost. This is a concrete design hook.

Spec 4.2 / M1 transaction pipeline: adopt R4's exact batch normalisation (E- := (E- ∩ E) \ E+; E+ := E+ \ E) at stage time, then run delete phase before insert phase per stratum (SCC) in topological order. This also answers the 'node invalid then restored in same txn' trap: such a node lands in D and then in A, and only the final state (I\D) ∪ A is published.

Oracle for V1 (spec 4.1 must change): with cycles, 'topological recompute' is undefined. The oracle must be the least fixpoint: naive or semi-naive forward chaining from base facts only (never from previous state). The oracle should also emit expected (cnr, cr) per node, so the counter-compatibility invariant of R4 Thm 1 can be property-tested at every epoch (spec 8 'Property-based model checking').

Metric (spec 9.3 'rule evaluations per update'): report counts of rule instances considered in overdeletion, rederivation (or backward checks) and insertion, separately. Compare them with the optimal set instr[I] Δ instr[I'] (the optimality notion used by R4 and formalised in Motik et al. AIJ 2019 Def 26). Add Remat, Remat-1C and Remat-2C baselines to measure counter overhead, as R4 does (spec 9.2 baseline 1).

Dynamic SCCs are a new problem that R4 does not face. R4 assumes a fixed program stratification λ. In ContextDB, adding a justification can merge SCCs, which flips other justifications from nonrecursive to recursive and moves counts from cnr to cr. Removing one can split SCCs. V1 needs incremental SCC / topological-order maintenance plus counter reclassification inside the same staged transaction. This is a genuine research and engineering gap and a possible novelty point. A simpler, sound fallback: allow all justifications to be treated as recursive within coarse, conservative 'cycle regions'. Correctness holds for any valid stratification, at the cost of more overdeletion. A finer stratification only improves efficiency.

Applying R4 at ground (per-node SCC) granularity rather than predicate-level strata is my extrapolation, not in the paper. The appendix proof is per-stratum and relies only on lower strata being final, so a ground-level condensation should satisfy it. This should be checked by the oracle-based property tests before it is claimed.
spec_gaps_or_errors: Spec 4.4 says 'DRed、B/F、Counting 的混合策略' but does not say that the hybrid needs TWO counters per node (nonrecursive vs recursive) and a recursive/nonrecursive classification per justification. The current single active_support_count in spec 3.2 cannot express V1 correctly. If the plain count is used with cycles, it reproduces the self-support bug of spec 2.7.

Spec 2.7 V1 says 'least fixed point + SCC / DRed 或 B/F'. R4 uses a STATIC stratification. The spec does not address dynamic SCC changes caused by justification insert/delete, or the cost of keeping SCCs and topological order current per commit. M0's cycle check (reachability c ->* p per insert) is also O(V+E) worst case per write. A dynamic topological order structure would amortise it. Neither is mentioned.

Novelty risk for spec 11 contribution 2 ('incremental maintenance algorithm with correct alternative-support handling and explicit cycle semantics'): R4 plus Motik et al. AIJ 2019 already give correct counting/DRed/B/F/FBF hybrids for recursive datalog, with proofs and evaluations. ContextDB cannot claim the recursive maintenance algorithm itself. A defensible contribution is the versioned-currency and certificate semantics over it, the dynamic-SCC ground setting, and the native layout.

Spec 1 says R4 provides 'algorithm baseline for SCC/cyclic dependencies'. That is correct, but R4's evaluation is on OWL/RDF benchmarks (UOBM, Reactome, Uniprot, ChemBL, Claros, SSPE) with millions of facts and non-ground rules. Its performance numbers are not transferable to ContextDB's ground agent-decision graphs. Only the mechanisms and the optimality metric are.

R4 handles stratified negation. The spec defers negation and contradiction to a separate phase (spec 4.4). That is consistent, but if contradiction ('A' vs 'not A') is later expressed as negated premises, the per-stratum delete-then-insert discipline and the C_nr/C_r split from R4 carry over directly. The spec should note this rather than design contradiction ad hoc.

extra_related_work: Motik, Nenov, Piro, Horrocks. 'Maintenance of Datalog Materialisations Revisited', Artificial Intelligence (2019; I did not verify the volume number, and one listing claimed vol 455, which looks wrong). Author preprint, accessed and partially read: https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/boris.motik/pubs/mnph19maintenance-revisited.pdf. It is the most important companion to R3/R4. (a) Example 5 shows the Nicolas-Yazdanian/Gupta counting applied to the recursive rule R(x,y)->R(y,x): after deleting R(a,b), counts leave R(a,b) and R(b,a) supporting each other. This is exactly the spec 2.7 self-support bug and makes a ready-made regression test. (b) It gives a correct RECURSIVE counting algorithm that keeps a multiset 'trace' of facts per semi-naive round (N_i^s) and undoes or redoes rule instances round by round. This is an alternative to the C_nr/C_r split, with higher memory. (c) Optimised DRed that does not repeat derivations, and FBF (Forward/Backward/Forward). (d) Formal optimality definition (Def 26: consider only instr[I] Δ instr[I']). Results: Counting is optimal on nonrecursive programs (Prop 27); no algorithm is optimal for deletions on recursive programs (Prop 29); DRed/FBF are optimal for instance-increasing updates (Prop 32). It is needed for the V1 design and for the benchmark metric definition.

Motik, Nenov, Piro, Horrocks. 'Incremental Update of Datalog Materialisation: the Backward/Forward Algorithm', AAAI 2015, pp. 1560-1568. This is the original B/F, cited by R4. I did NOT access it directly; the B/F description above comes from R4's Algorithm 3 (B/F^c).

Hu, Motik, Horrocks. 'Modular Materialisation of Datalog Programs', arXiv:1811.02304 (AAAI 2019; extended version reportedly in AIJ). Only arXiv metadata was verified. It answers R4's own open problem (cliques in Claros-LE) with plug-in modules for transitivity/symmetry. It is relevant if ContextDB's 'hub' or dense mutual-support workloads behave like cliques.
Nicolas & Yazdanian 1983, BDGEN (cited by R3 and R4). This is the historical evidence that naive counting on recursive rules is incorrect. Not accessed.
Staudt & Jarke 1996 (VLDB), DRed variant for externally materialised views; Ceri & Widom 1991/1992, production-rule IVM developed concurrently with DRed (cited by R3/R4). Not accessed.

Dowling & Gallier 1984, linear-time propositional Horn satisfiability (cited from memory, not accessed). It uses a per-clause unsatisfied-literal counter with a queue, which is exactly spec 4.2's unsatisfied_premise_count. It gives the theoretical O(total premise incidences) bound for a full recompute of the ground AND/OR graph, and is a prior-art risk for claiming the counter layout as novel.

Dynamic topological order and incremental SCC maintenance (cited from memory, not accessed): Pearce & Kelly 2006 (JEA); Haeupler et al. 2012 (TALG); Bender, Fineman, Gilbert, Tarjan 2016 (TALG). V0 needs these for cheap per-write CYCLE_DETECTED checks and a maintained processing order (spec 2.7, 4.2). V1 needs them to classify justifications as recursive or nonrecursive as SCCs merge and split, which R4 does not cover.

Doyle 1979 JTMS (spec R1): its relabelling of a node's consequences followed by searching for well-founded support is operationally a DRed/B/F scheme on ground justifications. Position ContextDB V1 against both the TMS and the datalog-maintenance lines, not only datalog.

papers.title: Differential dataflow (McSherry, Murray, Isaacs, Isard), CIDR 2013
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified. Read the full PDF from the MSR URL in the spec (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/differentialdataflow.pdf): CIDR 2013, Asilomar, 4 authors from MSR Silicon Valley. One correction: the spec's Focus list asks about 'arrangements (shared indexed state)', but R5 never uses that term. R5 only describes per-operator indexed difference traces (key -> version -> record -> count). Arrangements, meaning traces shared across operators and dataflows, come from McSherry, Lattuada, Schwarzkopf and Roscoe, 'Shared Arrangements', PVLDB 13(10) 2020, which I also read (see extra_related_work).
core_ideas: Differential computation: collection state is indexed by a PARTIALLY ordered set of versions, not by a sequence. Each difference is kept rather than folded into a 'current' state. A_t = sum over s<=t of dA_s, and dA_t = A_t - sum over s<t of dA_s.

Product order (epoch i, iteration j): (i1,j1)<=(i2,j2) iff i1<=i2 and j1<=j2. Version (i,j) can reuse work from both (i-1,j) and (i,j-1), so an input change and an iteration step are independent sources of change. The paper calls dA_11 'often completely empty'.
Lexicographic order (priority, iteration) gives prioritized fixpoints. Orders compose (product of total and lexicographic), and a nested loop adds one coordinate. SCC uses a 4-dimensional order.

Output differences can appear at versions t > tau even when the inputs have no difference at t. The candidate set is the least upper bounds of tau with existing non-zero versions, which is why a lattice is required, not just a partial order.

Loops are built from Ingress (adds an iteration coordinate; differential output +dX at i=0 and -dX at i=1), Feedback (advances the iteration coordinate) and Egress (sums over i). Convergence means no outstanding differences remain; there is no explicit convergence test.

Data-parallel keyed operators do work only for keys that appear in incoming differences. Linear operators (Select, Where, Concat, Except) need no state. Join uses z = A*b + a*B + a*b. Count and Sum keep per-key accumulated weights. Min and Max must keep the full trace.
Scheduling uses a causal partial order over (operator, version) pairs, and the scheduler repeatedly runs a minimal outstanding difference.

Compaction: once no updates can arrive for times below t0, differences up to t0 are consolidated into the equivalent of a checkpoint. The details are deferred, and the mathematics appears only later in the Shared Arrangements tech report.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Algorithm 1 (generic differential operator): for each version t in the lattice, rebuild A_t and B_t from the stored dA_s and dB_s for s<t, then dz_t = f(A_t+da, B_t+db) - f(A_t,B_t) - sum over s<t of dz_s. Only t that are lubs of tau and existing non-zero versions need visiting. Optimization: start from a previously rebuilt A_t' and apply only the {dA_s : (s<=t') != (s<=t)}.
Trace storage (Naiad): a triply nested sparse array of counts indexed by key, then lattice version, then record. Only non-zero counts are kept.
Fixed point: [Ingress(X)](t,i) = X_t if i=0, else 0. [Feedback(W)](t,i) = W(t,i-1). [Egress(W)]_t = W(t,i*) where i* is the first i with W(t,i)=W(t,i-1).
Prioritized fixpoint: PIngress adds (p,i) coordinates, and PFeedback feeds the converged result of priority p-1 into (p,0).
Join delta: z = A |><| db + dA |><| B + dA |><| db, using indexed traces of both inputs.

The DD Rust crate (verified on crates.io: differential-dataflow 0.25.1, 2026-07-15, MSRV 1.86; timely 0.31.0) implements these ideas with arrangements (arrange_by_key / arrange_by_self -> TraceAgent), iterate/Variable, join, semijoin, antijoin, count, reduce, distinct and threshold. I confirmed the API by building and running a prototype on the local Rust 1.95.0 / M1 Pro.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec 2.4 S_e semantics is exactly the least fixed point of a positive Datalog program, so DD can maintain it incrementally and correctly, including deletions, multiple supports (OR) and cycles (lfp, no self-support). This holds because DD indexes every difference by (epoch, iteration), so a retraction is replayed per iteration rather than reference-counted. Spec 9.2 #6 is therefore a real and strong baseline, not a strawman.

Prototype (scratch only, not in the repo): /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-jiucheng-Dev-ContextDB/1a270d89-8f2c-4a88-9d35-782a613801cb/scratchpad/ddproto/src/main.rs. It has two encodings: (A) pure positive Datalog with a premise-prefix chain, and (B) counting inside iterate. Both include currency for REQUIRES_CURRENT, enabled rules and a full-recompute oracle. Across 200 seeds x 12 epochs (2400 committed epochs) with random batched base, rule and head flips, both encodings had 0 mismatches against the oracle. A mutation test that breaks the oracle's currency check produced 1977/2400 mismatches, so the checker does catch errors.

Atomic batches (spec T08): every update at one DD timestamp is consolidated before output, so a node that flips and flips back inside a batch cancels out and observers never see the transient. Spec 4.2's 'staged state' trap comes for free in DD.

Spec 5.2 HISTORICAL(epoch)/SNAPSHOT and spec 6 DIFF: a DD arrangement is a multiversion index. Reading 'as of e' needs the trace handle's logical-compaction frontier held at or before e. The memory cost of keeping history has to be reported, because the native design stores immutable revisions in any case.

Spec 5.3 WHAT_IF: DD can model a speculative branch as an extra partially ordered time coordinate (for example Product<epoch, branch>), so main updates flow into the branch and branch updates never reach main. That is the 'differential' reuse R5 describes. The simpler alternative is branch-as-key relations, which duplicate derived state per branch. Either way it must be documented as part of the baseline, not left out.

Measured cost structure (single run, 1 timely worker, Rust 1.95, M1 Pro, release build, untuned). Flipping base at the root of a chain costs one iteration per level: encoding B took about 34 ms at depth 1K, about 340 ms at 10K and about 3.6 s at 100K. Encoding A took about 69 ms, 0.72 s and 7.6 s. A native event-driven counter (spec 4.2) in the same scratch binary took about 0.55 ms at depth 100K. A tree with fanout 8 and 1M nodes took about 0.57-0.98 s in DD versus about 3.7 ms native. A leaf-local flip stayed about 0.1-0.5 ms in DD at every depth, because DD jumps to sparse (epoch, iteration) times. Conclusion: DD's per-update cost grows with the number of fixpoint rounds the change crosses, roughly 35-70 us per round here. H1/H2 should be argued on depth-sensitive shapes (chain, hub) and must report shape statistics (spec 9.1) to be fair.

The native mini-counter does none of the snapshot, WAL or transaction work, so these ratios are upper bounds on any advantage, not results. Spec 9.4 discipline applies: same event log, per-epoch output check against the oracle, at least 3 seeds, environment reported, and DD tuned (worker count, batch size, arrangement reuse) before any comparison.

WHY and IMPACT (spec 6) are not maintained by default. A faithful baseline should materialize active(j,c) and support_count(c) as arranged views, and answer IMPACT and WHY either as maintained recursive views or as interactive 'query-as-input' dataflows over shared arrangements (the top-down Datalog pattern from the Shared Arrangements paper).

CYCLE_DETECTED (spec 2.7 V0) is a front-end write-validation concern. All baselines should share one validator and receive only DAG-preserving batches, so DD is not charged for cycle checking it would never be asked to do.
spec_gaps_or_errors: Arrangements, frontiers and compaction are attributed to R5 in the task's focus list, but they come from Shared Arrangements (PVLDB 2020) and, for compaction mathematics, its tech report. Add that paper to the reading list.

Novelty risk for H2 and spec 2.6: correct OR-alternative support with no false invalidation is not unique to a TMS. Any correct recursive Datalog IVM (DD, DBSP) gives the same outputs. The contribution has to be cost: depth-independent locality, compact native layout, and no per-iteration overhead or history. It also has to come from features DD/DBSP lack (certified reads, CAS transactions, per-dependency version certificates), not from correctness of multi-support.

Spec 4.4 / 2.7 V1 plans 'SCC + DRed/B/F' for cycles, but DD already maintains positive recursion with lfp semantics and no DRed over-deletion. That makes DD the natural V1 baseline for the cycle-heavy shape and shows R4-style algorithms are not the only option.

Spec 1 table: 'versioned, iterative incremental maintenance' is accurate. R5's own evaluation, though, is on graph analytics with a 2013 C#/.NET prototype (Naiad), not the Rust crate. Its numbers do not transfer.
papers.reported_results: Twitter mention graph, 24 h window, connected components. Sliding the window by 1 s processes about 67 differences, 0.003% of a full prioritized re-evaluation. Stored differences are only 1.5% more than the label set. Wall clock: Naiad handles a 1 s update in 24.4 ms, versus 7.1 s for a full differential run and 36.4 s for incremental (8 cores of a 48-core AMD Opteron, 64 GB, Windows Server 2008 R2). Table 1, ClueWeb Category B, 16 servers x 8 cores, running times in seconds: PageRank Naiad 1,404 vs PDW 8,970 / DryadLINQ 4,513 / SHS 90,942. SCC 234 vs 475 / 446 / 1,073. WCC 130 vs 4,207 / 3,844 / 1,976. ASP 3,822 vs 30,379 / 17,089 / 246,944. The Table 1 workloads are batch runs and do not exercise incremental updates.

papers.title: DBSP: Automatic Incremental View Maintenance for Rich Query Languages (Budiu et al.), VLDB Journal 34(4), article 39, 2025. Earlier version PVLDB 16(7):1601-1614, 2023 (VLDB 2023 Best Paper)
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: The citation exists and the DOI matches, but I could not read the journal text. Crossref for 10.1007/s00778-025-00922-y lists 'DBSP: automatic incremental view maintenance for rich query languages', The VLDB Journal vol 34, issue 4, article 39, published 2025-05-08, with 11 authors: Mihai Budiu, Leonid Ryzhyk, Gerd Zellweger, Ben Pfaff, Lalith Suresh, Simon Kassing, Abhinav Gyawali, Matei Budiu, Tej Chajed, Frank McSherry, Val Tannen. Springer (and the rdcu.be SharedIt link from Feldera's site) returned a JavaScript client challenge. Semantic Scholar's open-access pointer goes to arXiv 2203.16684 v1, a different 2022 preprint, not the journal text. Feldera's publications page calls the journal paper 'a longer version' of the VLDB 2023 paper. What I actually read in full: (a) the PVLDB 16(7) 2023 paper (https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol16/p1601-budiu.pdf; authors Budiu, Chajed, McSherry, Ryzhyk, Tannen); (b) the 87-page 'DBSP mathematical specification' tech report dated Dec 21, 2022 (https://mihaibudiu.github.io/work/dbsp-spec.pdf), including its Datalog compilation, negation/antijoin and implementation chapters; (c) arXiv 2203.16684 v1. Any journal-only content, such as a system evaluation, is UNVERIFIED by me.
core_ideas: IVM is defined on streams, not on query derivatives. A stream is N -> A with A an abelian group. Primitives: lifting ↑f (pointwise), delay z^-1, D(s) = s - z^-1(s), and I(s) = fix a.(s + z^-1 a). Then Q^Δ = D ∘ ↑Q ∘ I.

Algebraic laws (Prop 3.2): inversion; invariance (+, -, z^-1, I, D are their own incremental versions); push/pull Q∘I = I∘Q^Δ; chain rule (Q1∘Q2)^Δ = Q1^Δ ∘ Q2^Δ; addition; cycle rule (the incremental version of a feedback loop is the loop around the incremental body). Linear time-invariant ops satisfy Q^Δ = Q. Bilinear ops (join): (a×b)^Δ = I(a)×b + a×z^-1(I(b)).

Z-sets: finite-support functions A -> Z with negative weights for deletions, forming an abelian group. Sets and bags are special cases. distinct(m)[x] = 1 if m[x] > 0. Relational algebra maps to Z-set operators (Table 1): union = distinct(a+b), difference = distinct(a-b), and so on. distinct elimination rules (Prop 4.4/4.5) apply for positive inputs.
Incremental distinct is O(|Δ|) via H(i,d)[x] = -1 if i[x] > 0 and (i+d)[x] <= 0; +1 if i[x] <= 0 and (i+d)[x] > 0; else 0. It keeps the integrated input, so space is O(|DB|).

Recursion (Alg 5.3): bracket with δ0 (scalar -> stream) and ∫ (sum of a stream that is zero almost everywhere). The cycle rule then yields semi-naive evaluation, and Theorem 5.4 says the output equals the stratified Datalog least model when the input is a set.

Incremental recursion uses nested streams (2D time t0 = outer transaction, t1 = inner iteration). ↑z^-1 is strict in the inner dimension. Lifting a cycle lifts its operators (Prop 6.2), giving the circuit (↑(↑R)^Δ)^Δ.

Cost (Section 6.1): an incremental recursive circuit never runs more iterations than the non-incremental one. Each operator does asymptotically less work. Space is proportional to the total size of changes summed over all inner iterations and all outer steps, so state grows with the number of iterations.

Richer languages: indexed Z-sets Z[A][K] for GROUP BY (grouping is linear); COUNT and SUM aggregates are linear; MIN/MAX are brute force or custom (Reactive Aggregator, O(log n)); flatmap; window queries; relational while (non-monotone, not guaranteed to terminate); stratified negation; antijoin as join plus set difference.

DBSP vs DD, as the authors put it: DD's model is more powerful (time is an arbitrary lattice), while DBSP uses linear time plus nested time via lifting. DBSP's advantage is a syntax-directed incrementalization algorithm and modular addition of new operators.

Implementation notes (tech report Section 15.4): 'DBSP is not a database'. It keeps only the state needed for deltas and cannot answer whether a value exists at a given time without extra integration. Inputs must stay sets. Three options: trust the environment, normalize with distinct after I, or put a 'change manager' that validates commands and emits atomic input changes in front of the circuit.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Algorithm 4.6: (1) translate to a circuit using Table 1; (2) apply distinct elimination to convergence; (3) lift; (4) wrap in I/D; (5) push incrementalization inward with the chain rule, replacing linear ops by themselves, joins by the bilinear formula and distinct by H. Running time is linear in the number of operators.

Incremental join: two integrators (I with z^-1) holding the full input relations, plus two joins per bilinear op. In a recursive (2D) circuit a join expands to 4 joins with costs O(|ΔDB|^2), O(|DB||ΔDB|) twice, and O(|DB|) once (tech report Section 10).
State lives only in z^-1 operators. Checkpoint/restore means saving the z^-1 contents (tech report 15.4.1).

Datalog compilation (tech report Section 14): rule body = join chain; repeated heads = plus + distinct; a negated term over all variables = set difference; a negated term over a subset of variables = antijoin rewritten as C(v,z) :- I1(v,z), I2(v); O(v) :- I1(v,z), not C(v,z).

Rust library dbsp (Feldera). Verified on crates.io: dbsp 0.367.0 (2026-10-18) needs rustc 1.96.1, and so do all versions from 0.350 through 0.367. 0.349.0 (2026-09-12) is the newest version buildable on the local Rust 1.95.0 (MSRV 1.93.1); it builds in about 2.5 min on the M1 Pro with CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_RUST_VERSIONS=fallback.
