API: Runtime::init_circuit, add_input_zset -> ZSetHandle push(k,w), recursive(|child, streams| ...) with automatic distinct on recursive streams and support for tuples of mutually recursive streams, delta0, map_index/join/flat_map/plus, output().consolidate(), transaction().
implications_for_contextdb: A faithful Datalog encoding of spec 2.4 that I tested in both DD and DBSP. EDB: base(r); rule(j,c,n) with premises canonicalized and deduplicated per T09; premise(j,i,p,kind) for i in [0,n); enabled(j); head(l,r) (per branch: head(b,l,r)); logical(r,l). Stratum 0 (non-recursive): usable(j,i,p) :- premise(j,i,p,k), k != REQUIRES_CURRENT. usable(j,i,p) :- premise(j,i,p,REQUIRES_CURRENT), logical(p,l), head(l,p). rule_en(j,c,n) :- rule(j,c,n), enabled(j). HISTORICAL_REFERENCE edges are never premises. SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY edges go to the validation stratum, not to structural support. Stratum 1 (recursive, positive, monotone, so least fixed point): ok(j,0) :- rule_en(j,_,_). ok(j,i+1) :- ok(j,i), usable(j,i,p), S(p). S(c) :- base(c). S(c) :- ok(j,n), rule_en(j,c,n). Stratum 2 (non-recursive): active(j,c) :- ok(j,n), rule_en(j,c,n). support_count(c) = count of active(j,c). current(r) :- logical(r,l), head(l,r). pending(r) for a semantic dependency whose read revision differs from the current head with no ValidationRecord for that version vector. certified(r) :- current(r), S(r), not pending(r), authorized(principal,r). That is stratified negation, which DBSP and DD both support. A REVISE is a single atomic batch: head(l,old) with weight -1 and head(l,new) with weight +1 at the same time.

Alternative AND encoding B: active(j) iff count{i : usable(j,i,p), S(p)} = n(j), with aggregation inside the recursion. It is monotone in S, so it is also correct under DD's per-iteration semantics, and in my DD runs it was about 2x faster than the prefix chain. Encoding A is the textbook pure positive Datalog version and runs on any engine (DDlog, Soufflé, ascent, crepe), so it is the 'faithful, not weakened' reference. Report both.

DBSP correctness problem found and root-caused. With dbsp 0.349.0 the encoding-A circuit disagreed with the oracle on 117-118 of 2400 epochs. Minimal repro: rules {0}->1, {1,0}->4, {1}->5, {5,4}->6, base {0,5}; retracting base 5 wrongly drops 6, although 6 is still derivable at the same inner iteration through a different supporting path. A plain linear reachability recursion was correct. The cause is upstream Feldera PR #7284, '[dbsp] Bug in recursive join operators' (merged 2026-09-29, after 0.349.0). Before the fix, the join's future_outputs spine was inserted only if the map entry was Vacant, so a second batch of updates for the same future time was dropped. 0.349.0 still contains that code (src/operator/dynamic/join.rs line 1775). After I backported the fix into a scratch [patch] copy, both minimal repros were correct and the randomized check had 0 mismatches in 2400 epochs. Practical consequence: a DBSP baseline needs either a toolchain bump to Rust >= 1.96.1 with a dbsp release that contains #7284 (I did not verify which version first ships it), or the backport. The randomized oracle harness should be mandatory for every external baseline, not only for ContextDB. Repro files: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-jiucheng-Dev-ContextDB/1a270d89-8f2c-4a88-9d35-782a613801cb/scratchpad/dbspproto/src/bin/mini2.rs and .../dbspproto/src/main.rs; the patched crate is in .../scratchpad/dbsp-patched.

Cost structure differs from DD in a way that matters for the benchmark. DBSP's inner time is dense: each outer step steps the nested circuit until changes stop. Measured with patched dbsp 0.349, 1 worker: chain depth 1K root flip about 250 ms and leaf flip about 190 ms; depth 10K root about 2.5-2.9 s and leaf about 1.9-2.0 s; tree8 with 1M nodes root about 1.7-2.0 s and leaf about 2-4 ms. DD's leaf flip was about 0.2 ms at every depth. So DBSP latency grows with the DAG's maximum derivation depth even for local updates, while DD's grows with the depth the change actually crosses. Both are a factor of 100 or more above an event-driven counter on deep shapes. This supports H1/H2 on deep or hub shapes and predicts weak gains on shallow, wide 'modular' shapes. Those shapes must be in the report to avoid cherry-picking (spec 9.1, 9.4).

DBSP has no time travel (tech report 15.4.2). HISTORICAL(epoch) and DIFF in a DBSP baseline would need an external snapshot store or integrated views keyed by epoch, which must be counted in memory and latency. DD can serve as-of reads from arrangements if compaction is held back.

The DBSP 'change manager' that validates commands and emits atomic input changes is architecturally the same as ContextDB's transaction layer (spec 5.1). The fair baseline comparison therefore covers only the derived-state maintenance engine: same front-end (CAS, read-set validation, cycle rejection), swap only the maintenance kernel. This keeps guarantee levels aligned, as spec 9.2 requires.

State and memory: DBSP stores integrals for each join input and each distinct, plus iteration-indexed changes for recursion. Space grows with the number of iterations. Spec 9.3's bytes per revision, rule and premise incidence should be reported for the DD and DBSP baselines; I expect them to be several times the native layout, but that is a hypothesis to measure.
spec_gaps_or_errors: Citation: the spec says 'Budiu et al. (2025) ... VLDB Journal' with the correct DOI. It should also cite the PVLDB 16(7) 2023 version, which is open access and holds the theory and Lean proofs. The journal version has 11 authors and could not be accessed here.

The PVLDB 2023 paper has no performance evaluation ('Benchmark results ... will be discussed in future work'). Spec claims that DBSP is 'efficient' should cite asymptotic results only, unless the journal version (unverified) adds measurements.

Spec 9.2 #6 says 'according to available libraries'. Concretely: DD 0.25.1 builds on Rust 1.95. dbsp versions newer than 0.349 need Rust >= 1.96.1, and 0.349 has the nonlinear-recursion join bug (#7284). DDlog (vmware-archive/differential-datalog) has been archived since 2023, so it is not a maintained baseline. ascent, crepe and datafrog are non-incremental Datalog engines, usable only as 'full recompute in Datalog' references.

Novelty overlap: DBSP plus Feldera SQL support recursive views. Feldera issues mention 'DECLARE RECURSIVE VIEW'-style recursive SQL, for example #7495, #5452 and #3318. So 'incremental maintenance of justification closures' is commodity functionality. ContextDB's defensible deltas are the per-version currency and certificate semantics, transactional CAS heads, branch overlays, provenance queries (WHY/WHY_NOT), and depth-independent update cost. These need to be demonstrated, not assumed.

Spec 4.4 mentions 'multi-version' via DD/DBSP. Note that DBSP is single-timeline (linear time plus nesting) and gives no branch or what-if support. Only DD's lattice timestamps can express branches natively.
papers.reported_results: Theory paper. Results: DBSP has 4 core operators. The paper reports full SQL compilation (the SQL-to-DBSP compiler, based on Apache Calcite, passes all 7 million SQL Logic Tests). All definitions and theorems are machine-checked in Lean, about 5K lines on mathlib. The asymptotic results: linear ops O(|Δ|) time and 0 space; distinct^Δ O(|Δ|) time and O(|DB|) space; bilinear join O(|DB|·|Δ|); incremental recursion never runs more iterations than non-incremental, with space proportional to the number of iterations. The open-source Rust library (multicore sharding, spill to storage) is mentioned; the paper says its benchmarks 'are very promising' but reports no numbers. Journal-version results: not accessed.

extra_related_work: McSherry, Lattuada, Schwarzkopf, Roscoe. 'Shared Arrangements: practical inter-query sharing for streaming dataflows', PVLDB 13(10), 2020. https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p1793-mcsherry.pdf (accessed, read the mechanism sections). This is the actual source for 'arrangements': an append-only list of immutable batches, each bounded by lower and upper frontiers, sorted by (data, time) in columnar form. Batches are merged in the background (LSM-like, logarithmically many batches) with amortized work per batch. Updates are consolidated once every trace handle's frontier has passed them. Each reader holds a trace handle (a cursor plus frontier) and can import the arrangement into new dataflows. It also covers top-down interactive Datalog queries against maintained arrangements. Reported: 1.3-3x lower update latency and 2-4x less memory than non-shared indexing. It is the right model for maintaining ContextDB's rules_by_premise and rule_by_conclusion indexes once and serving WHY and IMPACT from them.

Budiu, Chajed, McSherry, Ryzhyk, Tannen. 'DBSP: Automatic Incremental View Maintenance for Rich Query Languages', PVLDB 16(7):1601-1614, 2023, VLDB 2023 Best Paper. https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol16/p1601-budiu.pdf (accessed, full text). This is the open-access version of R6.

papers.title: Is Agent Memory a Database? Rethinking Data Foundations for Long-Term AI Agent Memory
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: verified. arXiv:2605.26252, v1 only, submitted 25 May 2026, cs.AI. The authors are Abdelghny Orogat and Essam Mansour (Concordia University), and the full title matches spec §12. I read the whole 8-page PDF (vision paper with references). Spec §1's one-line summary ('GEM 讨论记忆状态演化，MemState 使用 property-graph backend') is accurate, and the backend is specifically Kuzu (embedded property graph). Code: github.com/CoDS-GCS/MemState exists (Python, Kuzu, last pushed 2026-09-25). Caveat: this is a vision paper with no quantitative evaluation at all. MemState is described only as a 'feasibility sketch'.
core_ideas: Agent memory is a new data-management workload. Correctness belongs to the state trajectory {M_t}, not to individual records, and the paper's answer to its title question is explicitly 'No'.

Four failure modes come from CRUD: unregulated growth, missing semantic revision, capacity-driven forgetting, and read-only retrieval. Four capabilities address them: relevance-driven retention, dependency-aware propagation, graded attenuation, and state-modifying retrieval. Table 1 claims that no DB paradigm and no memory system (MemGPT/MemOS, Mem0, Zep, MIRIX/EverMemOS, Mem-alpha/Memory-R1, Generative Agents) supplies all four.
GEM state is M_t = (D_t content as semantic units, S_t structure, P_t declarative policies ⟨event, condition, action⟩). Transitions follow M_{t+1} = U(M_t, I_t, R_t).

Four state-level operators replace CRUD: ingestion, revision (reconcile, propagate along S_t, keep superseded values with provenance), forgetting (salience-driven, graded compress → hide → archive), and retrieval (every read updates salience, so retrieval counts as a write).

Six correctness conditions. C1: query soundness (most recent non-archived value is returned as current; history only when asked). C2: transition soundness (P_t respected, and no superseded value is ever returned as current). C3: dependency consistency (an update to u_i over a typed propagation edge triggers evaluation of u_j under P_t). C4: provenance preservation. C5: bounded active state |D_active| ≤ β(n). C6: retrieval-induced adaptation.

Three informal 'structural observations' (the authors say they are not theorems): a pure-function retrieval cannot satisfy C6; C5 and C6 cannot both be enforced over CRUD; append-only storage without semantic units cannot satisfy C2; untyped propagation cannot satisfy C3.
algorithms_or_data_structures: MemState data model. The topic is the semantic unit: title, summary, dense embedding, and a set of fields. Each field holds a value history H_{i,f} = ⟨(v, t, π)⟩ that is appended to, never overwritten. Default reads return v_k, and temporal queries read any v_j plus its provenance.

Typed edges in S_t. EXTENSION edges carry entailment, so change propagates along them. ASSOCIATION edges mean 'related but independent' and are used only for retrieval context expansion. Revision traverses extension edges only.

Policy example (Listing 1): POLICY propagate-on-change ON field_updated WHEN EXISTS dependent_topic DO flag_for_revision(dependent_topic) WITH evidence={updated_field,timestamp}. Propagation marks dependents for revision. It does not declare them false.

Algorithm 1, the unified transition: dispatch(event) → begin transaction → the operator branch runs (ingest: an LLM picks the host topic, appends to the field history, refreshes the embedding, and flags extension-linked topics; revise: conflict/merge/propagate repair per evidence item; forget: attenuate units with salience < θ; retrieve: route, read, build output, increment salience) → evaluate P_t postconditions on the proposed M_{t+1} → commit atomically or abort. Ingest and retrieve are synchronous. Revise and forget run asynchronously as policy-triggered maintenance.

Dependency repair walks extension edges and halts at any topic whose policy condition does not fire. The paper argues topic granularity keeps the frontier small compared with entity-grain graphs (Zep).

Forgetting ladder: three thresholds θ_summary (compress history), θ_remove (hide field from active retrieval), and θ_archive (archive topic, recoverable by explicit lookup). Salience rises on access and decays on disuse.

Proposed native-engine agenda: field histories as first-class bitemporal attributes; propagation semantics attached to extension edges in the schema; policy postconditions compiled into the commit protocol; an I/O-aware page layout co-locating topics, histories and embeddings; a joint index over semantic similarity and history predicates; and a single read-modify-write primitive for retrieval plus salience.
implications_for_contextdb: Motivation (spec §1, §3). R7 explicitly calls for a native engine that attaches propagation semantics to edges and compiles policy checks into commit. ContextDB's native justification layout (§3.2–3.3) is a direct answer to that call, so cite R7 as the motivation and do not present a native engine as an unclaimed idea.

Typed edges (spec §2.3). R7's EXTENSION/ASSOCIATION split resembles ContextDB's SUPPORTS/SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY vs HISTORICAL_REFERENCE split. ContextDB goes further in two ways: AND hyperedges with OR alternatives, and REQUIRES_CURRENT exact-version currency. Section 2 of the paper should spell out this difference.

Propagation semantics (spec §4.2). R7's flag_for_revision is the same idea as ContextDB's 'mark PENDING, never FALSE', so that idea alone is not novel. ContextDB's novel parts must be the deterministic support counts, stopping propagation when an alternative support survives, and checking the result against the oracle. R7 has no counting, no OR support, no cycle semantics, and no oracle.

Read semantics (spec §5.2). GEM's C6 makes every retrieval a state-changing write. ContextDB deliberately keeps reads pure (snapshot/certified reads), which is the right call for certifiable reads. Any future relevance or salience feature (M5 context packing) should be kept out of the certified state, or it inherits R7's own multi-tenant leakage problem: salience written by one tenant leaks to another tenant through ranking.

Benchmarks (spec §9). R7 proposes a 'trajectory benchmark' with ground truth for current value per unit over time (C2), the set of dependents that change after each update (C3), and the active footprint (C5). ContextDB's oracle-based per-epoch comparison and its false/missed invalidation metrics (§9.3) already produce C2/C3-style ground truth, and could be packaged as a contribution against this stated gap.

Baselines (spec §9.2). MemState is open source (Kuzu, Python). It is a natural 'generic property-graph backend' baseline (§9.2 item 5) for propagation latency, but it runs LLM-driven ingestion and revision. For a fair kernel comparison, drive only its graph and policy layer with deterministic events.

Erasure (spec §10). R7 points out that verifiable erasure under provenance preservation is strictly harder than relational delete. ContextDB already declares that v0 does not meet right-to-erasure, which is consistent with R7. Cite R7 there.
spec_gaps_or_errors: Spec §1 says MemState is 'the direct research motivation for the native-kernel route', which is fair. However, the spec does not note that R7 has no experiments, so ContextDB cannot reuse any R7 numbers as a baseline. A baseline must be run, for example through the MemState repo.

Novelty risk: R7 already claims (a) typed propagation-bearing edges, (b) value histories with provenance (revisions are kept immutable), (c) atomic commit with policy postconditions, and (d) a 'native engine' agenda. ContextDB's §11 claims 1 and 3 need to be framed precisely against R7: separating structural support from semantic currency, with exact head-version certificates. A loose framing would overlap R7.

R7's correctness condition C2 ('no superseded value returned as current') applies at the level of a unit's own value history. It does not cover derived conclusions whose premises were superseded, which is ContextDB's D1→D2/D3 stale-plan problem. ContextDB should state this distinction explicitly. It is a real gap in R7: C3 only requires 'evaluation', with no guarantee about what readers may see while that evaluation is pending.

R7's propagation runs asynchronously (revision is background maintenance), so readers can observe un-revised dependents. Spec §4.5 STRICT reads and fail-closed certification are the differentiator here, and the spec should name R7's async model as the contrast case.
papers.reported_results: No quantitative results. MemState is presented as a feasibility prototype: C1, C2 and C4 are said to hold 'by construction' and C5 and C6 'under transitions'. The research agenda lists first targets: a 500-turn adversarial workload scoring Mem0, Zep and MemState; a policy-language prototype on LongMemEval and LoCoMo; and an RL controller constrained by C2–C5. None of these were evaluated in the paper.

papers.title: MemTX: Transactional Belief Commit for Stateful Agent Memory
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: verified, with additional detail. arXiv:2607.23929, cs.AI. v1 was submitted 27 Jul 2026 and v2 on 28 Jul 2026; the comment says 'Preprint. Under review'. 'Li et al.' is correct: Xiaoyang Li, Yiqi Wang, Haohui Lu, Zhi Chen, Mo Li, Pingan Song, Mingkai Zheng, Taotao Cai (USQ, Griffith, Sydney, Liaoning, SUSTech). The title matches exactly, and spec §1's summary (staged write, validate/commit, action gating, cascade repair) is accurate. I read the full v2 PDF (15 pages including appendices A–H). The code URL printed in the paper, github.com/lxy1134/MEMTX, returns 404. Repository github.com/lxy1134/MEMTX_ exists and contains src/memtx/*, the case JSONs and the scripts; I inspected its core source files (state_machine.py, dependency_graph.py, memtx_manager.py). I infer it is the paper's artifact, but the paper does not link to it.
core_ideas: 'A memory write is not a belief commit.' Recording an observation, committing it as a belief, acting on it, and repairing after retraction become distinct, auditable steps in a single state machine. The system is model-agnostic middleware between the agent and its memory.
Six state-corruption families: tool-result pollution, stale late writes, dirty reads of tentative state, semantic conflict, permission laundering, and cascading-rollback failures.
Memory correctness is extended from write time to action time (gating irreversible tool calls) and to post-hoc repair (typed cascade over the derivation DAG).
Two machine-checked invariants. I1 is action-safety gating. I2 is cascade-repair completeness. A corollary G3 states that no committed or action-safe record has a revoked transitive ancestor.

Self-reported open problem: protections are scoped to a single commit or transaction, so transcription without a declared parent, and retry in a fresh transaction, both step around them. Fixing this needs 'provenance that follows content to action time'.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Record schema: entity, attribute, value; source with an authority weight; permission block (owner, reader/writer roles, scope ∈ {private, shared, public}); derived_from edges forming a derivation DAG; type ∈ {belief, summary, profile, index entry, shared copy, tool action}; validity interval checked against a logical clock (sim_now); writer confidence; version counter.

Eight-state lifecycle (code: state_machine.py TRANSITIONS). RAW→{TENTATIVE, REVOKED}. TENTATIVE→{VALIDATED, QUARANTINED, REVOKED}. VALIDATED→{COMMITTED, QUARANTINED, REVOKED}. COMMITTED→{ACTION_SAFE, SUPERSEDED, QUARANTINED, REVOKED}. ACTION_SAFE→{SUPERSEDED, REVOKED}. QUARANTINED→{VALIDATED, REVOKED}. SUPERSEDED→{REVOKED}. REVOKED is terminal. Any other move raises an error.

Five isolation levels, each defined by which lifecycle states are visible: raw-read, committed-read, verified-read, causally-stable-read (also hides records with any revoked transitive ancestor), and action-safe-read. Four risk tiers map onto them: low→committed, medium→verified, high→causally-stable, external_action→action-safe. The tier comes from trusted harness configuration and is never an agent argument.

Transaction: begin_tx captures snapshot_ids, the list of record IDs visible at the tier's isolation level at open time. stage_write adds TENTATIVE records plus provenance edges. Staged records are invisible to others at committed-read and above.

Commit pipeline, applied per staged record in order. (1) Evidence: confidence ≥ 0.6 unless source authority ≥ 0.9, both inclusive. (2) Validity interval contains the logical now. (3) Rule-based semantic conflict on the same (entity, attribute) slot: temporally disjoint values coexist; if a rival committed after the snapshot, the write is a stale late write and aborts before any authority comparison; otherwise the higher-authority value supersedes, the lower one aborts, and equal authority from different sources is quarantined for user review. This check also blocks children of revoked parents and private→wider-scope republishing (laundering). (4) Dependency stability: reject if any transitive ancestor is in the revoked set. A record that fails is QUARANTINED with a reason. A record that passes becomes COMMITTED, or COMMITTED→ACTION_SAFE in external-action transactions. A transaction can commit, partially commit, or abort. Each conflict adjudication is metered as one verifier call.

Action gate, consulted before any irreversible tool (tools are statically partitioned into reversible and irreversible). It blocks if ANY TENTATIVE record anywhere in the store is outside the transaction's snapshot, including the agent's own uncommitted staging. For external_action tier it also blocks if the snapshot contains NO ACTION_SAFE record. The second condition is existential: any action-safe record satisfies it, even one unrelated to the action, and the paper admits this in Appendix C. A blocked call returns a structured refusal.

Typed cascading repair. There are two entry points, transaction abort and revocation of a committed record, and both share one routine. A BFS over transitive descendants in the derivation DAG dispatches by type: beliefs → REVOKED; summaries/profiles/index entries/shared copies → QUARANTINED for rebuild (and added to the revocation registry); tool actions → compensated if reversible, otherwise logged as 'leaked'. Every step is written to a rollback log. In code, every descendant is added to _revoked_ids whatever its alternative parents are: there is no AND/OR support semantics, and any revoked ancestor kills the whole subtree.

Verification: property-based testing over 10,000 random traces (all 4 tiers, 6 record types), plus bounded exhaustive enumeration with symmetry reduction (4 records, 3 concurrent transactions, depth 10, reduced 2-tier/2-type alphabet): 5,530,160 canonical states and 10,537,260 transitions with 0 violations. The checker recomputes reachability from each record's own provenance fields. Verifying G3 exposed a missed-cascade bug on the abort path, which is kept as a regression test.
Agent interface: five memory tools (read, stage, commit, abort, revoke) plus 11 deterministic mock domain tools, 6 of them irreversible (refunds, outbound email, and similar).
implications_for_contextdb: Closest prior art for spec §5 and §6 (action gate, certified read). ContextDB must position itself explicitly against MemTX. The differences I could confirm from the paper and code: (a) MemTX's gate is global and existential ('no tentative record in flight anywhere' plus 'at least one action-safe record exists'). It is NOT scoped to the action's actual dependencies. ContextDB's VALIDATE_CERTIFICATE compares the exact head-version vector of the plan's dependency read set (spec §2.2 ValidationRecord, §3.2 note, M3), which is exactly the 'provenance that follows content to action time' MemTX lists as its main open problem. (b) MemTX's cascade revokes every transitive descendant, with no alternative support. That is precisely spec §9.2 baseline 4 ('No alternative-support tracking ablation'), so ContextDB can implement a MemTX-style BFS-revoke as a named baseline and measure false invalidation against it (spec H2, T02).

Supersession gap (spec §2.3 REQUIRES_CURRENT, T06/T16). In the MemTX code I inspected, a 'supersede_old' adjudication moves the old belief to SUPERSEDED but does NOT cascade to records derived from it. has_pending_invalidation consults only the revoked set. So MemTX's own repair machinery does not catch ContextDB's motivating case, where D1@v1 is superseded by D1@v2 and D2/D3 stay committed. Turn this into a head-to-head stale-plan test. Caveat: this is my reading of the public repo snapshot, not a claim the paper makes.

Atomicity and isolation (spec §5.1, T08, T12). MemTX allows partial commit, so a transaction is not all-or-nothing, and its 'snapshot' is a list of visible record IDs captured at begin. Stale-write detection is first-committer-wins on the same (entity, attribute) slot. There is no read-set validation, so cross-record write skew is not prevented. ContextDB's atomic batch publish and real read-set certification are concrete, testable differentiators. Add a write-skew test (two plans each reading A and B and writing different keys) to the T-matrix.

Retry escape (spec §5.1 CAS). MemTX reports that a correctly aborted stale write, retried in a fresh transaction, is no longer 'late' because the new snapshot already contains the rival, so authority adjudication takes over. ContextDB's REVISE(expected_revision) CAS has the same hole if a client blindly re-reads and retries. Mitigations: the new revision must carry justifications that reference the head it actually read, and the spec should state that CAS prevents lost updates but does not stop an agent from overwriting after seeing the conflict. Add a golden test for it.

Undeclared provenance (spec §9.3 'Dependency discovery precision/recall', M5). MemTX's source-scope family failed for every method because agents transcribed content without declaring the parent. ContextDB's guarantees are equally conditional on declared justifications. The spec's 'clients that do not use the action gate are out of scope' boundary should be extended to undeclared dependencies, and the M5 auto-dependency-extraction dataset is where this gets measured.

Verification methodology (spec §8, M1 exit). MemTX's bounded exhaustive enumeration (with symmetry reduction) on top of property tests is a stronger bar than '10,000 fixed seeds vs oracle'. Consider adding bounded exhaustive model checking of small DAGs (for example ≤4–5 revisions, ≤3 rules, depth ≤10 commits) against the oracle, along the lines of a stateright or loom exhaustive search in Rust.

Lifecycle vs orthogonal dimensions (spec §2.5). MemTX collapses state into one 8-state enum. ContextDB's orthogonal dimensions (head currency × structural support × semantic validation × conflict × visibility) are a stated design difference. The paper should argue it with an example MemTX's enum cannot express, such as CURRENT + SUPPORTED + PENDING validation.

Evaluation reuse (spec §9). MemTX's 90-case and 56-case declarative JSON suites (initial store, turn schedule, logical clock, ground truth: committed beliefs, aborted values, forbidden/required actions, required retractions) and its 24 downstream refund episodes are public in the MEMTX_ repo. ContextDB could run a scripted adapter over the stale-late-write, dirty-read and cascading-rollback families as an external conformance check. The 'trap + control pairs so blanket refusal can't score' design should be copied into the stale-action metric (spec §9.3: report the stale-action acceptance rate together with the legitimate-action allow rate).

Scale gap and opportunity. MemTX's cases have 1–3 agents and 1–4 turns, revocation chains of 4–5 nodes, and scripted latency of about 0.2 ms. It has no systems-performance evaluation at all, so ContextDB's 10K–1M revision workloads with update locality and tail latency (spec §9.1) do not overlap. That is where ContextDB's systems contribution can be clearly separate.

Typed repair (spec §4.2). MemTX's type-dispatched repair (beliefs revoked, derived views quarantined for rebuild, tool actions compensated or leaked) maps onto ContextDB's distinction between structural loss of support and PENDING semantic revalidation. The 'leaked irreversible effect' audit entry is a useful idea for ContextDB's action log once actions are recorded as Evidence.
spec_gaps_or_errors: Spec §1 lists MemTX's contribution as 'staged write、validate/commit、action gating、cascade repair' but does not say what ContextDB does beyond it. Given how close MemTX is, the novelty boundary paragraph in §1 should name MemTX explicitly and state three concrete deltas: dependency-scoped, exact-version certificates vs a global or existential gate; AND/OR support with alternatives vs revoke-all-descendants; supersession-triggered currency invalidation vs revocation-only cascade.

MemTX already ships five isolation levels, including a 'causally-stable-read' that hides records with invalidated ancestors. That is semantically close to spec §5.2 CERTIFIED_CURRENT and STRICT reads. The spec's read modes need to be defined against MemTX's levels to avoid looking like a renaming.

MemTX already machine-checks invariants on 5.5M states. Spec §8's correctness story (oracle plus proptest) will not read as stronger unless bounded exhaustive checking is added or the checked invariants are richer (OR support, currency, atomic batch).
The spec does not mention the retry-escape or undeclared-provenance failure modes that MemTX found empirically. Both apply to ContextDB's design and should be added to §10 Risks.
The paper's printed code URL (lxy1134/MEMTX) is a 404, and the artifact appears to live at lxy1134/MEMTX_. If the spec cites the code, it should use the working URL and note the discrepancy.

Isolation sweep (Appendix G): every level from committed-read upward scored identically on the suite. MemTX's benchmark therefore does not separate its stronger isolation levels, so ContextDB should not assume MemTX's suite can validate certified-read benefits. A purpose-built stale-plan workload is needed (spec §9).
papers.reported_results: Main suite (90 cases = 6 families × (10 traps + 5 controls), temperature 0). MemTX task success: Qwen3-8B 0.956, Qwen2.5-14B 0.811, GLM-4.7-Flash 0.944, GPT-5.4-mini 0.922, GPT-5.5 0.756. On GPT-5.5 it statistically ties 'Cordon + revocation' (0.778). The MemState baseline scored 0.333–0.411. Of 40 McNemar comparisons, 39 are significant at p<0.005 after Holm. Downstream harm (24 refund episodes): MemTX is the only method at 0.000 on every backbone; baselines range 0.125–0.5. Abort recall 0.922–1.0. Hardened suite (56 cases = 40 traps + 16 controls): MemTX 0.875–0.929 on strong backbones (scripted 0.893) vs ≤0.768 for the best baseline. At temperature 0.7 with 3 seeds, MemTX ranks first in 9 of 9 model-seed runs (std ≤0.023). Ablations: removing semantic-conflict adjudication, permission inheritance or cascading rollback each costs about 11 points. Removing dependency-stability, typed repair, validity interval or the evidence gate makes no difference on task success. Cost: about 1.36–1.58 verifier calls per case, tokens up to +14%, latency within the baseline band. Isolation sweep: raw-read 0.689 with 0.111 dirty reads per case; every level from committed-read upward is identical (0.800). Negative results: the source-scope (undeclared-transcription) family fails for all methods, and the temporal-scope retry escape empties stale-abort recall on 3 of 5 backbones. Formal check: 5,530,160 states and 10,537,260 transitions with 0 violations, plus 10k random traces.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Memory from a Computer Architecture Perspective: Visions and Challenges Ahead
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: verified. arXiv:2603.10062 (v1 9 Mar 2026, v2 30 Mar 2026), primary category cs.AR. 'Yu et al.' is correct: Zhongming Yu, Naicheng Yu, Hejia Zhang, Wentao Ni, Mingrui Yin, Jiaying Yang, Yujie Zhao, Jishen Zhao (UCSD; one Georgia Tech). The title matches. It is a short position paper (about 3 pages of text plus references) whose header reads 'Architecture 2.0 '26, March 23, 2026, Pittsburgh, PA', which I read as a workshop venue. Spec §1's summary ('将 memory consistency 界定为核心开放问题') is accurate: the paper says 'the most pressing open challenge is multi-agent memory consistency'. I read the full PDF. It has no data model, no protocol, and no evaluation.
core_ideas: Multi-agent memory is framed as a computer-architecture problem: the bottleneck is memory hierarchy, bandwidth and consistency, but over semantic context instead of bytes.

Two prototypes. In shared memory, all agents use one pool (a vector store or document DB): reuse is easy but coherence is needed, otherwise agents overwrite each other, read stale data, or rely on inconsistent versions. In distributed memory, each agent has local memory with selective synchronization: better isolation, but state diverges. Real systems are hybrids: local working memory plus selectively shared artifacts.

Three-layer hierarchy. I/O layer: ingest and emit (audio, text, images, network calls). Cache layer: compressed context, recent trajectories and tool calls, KV caches and embeddings. Memory layer: full dialogue history, vector/graph/document DBs. Agent performance is 'an end-to-end data movement problem'.

Two missing protocols. (1) An agent cache-sharing protocol, analogous to cache transfers in multiprocessors, so one agent's cached artifacts can be transformed and reused by another (prior KV-cache sharing work exists, but no principled protocol). (2) An agent memory access protocol covering permissions, scope, read-only vs read-write, and access granularity (document, chunk, KV record, or trace segment). MCP is treated as the 'agent context I/O' layer: necessary but not sufficient.

Consistency breaks into two requirements. Update-time visibility and ordering: when one agent's writes become observable to others and in what order concurrent writes are seen, analogous to SC/TSO/release consistency. Read-time conflict resolution: how to reconcile conflicting or stale artifacts when records evolve across versions under concurrent revision. Both are harder than in hardware because artifacts are semantically heterogeneous (evidence, tool traces, plans), inter-agent dependencies are implicit rather than declared, and conflicts are semantic and coupled to environment state.

Figure 3 lists the to-dos: a formal definition of multi-agent consistency models, and a verification framework that detects and classifies violations. It notes that multi-agent memory has 'no global clock or strict order' and 'implicit inter-agent communication'.
algorithms_or_data_structures: None. The paper is conceptual and specifies no data model, protocol, algorithm or evaluation. The only structure is the three-layer hierarchy (I/O, cache, memory) and the protocol boxes in Figure 2 (MCP/JSON-RPC for context I/O, 'Cache Protocol / Cache Reuse' for cache sharing, 'e.g. Agent-RDMA' for memory access).
implications_for_contextdb: Consistency model (spec §5, §10 '是否强一致'). R12 asks for a formal multi-agent consistency model. ContextDB can provide a concrete, scoped answer and should state it in those terms. Per branch, the single serialized writer plus atomic epoch publish gives a total commit order: commits are linearizable at the engine, and SNAPSHOT(e) reads are consistent cuts. CERTIFIED_CURRENT adds read-time validation against current heads. Map it explicitly to R12's two requirements: update-time visibility/ordering = epoch publish order; read-time conflict resolution = currency/certificate validation plus CONFLICTED status.

R12 says 'inter-agent dependencies are implicit rather than declared'. ContextDB's design choice is the opposite: dependencies are declared as typed justifications. That is a direct response to R12, but it moves the problem to dependency capture (spec §9.3 dependency discovery precision/recall, M5). The paper should admit this.

Hierarchy placement (spec §3.4). ContextDB sits in R12's 'memory layer' as the coherent shared store. The certificate (exact head-version vector) acts like a cache-line validity tag that lets an agent's cached context be checked cheaply before use. Framing it as a coherence or validation protocol (an analogue of read-set or version validation) would connect to R12's audience (MLSys/architecture).

Memory access protocol (spec §6, T17). R12's open questions about permissions, scope, read-only vs read-write, and unit of access line up with ContextDB's trusted-principal binding and Visibility dimension. Spec §6 should fix the unit of access (Revision) and the scope model (branch/namespace) explicitly.

Verification framework (spec §8). R12 asks for a framework to detect and classify consistency violations. ContextDB's oracle-based per-epoch checking, plus a taxonomy of the violations it detects (stale-plan execution, missed invalidation, transient partial state, lost update), could be presented as a partial answer to that call.
spec_gaps_or_errors: Not an error, but R12 gives only a problem statement: no definitions, no system, no data. ContextDB can cite it for motivation, but not as a baseline or for any technical claim.

Spec §1 says R12 should inform 'Shared/private context 与一致性协议'. The spec itself has no private/shared memory split (no per-agent private workspace vs shared branch semantics beyond copy-on-write branches in §5.3). If that framing is kept, define how an agent's private branch relates to main, for example the visibility of uncommitted branch heads and the merge as an explicit transaction, so the R12 shared vs distributed paradigms are actually addressed.

Overlap risk is low because R12 proposes no mechanism. However, MemTX (R8) already cites R12 as motivation for transactional belief commit, so the 'we answer R12's consistency challenge' framing is already in use.
papers.reported_results: None. Position/vision paper with no experiments.

extra_related_work: Khan (2026), 'Verified Detection and Prevention of Concurrency Anomalies in Multi-Agent Large Language Model Systems', arXiv:2606.17182, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17182. I read the abstract only. It formalizes four anomalies in TLA+: stale-generation, phantom-tool, causal-cascade, and tool-effect reordering. It machine-checks a consistency hierarchy L0⊊…⊊L4 with 274 Verus obligations and ships three Rust runtimes (pessimistic locking, SSI, default SI). Highly relevant: it is a Rust, verified transactional baseline that overlaps ContextDB spec §5 (read-set validation, write skew, cascade). MemTX uses it as a baseline.

Chen et al. (2026), 'Cordon: Semantic Transactions for Tool-Using LLM Agents', arXiv:2606.17573, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17573. I read the abstract only. Task-scoped transactions with shadow state, an effect outbox for irreversible actions, and result-lineage tracking. It is the strongest MemTX baseline (with revocation added). Relevant to ContextDB's action-time guard and the external TOCTOU discussion (spec §5.2): an outbox or conditional-release pattern is a concrete mitigation.

Wang (2026), 'TOKI: A Bitemporal Operator Algebra for Contradiction Resolution in LLM-Agent Persistent Memory', arXiv:2606.06240, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06240. I read the abstract only. It treats contradiction resolution as write-time concurrency control and gives four soundness theorems over a bitemporal dual-row schema with audit rows. Relevant to ContextDB's CONFLICTED dimension and supersession semantics (spec §2.5, §5.1).

Margalit et al. (2026), 'Governed Shared Memory for Multi-Agent LLM Systems' (MemClaw / ArgusFleet), arXiv:2606.24535, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24535. I read the abstract only. A production multi-tenant memory service with scoped retrieval, temporal supersession, provenance tracking (reconstructing depth-4 derivation chains), and policy-governed propagation. A practical baseline for spec §9.2 item 7, and relevant to the scope/permission layer (T17).

Chao et al. (2026), 'STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid?', arXiv:2605.06527. I verified the title only. It isolates implicit invalidation, where a later observation invalidates an earlier memory without explicit negation. Relevant to SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY/PENDING (spec §2.3) and could serve as an end-to-end benchmark source.

Ren et al. (2026), 'GateMem: Benchmarking Memory Governance in Multi-Principal Shared-Memory Agents', arXiv:2606.18829. I verified the title only. A multi-principal access-control benchmark, relevant to spec T17 and the M5 permissions layer.

Rezazadeh et al. (2025), 'Collaborative Memory: Multi-User Memory Sharing in LLM Agents with Dynamic Access Control', arXiv:2505.18279. I verified the title only. Private and shared memory tiers under time-evolving access control. Relevant to R12's shared vs distributed split and to ContextDB's branch/visibility model.

Yadav (2026), 'Temporal Validity in Retrieval Memory: Eliminating Stale-Fact Errors for AI Agents over Evolving Knowledge', arXiv:2606.26511, and Ganesan (2026), 'WorldDB: A Vector Graph-of-Worlds Memory Engine with Ontology-Aware Write-Time Reconciliation', arXiv:2604.18478. I verified the titles only. Both deal with supersession or temporal validity in memory engines; relevant to novelty positioning around head currency (spec §2.5).

papers.title: PACMI: Provenance-Aware Cascading Memory Invalidation for Long-Term LLM Agents (Wang, Liu, Zhang, Wu, Duan, Zheng, Cai; arXiv 2610.05732v1, 5 Oct 2026, cs.LG)
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: verified. The ID, title and first author match the spec. I read the full arXiv HTML v1, including the methods, experiments and appendices A-K. Two of the authors (M. Zheng, T. Cai) are also authors of MemTX [R8], so this is the same research group. Code and data are 'will be made publicly available'; the paper gives no released artifact.
core_ideas: Stale-memory handling is framed as dependency-aware validity management over a memory provenance graph G_t=(V_t,E_t). Nodes are prior memories plus new evidence. Edges are typed: supports, used-by (both given by annotation), and updates/contradicts (added by an LLM classifier). derived-from exists in the code but is not exercised.

There is a single four-state validity lattice: active < needs-verification < historical-only < superseded. The paper says the ordering is operationally defined by the retrieval biases (+0.12, +0.04, -0.10, -0.22 for current queries). Two more states (stale, invalidated) exist in the code but were never tested.

Invalidation is non-destructive. Original text is kept, so superseded records still answer historical queries. In-place LLM rewriting (the LLM-Only Update baseline) collapses historical accuracy to 0.42.

The paper explicitly positions itself as 'a truth maintenance system over natural-language agent memory' (it cites Doyle and de Kleer, plus Gupta & Mumick IVM and PROV-DM) and calls symbolic TMS 'a natural upper bound'.
At query time, a premise checker (LLM) compares superseded facts against current facts and injects a correction block when the question assumes an outdated fact.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Candidate ranking: s = 0.82*cos + 0.18*tokenJaccard + 0.08*[same semantic slot]. Keep the top k=6 candidates, then make one batched LLM call that classifies each as DUPLICATE/REFINE/UPDATE/CONTRADICT/TEMPORALLY_COMPATIBLE/UNRELATED. Deterministic slot, stability and temporality constraints then override the labels. Only UPDATE/CONTRADICT on a single-valued slot can create a direct target. A candidate that has an incoming supports/used-by edge is treated as downstream, never as a direct target.

Cascade (Algorithm 1): BFS from the accepted direct targets over outgoing dependency edges. Each edge type maps to a downstream state (supports -> needs-verification, used-by -> historical-only). When several paths reach a node, 'the stronger state in the lattice wins', i.e. a monotone max-join. Nodes not reached stay active. There is no counting of alternative supports and no AND/OR semantics: reaching a node by any path is enough to demote it.
Retrieval: score = cos + state bias + 0.06 new-evidence + 0.05 slot + 0.04 recency, top-5. Historical queries use flipped biases (0.04, 0.04, 0.12, 0.12).

Metrics, formally defined in Appendix B: DR (direct stale recall), AR (affected-node recall), OI/UI (the fraction of cases whose predicted non-current set has a false positive or a miss), SIC (stale-in-context fraction), CVER (current valid-evidence recall), Recall@Depth(d), Final accuracy, Stale Reuse, Premise Resistance (Q2), Historical Preservation (Q3). Statistics: 10,000-sample case bootstrap (seed 20260728) and exact McNemar tests.
papers.reported_results: On 100 cases / 300 queries / 5 domains (each case has 6 memories, 1 new evidence item, and a fixed 2-hop chain M1-supports->M2-used-by->M3): Final accuracy is 0.99 vs 0.90 for A-MEM-style, the strongest baseline (McNemar p=2.6e-6), with the whole gap on stale-premise Q2. Removing cascading raises errors from 3 to 11, which is not significant (p=0.057). Removing the premise check drops Final to 0.83 and Q2 to 0.50. Removing historical preservation drops Q3 to 0.36. The premise detector scores P=R=F1=1.0 on the controlled distribution. Costs are counted as LLM calls only (PACMI 400 auxiliary calls vs 100 for the others); no latency or token numbers are given. The authors themselves state that AR/UI are a deterministic function of the supplied topology (A1-A3), that OI cannot be exercised, and that multi-path resolution is never tested.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec 2.6 / T02 / H2: PACMI's 'stronger state wins' max-join over paths is exactly the non-counting behaviour ContextDB argues against. A node with J1:A&B->D and J2:E->D would be demoted by PACMI when A fails. Build a 'PACMI-style typed-BFS max-lattice' baseline into spec 9.2. It is the concrete, citable form of baseline 2 (naive eager BFS invalidation) and of baseline 4 (no alternative support). Then measure false invalidation on the multi-support workload (spec 9.1).

Spec 9.3 metrics: reuse PACMI's formal OI/UI/AR/Recall@Depth definitions (Appendix B) for 'false/missed invalidation rate', so the numbers are directly comparable. Apply them to topologies PACMI could not test: confluence, branching, and 'dependency-connected but should stay active' nodes. PACMI's Appendix J lists exactly these as needed extensions, so ContextDB's synthetic generator can fill a gap the authors acknowledge.

Spec 2.5: PACMI folds head currency, structural support and semantic status into one ordinal lattice that is driven by retrieval bias. ContextDB's orthogonal dimensions are a defensible difference. PACMI's mapping is still useful as an adapter/golden-test vocabulary: superseded=SUPERSEDED head, needs-verification=semantic PENDING, historical-only~HISTORICAL_REFERENCE.

Spec 5.2 read modes: PACMI's Q1/Q2/Q3 query types (current / stale premise / historical) map onto CERTIFIED_CURRENT vs HISTORICAL(epoch). The PACMI 100-case dataset (if released) can be replayed as a tiny end-to-end sanity check for the HISTORICAL vs CURRENT split. It is too small to say anything about systems performance.

Spec 10 'automatic dependency inference': PACMI's LLM relation classifier plus deterministic slot constraints is one design for M5's dependency extraction. PACMI did not evaluate edge induction (A1), so the graph-quality degradation study it names (oracle vs LLM-induced vs corrupted edges) is open and fits ContextDB M5.
spec_gaps_or_errors: The spec's one-line summary is accurate ('needs research on automatic dependency construction, scale, complex workloads'). It understates one novelty risk: PACMI already claims the 'TMS for agent memory' framing in prose. ContextDB cannot claim conceptual novelty for 'TMS + agent memory + cascading invalidation'. The contribution must sit in correct OR/AND support counting, versioned transactional semantics, native layout, and scale (the spec's own Novelty boundary statement in section 1 is right and should name PACMI explicitly).
The spec 9.2 baselines do not list PACMI (or any R9-R11 system) by name. Add a faithful PACMI-style propagation baseline.

Spec 2.3 edge types: PACMI's used-by -> historical-only rule (a downstream decision becomes 'historical', not 'pending') is a semantic choice that differs from ContextDB's SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY -> PENDING. Spec section 1 could note this difference explicitly.

papers.title: Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Derivation Currency for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory (v2) / ...: Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory (v1) (Evan Chen, Shiqiang Wang, Christopher G. Brinton; arXiv 2609.03340, v1 3 Sep 2026, v2 27 Sep 2026)
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified, with a title mismatch. The ID, authors (Chen, Wang & Brinton; Purdue / Exeter) and the PlanFence system match. The spec cites the v1 title 'Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory'. The current v2 is titled 'Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Derivation Currency for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory' and was substantially rewritten (it adds the observation- vs derivation-currency definitions, Proposition 1, the S-Bus evidence ablation, and the cost model). I read the full v2 HTML (all appendices) and the v1 abstract and introduction. The spec citation should be updated to v2.
core_ideas: Observation currency (the executor's local copy equals the owner's head, C_a(x)=H(x)) differs from derivation currency (the inputs the plan was derived from equal the owner's head, F_a(x)=H(x)). Neither implies the other, and both constructions are proved in Appendix B. 'Fresh memory, stale plan' is the case where observation currency holds and derivation currency fails.

Stored plans carry exact parent links (immutable record IDs). Before a protected action, the executor reconstructs an action-specific dependency frontier from the plan roots, asks each declared key's owner for its current head, refreshes the inputs that changed, allows one replan, and otherwise blocks (fail-closed). The application supplies the parent links and declares the dependency scope D(a). The model is never asked what it depended on.

Proposition 1 (frontier invariance and conditional soundness): installing newer versions or advancing heads never changes the recorded frontier, so refreshing memory cannot mask a stale plan. Under the recorded-input contract (Assumption 1), release implies that every covered input matched its owner's response during that pass. The paper is explicit that this is NOT a common multi-owner snapshot and NOT atomic with the external effect.
There is no shared memory service. Each key has a single authoritative owner (single writer). The paper argues against centralized lineage (a shared store) on cost grounds in an edge/LTE setting.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Record model: each public version stores the semantic key, an immutable record ID (a content digest that binds content, key and parent list), the authoritative owner, a monotone owner sequence, exact parent IDs, record type, size and payload. An owner accepts a head update only if the author equals the owner and the sequence increases. Duplicate sequences are treated as conflicts. Because IDs are digest-bound, parent cycles are impossible.

Frontier algorithm (Algorithm 1, Appendix E): a worklist starting at L(a) with a visited set. A record whose key is in D(a) adds its ID to B(key) and stops that branch. Otherwise its parents are enqueued. A missing record before or at a boundary blocks. After the traversal, every declared key must have |B(x)|==1, otherwise block (an empty set means a missing input; more than one ID means an ambiguous version, which catches conflicting branches). Owners are then queried concurrently for H(x). Records where H != C_a are fetched and verified. Release iff F_a = C_a = H. On a mismatch, return replan-required with the owner IDs, unless a replan has already been used, in which case block.

Cost model (bytes): W_sync ~ rho(N-1)c_h, W_scoped ~ nu*d(c_r+c_e), W_all ~ nu(M*c_r+|X|c_e). Crossover rho* = nu*d(c_r+c_e)/((N-1)c_h): sync wins below about 1 update per action, action-time validation wins above. Scope difference: W_all - W_scoped ~ nu[(M-d)c_r+(|X|-d)c_e], so the gain disappears at full scope.

Metrics: invalid/issued (the action's recorded inputs fail F=H), available/scheduled, complete (meets the current requirement), coordination stall in ms/action (generation excluded), traffic in KiB/action, successful replans, redundant auditor actions, and 'Gap' (the input changed between the last owner response and the effect, i.e. measured TOCTOU). A difference below 10% is treated as a tie. Bootstrap is two-stage, over families then templates.
papers.reported_results: The S-Bus validator held fixed detects 0/30 inherited-plan conflicts with session logs only and 30/30 when given the inherited versions. Live, 5 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B agents across reservation, fulfillment and deployment (10 seeds each): owner-head freshness acts stale 30/30 times. Centralized lineage and PlanFence each complete 30/30, with 1 replan each. Of the exploratory unvalidated runs, 15/30 are fresh-memory/stale-plan cases. Replay at rho=4 (AT&T LTE trace, 8 keys): PlanFence stall is 230.8 ms/action at 8.1 KiB, vs centralized lineage 508.6 ms / 15.6 KiB, metadata sync 403.4 / 23.5, and batched all-key 258.4 / 16.4. Across rho in {0.25,1,4,16}, PlanFence stays at 143-237 ms while sync grows from 52 to 1196 ms; PlanFence is 1.5-7.1x better at rho>=4, and sync is cheaper at rho<=1. Keyspace 8->128: scoped traffic stays flat at 8.1 KiB while all-key grows 16.4->81.7 KiB. At d=|X| the two are tied. Updates during replanning: at delta=2s and lambda=2/s both policies block 30/30. Effect-time gap: 1 of 252 issued actions. Learned policy selectors do not beat the 'sync if rho<=1 else PlanFence' rule out of distribution.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec 2.3 REQUIRES_CURRENT plus 3.3 dependency_reads[plan_id] plus 5.2 CERTIFIED_CURRENT/VALIDATE_CERTIFICATE plus T06/T16 are essentially PlanFence's derivation-currency check. Adopt their terminology (observation vs derivation currency) and cite it. Reuse their recorded-input contract (Assumption 1) as the precondition statement for ContextDB certificates.

PlanFence's frontier rule (stop at the first declared key; set-valued boundaries; block on |B|!=1) is a ready-made spec for building a certificate's exact dependency version vector (spec 3.2 'head-version vector'). Implement it in VALIDATE_CERTIFICATE and add a golden test for two branches that reach different versions of the same key, which must block. This conflict case is not in spec section 8.

Where ContextDB can go beyond PlanFence: (a) a single-store epoch snapshot gives a multi-key consistent certificate, which PlanFence explicitly cannot; (b) transitive derived-state maintenance, because PlanFence only compares leaf input IDs and has no OR alternative support, so any changed declared input forces a replan even if the plan has another valid justification; (c) separating structural from semantic invalidation (PlanFence treats every ID mismatch as replan, and its G.1 control shows version validity != semantic correctness). These three are the defensible delta for H3.

Spec 9 benchmarks: reuse PlanFence's stale-plan race workload (update rate rho per protected action in {0.25,1,4,16}; keyspace 8-128; declared scope d in {1,2,8}), its outcome accounting (invalid/issued, available/scheduled, replans, blocks), and its Appendix F 'updates during replanning' design (Poisson lambda, replan delay delta, Gap counter). These give 'stale action acceptance rate' (spec 9.3) and a measured TOCTOU window (spec 5.2). Include their unsafe baselines (local replica, owner-head freshness) and an all-key-validation baseline so H3 overheads are reported against the same guarantee levels (spec 9.2's 'do not mix guarantee levels').

Architectural risk: ContextDB is a centralized lineage store, i.e. PlanFence's losing baseline (about 2x stall at rho>=4 over emulated LTE). ContextDB should either scope its claims to co-located or single-site deployment, where the store is in-process (spec 5.1 single-writer), or report its certification latency under the same emulated-link setting. Their stall measurements exclude local processing, so an in-memory Rust validator is not directly comparable.
spec_gaps_or_errors: The title is out of date: v2's title is 'Derivation Currency for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory'.

The spec credits R10 only with 'exact dependency versions and pre-action validation'. In fact it also delivers a formal soundness proposition, a cost model, and a decentralized (no shared service) design that argues against a central store. That is a direct positioning challenge for ContextDB's H3 that the spec does not address.

Spec section 8 lacks PlanFence's ambiguity case (the same key reached at two versions through different derivation branches) and the 'one replan then block' bounded-recovery policy. Spec 5.2 mentions TOCTOU but defines no metric for it. PlanFence's 'Gap' count is one.
Spec 9.2 baselines omit derivation-current competitors (PlanFence, S-Bus with an inherited version set, MemTX). Without them, H3 is not compared against the strongest prior art.

papers.title: MemTrace: State-Consistent Memory for Long-Horizon Coding Agents (Hongming Xu, Le Zhou, ZhongHe Jin, Xiang Zhang, Bo Tang, Zhiyu Li, Xuanhe Zhou, Juncheng Zhang; arXiv 2610.04838v3, v1 4 Oct, v3 10 Oct 2026)
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified: the ID, title and first author (Xu) match. I read the full v3 HTML, including Appendix A.1-A.5 and the repository README. Code is public under Apache-2.0. The abs page links github.com/Homy-Xu/MemTrace and the HTML links github.com/theseus-labs-rsi/MemTrace; both resolve. Per its README, the repo releases only the DeepSWE entry points; SWE-EVO and SWE-Milestone reproduction are not claimed. Note: MemTrace is single-agent (one coding agent across context refreshes), not multi-agent shared context.
core_ideas: Long-horizon coding suffers 'state-memory misalignment': recalled history (e.g. an old test failure) no longer matches the current repository or task state after edits and context refreshes.

Completed work is sealed into immutable Memory Traces tau=(x_tau evidence+provenance, rho_tau repo state at creation, E(tau) bound files/symbols/tests, alpha_tau anchor). Corrections create new traces and relations, and nothing is mutated.

Two graphs. The Memory Trace Graph (MTG) has depend, verify, correct and supersede relations plus execution order. The Repository State Graph (RSG) has files, symbols and tests with defines/calls/imports/covers relations, updated incrementally around the frontier. The projection Pi links traces to entities.

Restoration is validated lazily: applies(tau;R_t,m_t) = aligned(tau,R_t) AND NOT superseded(tau,m_t). Supersession needs an explicit MTG edge, not temporal order. For a test result, both the test and its recorded dependencies must be unchanged. Unverifiable evidence is not reused, and the agent re-reads or re-runs instead.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Candidate retrieval starts from anchors, frontier traces, or repo references, then does bounded RSG expansion, then at most 2 MTG hops along depend/verify/correct/supersede in both directions. Results are deduplicated, then filtered with applies(), then packed by budget (oversized blocks are deferred, not truncated).

Revision-time closure policy, from code SemanticStore.advance_workspace_revision (Appendix A.3): on each workspace revision, every record marked CURRENT with an open validity interval (valid_to_cursor IS NULL) whose revision differs from the new one is closed IF its type is global (TOOL_RESULT, TEST_RESULT, TEST_FAILURE, VERIFIER_RESULT, REQUIREMENT_REVIEW; closed on ANY revision regardless of files), or IF its type is entity-scoped (CODE_CHANGE, CODE_OBSERVATION) and _entity_affected matches a bound file/symbol/test. Closure sets the validity endpoint and adds an INVALIDATED_BY relation; the trace itself is kept. This is an interval-based (temporal-validity) store with coarse type-level rules and no transitive support propagation.
Exposure metric x_tau = 1[exists later revision touching a bound file]. Kaplan-Meier survival of 'bound files unchanged' over event-step age. Per-task revision and invalidation counts.
papers.reported_results: Codex CLI with deepseek-v4-flash: DeepSWE pass@1 is 56.6 vs 35.4 Native (+21.2 over the best baseline); SWE-EVO Resolved is 69.6 vs 65.2 (+4.4); SWE-Milestone Score is 46.4 vs 28.6 (+17.8). mini-swe-agent: DeepSWE 66.4 vs 48.7. Ablation on DeepSWE: Trace Store only 32.1, +MTG 44.2, +RSG 56.6. On SWE-EVO the RSG adds nothing. Wall-clock is often higher (DeepSWE Codex 54.2 vs 42.0 min). Diagnostics over 85 trajectories: 57.0% of 9,226 file-bound traces see a later bound-file change. Survival of unchanged bound files falls to about 0.50 by around 1,000 event steps. 2,897 revisions produced 16,197 recorded invalidations (about 5.6 per revision), and revisions correlate with invalidations (Spearman 0.84). Median 79/102.5/129 traces per short/medium/long task. Single run per configuration, no seeds or CIs on the main table.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec 10 ('evidence anchors include commit/file/symbol/test version'): MemTrace's tau tuple (rho_tau plus entity bindings E(tau)) is a concrete Evidence schema for spec 2.2. Model the file/symbol/test bindings as base Evidence revisions whose heads advance on WORKSPACE_REVISION. Then MemTrace's closure rules become REQUIRES_CURRENT edges, and ContextDB can show the transitive and OR-aware consequences that MemTrace's flat type rule cannot express.

MemTrace closes ALL global-type records (test results, tool results) on every revision regardless of file overlap. That is deliberate over-invalidation. A ContextDB experiment can replay MemTrace's released DeepSWE traces/receipts as a coding-workflow workload (spec 9.1, 'real coding-workflow traces') and compare false-invalidation counts and revalidation work between MemTrace-style type-closure and ContextDB's justification-scoped invalidation. Their published statistics (about 34 revisions per task, about 5.6 invalidations per revision, about 100 traces per task, 57% exposure) can calibrate the synthetic generator's churn rates.

Spec 4.5 eager/lazy: MemTrace is the lazy, read-time-validation extreme (it checks applicability at restoration). That makes it a natural 'lazy' baseline for H4, against ContextDB's eager counter maintenance.

The scale is small (about 100 traces per task, a single agent). It does not stress the DB-layer questions (multi-writer, snapshots, 1M revisions), so MemTrace is a source of workload realism, not a systems competitor.
spec_gaps_or_errors: The spec's description ('Coding Agent trace and repository-state consistency') is accurate. The spec does not mention that MemTrace is single-agent and does no transitive propagation or multi-support reasoning. Those are useful novelty points for ContextDB and should be stated.

Spec 9.1 asks for 'real coding-workflow traces' but names no source. MemTrace's public repo (DeepSWE adapters, receipts, Codex/mini-swe-agent backends) is the most directly reusable one. Caveat: only the DeepSWE entry points are released.

MemTrace's end-task gains (pass@1) come from a whole memory system (offloading, anchors, retrieval) and cannot be attributed to validity checking alone. The spec should not cite them as evidence for version validation per se.

papers.title: CoMemBench: Benchmarking Collaborative Memory Boundaries across Multi-Agent Workflow Topologies (Sen Zhao, Ruiqi Kong, Zuyu Zhang, Lifeng Shen, Xinyu He, Ding Zou, Xu Zhang, Qinghua Zhang; arXiv 2609.32192v2, v1 26 Sep, v2 29 Sep 2026)
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified: the ID, title and first author (Zhao) match. I read the full v2 HTML, including Appendices A-G, and checked that the project site http://comembench.world is live (task browser and leaderboard). The paper says the data, schemas and evaluation code 'will be released'. Private evaluator oracles and pollution plans are distributed only with an 'operator package'.
core_ideas: A 'collaborative memory boundary' is the task- and state-conditioned split between information that is applicable to a consumer node (and must be shared) and information that is inapplicable (a sibling-branch result, unverified, wrong entity, incompatible, superseded) and must not change the consumer's verified behaviour.

Workflow topology is the stress dimension. There are five motifs: chain, split-join, reuse, overlap (partially shared predecessors), and bounded revision (a verifier-triggered repair that supersedes an artifact). The labels are multi-label.

The benchmark is execution-grounded: 800 workflows (200 each for stateful tool use via 25 MCP servers, SWE-bench Verified repository code, BrowseComp+ offline retrieval, and Lean 4.7 formal math), recovered from source dependency evidence, never synthetic edges.
Matched clean/polluted pairs: exactly one inapplicable artifact is injected into one target consumer's incoming view, and the polluted target is scored only if the clean target succeeds.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Workflow W=(q, G=(V,E), node-local specs X, resources R, native evaluator Phi). Each required edge carries a handoff contract h_e=(producer u, consumer v, semantic type tau, entity scope z, version nu, verification requirement sigma).

Artifact record: semantic type, producer, scenario/entity scope, version, verification state, payload, provenance. A node_view holds role, task, authorized context, declared incoming artifacts, handoff contract, output type and a capability token. An optional memory_proposal (artifact, producer, proposed recipients) is logged. Only a verified receipt lets an artifact satisfy a downstream dependency.

Six pollution operators: sibling crosswire, incompatible payload, unverified result, completed-as-pending, wrong entity, stale version (the last applies only in bounded-revision workflows, 414 of 800).

Metrics: SR (terminal success); VNCR (macro-average verified-node fraction); VHS = |H+|/|H| (consumers whose mandatory predecessors verified, and whose required artifacts were exposed, current, receipt-valid, explicitly consumed, and natively verified); ICS = |P+|/|P| (polluted-target success among pairs whose clean target succeeded, micro-pooled); tokens (mean, median, per verified node). Failures are attributed as method, benchmark or infra.

Certification gates: schema, graph closure and acyclicity outside declared revision edges, topology witnesses, node-local closure, a gold-plan replay with targeted negative mutations, and human repair-oriented review. The split is 177 dev / 623 test families, grouped by source.
papers.reported_results: No system solves any Stateful-Tool or Formal-Math workflow end to end. The best SR is 8.0 (code) and 18.0 (retrieval). VNCR reaches 84.2 and VHS 89.4 even at SR=0. Sharing and isolation do not improve together: e.g. with Qwen3.8-27B, SMoA has 72.4 VHS on Stateful Tool but only 10.1 ICS, while Deep Agents has 38.1 ICS with weak progress. In the controlled memory comparison (fixed supervisor-worker executor), Local-only gets ICS 97.1/89.4 (tool/code), while Full Context drops it to 72.4/71.9 and Shared Flat RAG gets 70.6/73.9. A-Mem reaches 18.4 code SR but 63.9 code ICS, and PlugMem gets 91.3 code ICS but 0 SR. Tokens: Local-only 489k vs Full Context 672k per task. Isolation rankings shift across topology and across operators (e.g. EvoMAS: 72.7 ICS on split-join, 14.3 on reuse).
implications_for_contextdb: Spec 9 end-to-end evaluation (M5): CoMemBench's controlled memory-mechanism harness (a fixed executor where only the cross-worker exposure policy changes) is the right place to plug ContextDB in as one more 'memory mechanism' row next to Local-only, Full Context, Shared Flat RAG, Mem0, A-Mem and PlugMem. ContextDB's CONTEXT query with typed dependencies, version currency and verification state is designed to get high VHS AND high ICS at once, which is precisely the trade-off CoMemBench shows no existing mechanism breaks.

Map the handoff contract h_e=(u,v,tau,z,nu,sigma) directly onto ContextDB objects. The producer/consumer edge becomes a Justification or REQUIRES_CURRENT edge. nu becomes the exact revision. sigma becomes the semantic validation state (VERIFIED/PENDING). z becomes namespace/scope. The six pollution operators then become CONTEXT read-filter test cases: stale version -> head currency; unverified result -> PENDING not actionable (T15); sibling crosswire and wrong entity -> scope/branch isolation (T14); completed-as-pending -> effect/idempotence state. Add these as golden tests in spec section 8.

Reuse the metrics VHS (required-sharing recall) and ICS (isolation robustness) as the end-to-end counterparts of spec 9.3's 'handoff validity' and 'context token cost'. Tokens per verified node is a good budget-efficiency metric for spec 6 token packing.

Caveat for spec 9.1: CoMemBench injects one static polluted artifact. It does not commit live mid-workflow revisions that cascade through derived artifacts, and only the stale-version operator touches versioning. ContextDB's core revision/cascade workload is therefore only partly exercised. A 'live revision' extension (commit a new upstream revision during execution, as PlanFence does) would be a contribution in its own right.

Cost and feasibility: the full benchmark needs SWE-bench Docker images, 25 MCP servers with PostgreSQL-backed apps, and Lean 4.7 toolchains, and the private oracles come only with the operator package. Start with the retrieval or code domain subset.
spec_gaps_or_errors: The spec's 'real multi-agent stress test' is partly accurate. The workflows are real and executable, but the isolation challenges are single synthetic injections, and the benchmark tests exposure policy, not version maintenance under concurrent revision.
The spec does not note that CoMemBench's strongest isolation result comes from Local-only (minimal sharing). Any ContextDB claim must beat Local-only on ICS while beating Full Context on VHS and SR.
The spec does not mention the benchmark's own schema (node_view / artifact / memory_proposal). ContextDB's MCP adapter (M5) could target that schema directly to lower integration cost.

extra_related_work: S-Bus: Automatic Read-Set Reconstruction for Multi-Agent LLM State Coordination (Khan, arXiv 2605.17076; existence verified, abstract page only). A session-level read-set (DeliveryLog) plus an explicit declared read-set validator against a logical registry, with replicated deployment through Raft. This is OCC for agents. PlanFence uses it as the native validator in its evidence ablation. It directly overlaps ContextDB's 'real read-set validation' (spec 5.1) and should be a spec 9.2 baseline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17076

Temporary Authority, Permanent Effects: Commit-Time Authorization for LLM Agents / CommitGuard (Santos-Grueiro, arXiv 2607.10487; existence verified). Tracks authority witnesses through derived state to the durable-effect boundary (freshness, causal priority, effect binding). This is the effect-side complement to spec 5.2's TOCTOU discussion and to 'Authorized_e(r)' in spec 2.4. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10487

When Memory Updates but Behavior Does Not: Repairing Implicit Stale Dependencies in Personalized Agent Responses / StateAuditor (Sun & He, arXiv 2608.01619; existence verified). Combines LLM judgments with deterministic provenance and chronology checks to find responses that still depend on an obsolete premise. This is the closest prior work to ContextDB's SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY -> PENDING validator adapter (spec 2.3, M3). https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01619

STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid? (Chao et al., arXiv 2605.06527; existence verified). A benchmark for implicit-update stale-memory detection and premise resistance. PACMI adapts its CUPMem baseline from it. It could supply the semantic-validator test sets for spec 9.3 'semantic validator invocations'. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06527

MemConflict: Evaluating Long-Term Memory Systems Under Memory Conflicts (Tao et al., arXiv 2605.20926; existence verified). Defines memory validity as query-conditioned fitness-for-use. Relevant to the spec 2.5 Conflict dimension. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20926

Turning Interaction History into Execution State: A Runtime Layer for Long-Horizon Coding Agents / Ledger (Wang et al., arXiv 2608.00808; existence verified). Uses change counters to track observation freshness. A simple version-counter baseline for coding agents, cited by MemTrace. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.00808

Beyond Semantic Organization: Memory as Execution State Management for Long-Horizon Agents / MAGE (Chen et al., arXiv 2606.06090; existence verified). A hierarchical state tree with summary validation and rollback, related to spec 5.3 branch/what-if. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06090

GateMem: Benchmarking Memory Governance in Multi-Principal Shared-Memory Agents (Ren et al., arXiv 2606.18829; existence verified). Covers access control and active forgetting in a shared pool. Relevant to spec 2.5 Visibility, T17 (untrusted principal) and the spec 10 right-to-erasure gap. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18829

MemTX [R8, already in spec] (arXiv 2607.23929, verified to exist). PlanFence's Appendix A characterizes it as a derived-from index with a service that walks descendants forward and does typed repair. Together with PACMI (the same Zheng/Cai group) it forms a family that ContextDB must differentiate from explicitly through OR-aware counting and transactional snapshot certificates.

papers.title: Introducing Context Repositories: Git-based Memory for Coding Agents (Letta blog, 2026-02-12), cross-checked against letta-code source v0.34.18 (commit e8073d4, 2026-10-19)
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified, with one qualification. The post exists at the cited URL, is dated Feb 12 2026, and is credited to 'Letta' with no individual authors. It is a product/engineering blog post, not a paper, and it reports no evaluation numbers at all. The spec's summary, 'Git-backed shared context and branching', is accurate for one agent and its subagents (worktrees merged back into main). Cross-agent sharing ('shared memory repositories' attached to several agents) is not in the blog. I found it only in the current letta-code source (src/skills/builtin/managing-shared-memory/SKILL.md), so treat it as a 2026 product feature, not a claim from the blog.
core_ideas: Agent memory is a directory of Markdown files cloned locally as a git repo (MemFS). Agents edit it with ordinary shell, file and script tools instead of special memory-tool calls. Every change is committed with an informative commit message.

The file tree is always in the system prompt, and each file has YAML frontmatter with a `description`. Files under `system/` are pinned (always fully loaded). Agents may reorganise the hierarchy or move files in and out of `system/`. Current code also supports a newer 'root layout' with MEMORY.md index files.

Concurrency comes from git. Each subagent (init, reflection/'sleep-time', defragmentation) works in its own git worktree on its own branch, then merges back into main. In the blog's words, git provides the missing 'mechanism to coordinate concurrent writes', via 'git-based conflict resolution'.

Built-in skills: memory initialisation (fans out over Claude Code and Codex history with parallel subagents), background reflection (runs in a worktree and auto-merges), and defragmentation (backs up, then restructures memory into about 15 to 25 focused files).

Cross-agent shared memory (code, not blog): an org-owned git repo hosted on Letta Cloud and mounted per agent. The harness pushes clean commits after each turn. A rejected push is retried once after `pull --rebase`. Dirty files and conflicts are not touched automatically; the agent gets a reminder instead.
algorithms_or_data_structures: Worktree branch creation (src/agent/memory-worktree.ts): `git worktree add <memory-worktrees>/<label>-<id> -b letta/<label>/<id> <baseHEAD>`. Branch = isolated subagent context; the base is the parent's HEAD at spawn time.

Finalize/merge: if the worktree has no commits, the result is `no_changes`. If the parent checkout is dirty, the result is `parent_dirty`. Otherwise it runs plain `git merge <branch> -m <msg>` (a textual three-way merge). On failure it runs `git merge --abort`, force-deletes the worktree and branch, and returns `merge_conflict` with retryable=true: the reflection is thrown away and the transcript can be reprocessed later. Status enum: merged / no_changes / discarded / merge_conflict / failed / dirty_uncommitted / parent_dirty.

Remote sync: if origin/main is an ancestor of HEAD, nothing to do. If HEAD is an ancestor of origin/main, `merge --ff-only`. Otherwise `rebase origin/main`, aborting on error. After a turn, a rejected push leads to `pull --rebase` and a push retry. If the rebase conflicts, the harness launches a background 'memory' subagent (an LLM) to resolve the conflict markers. That attempt is tracked in `letta-memory-repair.json`, with a token and a lease-based claim (src/agent/memory-conflict-repair.ts), using MERGE_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD and REVERT_HEAD as operation signatures.
Provenance = git history. `git log -- <path>`, commit messages and the per-commit author are the only provenance. Files do not record which other files' versions they relied on.
Versioning unit = git commit (a content-addressed tree) plus blob hashes per file. This gives exact, cheap content identity for any file at any commit.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec 9.2 #7 (Git-backed baseline). Build a deterministic 'GitMemory' adapter in Rust over a real git repo, preferably with gix/gitoxide or git2 (libgit2). Report the cost of spawning the git CLI separately, because Letta shells out to git and a library-only number would flatter or penalise the baseline unfairly. Mapping: LogicalRecord -> file path (e.g. `decisions/architecture.primary_db.md`). Revision -> blob OID at a commit. Epoch -> commit OID. Branch -> git branch or worktree. CURRENT -> `HEAD:path`. HISTORICAL(epoch) -> `<commit>:path`. DIFF -> `git diff --name-status A B`.

Do not strawman the baseline. Give it the best git-native dependency encoding a careful agent would write: frontmatter `depends_on: [{path, blob_oid}]`.
