Then stale-plan detection becomes 'compare the recorded blob_oid with the current `HEAD:path` OID'. That is an O(#deps) exact version-vector check that git provides almost for free. ContextDB's advantage must be shown on what git lacks: a reverse index (IMPACT needs a full-tree scan or grep), transitive AND/OR support with alternative-support short-circuiting (H2), and atomic publication of derived state. Single-record staleness checks are not that advantage. Run two variants: (a) a plain grep/scan IMPACT, and (b) a 'git + maintained reverse-index file' variant. Without (b), reviewers will say the baseline was weakened.

Merge semantics: a new correctness test. Spec 5.3 says a merge 'is not merging two text files'. Letta's merge is exactly a textual three-way merge plus LLM conflict repair. Add a regression and benchmark case, 'semantic merge skew': branch B writes D2 depending on D1@v1 while main revises D1 to v2. The files differ, so git merges cleanly and silently produces a stale D2 on main. ContextDB's merge transaction must detect this (D2's REQUIRES_CURRENT or SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY on D1@v1 against the new head) and return CONFLICT or PENDING. Measure stale-action acceptance after merge as the headline safety metric (spec 9.3).

Treat Letta's 'abort and discard the branch on conflict, then retry' policy as a baseline behaviour to measure: wasted validator/LLM work per conflict. Contrast it with ContextDB's explicit rebase and CONFLICT reporting (spec 5.1).

The spec 5.3 branch design (copy-on-write head overlay) should be benchmarked against git worktree creation time and disk footprint for the branch-heavy workload (spec 9.1). Git worktrees check out the whole tree.

The spec 9.1 'concurrency' row: Letta's model is optimistic, with push rejection and rebase-and-retry, and it has no read-set validation. Use it to demonstrate the write-skew case from spec 5.1 (two agents each update different files based on reading the other's old version; both rebase cleanly).

The novelty boundary (spec 1) is confirmed. Git-versioned, branchable, mergeable agent memory with worktree isolation is already shipped (Letta, Feb 2026) and published (GCC, arXiv 2508.00031). ContextDB cannot claim versioning, branching or merging as contributions. Only dependency-aware merge and certification are new.
spec_gaps_or_errors: The citation lists the year as 2026 with no exact date and no author. Use 'Letta (2026-02-12), blog post'. No peer review and no quantitative results, so it cannot serve as a performance reference. It can only describe behaviour.

The spec says 'shared context'. The blog's sharing is within one agent's subagent tree. Cross-agent shared memory repos are documented only in current code and docs. Cite those separately (letta-code SKILL.md, /v1/repositories) if the paper claims Letta supports multi-agent sharing.

The spec gives no adapter mapping for #7, and 'only compare end-to-end workflows with matching features' is underspecified. State explicitly which ContextDB operations have git equivalents (CURRENT, HISTORICAL, DIFF, branch isolation) and which must be marked 'not supported / emulated by scan' (IMPACT, WHY transitive, alternative support, CERTIFIED_CURRENT).

Letta behaviour is a moving target: v0.34.18 code differs from the blog (root vs. existing layout, LLM-driven conflict repair). Pin the letta-code version and commit in the experiment environment (spec 9.4).

papers.title: Graphiti, temporal context graphs (Zep docs plus github.com/getzep/graphiti v0.31.1, commit 6e3e3cb, 2026-10-19) and Rasmussen et al., 'Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory', arXiv:2501.13956v1 (20 Jan 2025)
papers.exists_and_matches_spec: Verified. The docs URL exists. On that welcome page the wording is 'Context Graphs' / 'temporal knowledge graphs'; the phrase 'temporal context graphs' appears in the GitHub README ('Graphiti is a framework for building and querying temporal context graphs for AI agents'). The arXiv paper exists: one version, 5 authors (Rasmussen, Paliychuk, Beauvais, Ryan, Chalef), all Zep AI. I read the full PDF, including methods, experiments and appendix prompts. The spec's characterisation ('temporal KG, provenance, history, hybrid retrieval; not equal to TMS proof maintenance') is accurate. The spec does not cite the arXiv paper itself, only the docs, and it should.
core_ideas: Three-tier graph G=(N,E,phi): an episode subgraph (raw messages, text or JSON; 'non-lossy'), a semantic entity subgraph (entities plus fact edges), and a community subgraph (label-propagation clusters with summaries).

Bi-temporal model (paper §2.1, §2.2.3): timeline T is event/valid time and T' is transaction/ingestion time. Each fact edge stores four timestamps: t'_created and t'_expired in T', and t_valid and t_invalid in T. Relative dates ('two weeks ago') are resolved against the episode reference timestamp t_ref.

Edge invalidation (paper §2.2.3): 'The system employs an LLM to compare new edges against semantically related existing edges to identify potential contradictions. When the system identifies temporally overlapping contradictions, it invalidates the affected edges by setting their t_invalid to the t_valid of the invalidating edge... Graphiti consistently prioritizes new information.' Facts are invalidated, never deleted, so history survives.

Provenance: episodic MENTIONS edges plus 'bidirectional indices' between episodes and the semantic edges derived from them (edge.episodes and episode.entity_edges), so that facts can be traced to sources for citation. The paper says these 'are not directly examined in this paper's experiments'.

Retrieval f(α)=χ(ρ(φ(α))): search (cosine plus BM25 via Neo4j/Lucene, plus BFS n-hop from seed nodes), rerank (RRF, MMR, episode-mentions, node distance, cross-encoder), and a constructor that emits facts with 'Date range: from - to' and entity summaries. Interpreting the validity ranges is left to the downstream LLM.
Graph writes use predefined Cypher (not LLM-generated). Backends per current README: Neo4j 5.26, FalkorDB, Amazon Neptune. Kuzu is deprecated.
algorithms_or_data_structures: EntityEdge fields (graphiti_core/edges.py): uuid, group_id, source/target_node_uuid, name, fact, fact_embedding, episodes: list[episode_uuid] (provenance), created_at (T' start), expired_at (T' end), valid_at (T start), invalid_at (T end), reference_time, attributes. EpisodicNode: content, source, valid_at (= reference time), entity_edges list. group_id is a namespace/partition; on FalkorDB each group_id is a separate graph.

Invalidation candidate discovery (edge_operations.py resolve_extracted_edges): for each new edge, (1) duplicate candidates are a hybrid BM25+cosine RRF search restricted to the same endpoint pair; (2) invalidation candidates are the same hybrid search over the whole group_id with no endpoint filter, capped at DEFAULT_SEARCH_LIMIT=10. One LLM call (`dedupe_edges.resolve_edge`) returns duplicate_facts and contradicted_facts indices. A contradiction that falls outside the top-10 retrieved candidates is never considered, so invalidation is recall-bounded by retrieval.

Temporal rule after the LLM verdict (_apply_temporal_invalidation and resolve_edge_contradictions): if the new edge already has invalid_at, set its expired_at=now. Else, if any contradicting candidate has a later valid_at, the new edge itself gets invalid_at = that candidate's valid_at and is expired (late-arriving old facts don't override newer ones). For each contradicting candidate: skip if the intervals don't overlap (cand.invalid_at <= new.valid_at, or new.invalid_at <= cand.valid_at). Otherwise, if cand.valid_at < new.valid_at, set cand.invalid_at = new.valid_at and cand.expired_at = now (if not already set). Edges with null valid_at are never invalidated by this rule.

Future-tense normalisation (temporal_edge_utils.py): a regex detects 'will / plans to / scheduled to...'. For such facts valid_at is clamped to the reference time, and a soft-deadline invalid_at ('by Friday') is dropped. This is a heuristic, not a formal semantics.

Provenance-counted retraction (graphiti.py remove_episode): remove the episode uuid from each mentioned edge's `episodes` list. Edges with remaining episodes are kept; edges with none are deleted. Entity nodes mentioned only by that episode are deleted, and summaries of surviving nodes are rebuilt by LLM. This is a one-level OR support count over source episodes, with no transitive propagation. Invalidations caused by the removed episode are NOT reverted: the `invalidated_by` map is only an in-memory out-parameter and is never persisted, so an old fact stays expired after its invalidator is retracted.

Point-in-time queries: SearchFilters has valid_at, invalid_at, created_at and expired_at as DNF lists of DateFilter (operators =, <>, <, <=, >, >=, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL). The default SearchFilters() applies no temporal filter, so ordinary search returns invalidated facts alongside current ones (with date ranges). An 'as-of (t, t')' bitemporal read must be composed explicitly: valid_at<=t AND (invalid_at IS NULL OR invalid_at>t) AND created_at<=t' AND (expired_at IS NULL OR expired_at>t').

Ordering and concurrency: the add_episode docstring says 'each episode is added sequentially and awaited before adding the next one'. There is no multi-episode transaction, no CAS on facts, no branch/fork primitive, and no merge. add_episode_bulk exists, and the docs claim it also resolves invalidations. add_triplet (direct fact insertion) still runs the LLM dedupe/contradiction step.
Communities: incremental single-step label propagation (a new node joins the plurality community of its neighbours). The paper admits this drifts and needs periodic full refresh.
implications_for_contextdb: Spec 9.2 #5/#7 adapter design. Build two Graphiti baselines and never mix them in one ranking (spec 9.2 last paragraph). (A) Graphiti-structural, for kernel comparison #5: write EntityEdge and EntityNode objects directly to Neo4j or FalkorDB with workload-supplied valid_at, invalid_at and expired_at. Implement 'revise D1' as invalidate-old plus insert-new with the same deterministic rule Graphiti uses. Implement dependency edges (Plan -[DEPENDS_ON]-> Decision) as ordinary RELATES_TO edges and do downstream invalidation as a Cypher BFS. This is the fair 'temporal graph backend' with an identical event stream. (B) Graphiti-native, for end-to-end #7: real add_episode, or a scripted 'oracle LLMClient' that answers the dedupe/contradiction prompts from workload ground truth. The oracle client separates storage and propagation cost from extraction quality and makes runs reproducible (spec 9.4). Then run (B) with a real LLM only for the end-to-end workflow, reporting tokens and dollar cost per write (spec 9.3 'semantic validator invocations / tokens').

Map ContextDB concepts onto Graphiti honestly. Revision = EntityEdge (immutable fact plus timestamps; but Graphiti mutates invalid_at and expired_at in place, so it is not append-only). Logical identity = (source, relation name, target) or entity, which is implicit and LLM-resolved, with no stable key and no CAS. SUPERSEDES = invalidation by timestamp, with no explicit supersedes edge stored. Provenance = edge.episodes. Epoch/snapshot = filter on created_at and expired_at (transaction time). Branch = separate group_id or graph copy (no copy-on-write). Mark WHY-transitive, alternative support, PENDING semantic state and certificates as 'not representable'.

Correctness tests to add, derived from observed Graphiti behaviour. (1) Missed downstream invalidation (spec T04/T06): D1 is revised, but the derived plan fact D3 is not contradicted textually, so Graphiti leaves D3 valid. Measure the missed-invalidation rate. (2) Retrieval-bounded invalidation: the contradicting fact ranks outside top-10, so there is no invalidation. Measure as workload size grows. (3) Retraction of the invalidator: remove the episode that caused invalidation and check whether the old fact is restored. Graphiti: no; ContextDB: head semantics must define this explicitly. Add a golden case. (4) Null valid_at facts are never invalidated. (5) Out-of-order arrival (late old fact): Graphiti expires the late edge itself. ContextDB's transaction-time head CAS should give a defined answer.

Bi-temporal lesson for spec 2.1/2.5. ContextDB's epoch is transaction time only. Graphiti shows agents need valid time too ('decided last week', 'effective from release 2.0'). Decide explicitly: either add an optional valid-time interval on Revision, orthogonal to the head-currency dimension in 2.5, or state 'transaction-time only' as a v0 non-goal. Never conflate 'head superseded' (T') with 'fact no longer true in the world' (T). Graphiti keeps the two clocks separate, and the spec's 'Head currency' dimension corresponds to T' only.

Provenance lesson for spec 2.6. Graphiti's edge.episodes is a de-duplicated source list, the kind of one-level support count that spec 2.6 warns about. Repeated mentions from the same source are merged by LLM dedupe, not counted. ContextDB should record Evidence identity (content hash plus source) so that 'independent support' is not inflated by duplicate ingestions of the same source.

Benchmark fairness (spec 9.4). The Zep paper's latency numbers include WAN latency to AWS for Zep but not for the baselines, and they measure retrieval only, not ingestion. For #5/#7, colocate Graphiti's DB on the same M1 Pro machine, pin the Neo4j or FalkorDB version and Graphiti 0.31.1, set SEMAPHORE_LIMIT, report ingestion (write) latency including LLM calls separately from read latency, and use identical event sequences. Report per-write LLM calls; Graphiti makes several (extraction, node dedupe, edge dedupe/contradiction, timestamps, summaries).

Novelty boundary (spec 1, 11). 'Temporal graph + provenance + invalidating outdated facts while keeping history' is already shipped by Graphiti and published (arXiv 2501.13956). ContextDB's paper must not frame invalidation-with-history as new. The differentiators to emphasise: invalidation by explicit typed dependency and justification structure (AND/OR, transitive, short-circuited by alternative support), not by LLM contradiction detection over retrieved neighbours; atomic multi-record transactions with CAS and read-set validation; and certified reads for action gating.
spec_gaps_or_errors: R15 cites only docs. Add the arXiv paper (Rasmussen et al., arXiv:2501.13956, Jan 2025) as the citable research source, and pin the Graphiti version and commit used for the baseline.

Spec 1 says Graphiti covers 'history'. True for valid/transaction-time history of individual facts, but there is no snapshot isolation or epoch-consistent read across a multi-fact commit. Ingestion is per-episode and non-transactional across episodes, with invalid_at and expired_at mutated in place. The spec should say so, so that a 'SNAPSHOT(epoch)' comparison is not presented as feature-equivalent.

Graphiti 'invalidation' is contradiction-driven (semantic, LLM-judged, among the top-k retrieved neighbours). ContextDB 'invalidation' is dependency-driven (structural). These are different problems with different failure modes: false or missed contradiction versus missed dependency extraction. The spec 9.3 metrics 'false invalidation rate / missed invalidation rate' need separate definitions for each, or the comparison is not like-for-like.

The Zep paper's evaluation does not test edge invalidation, provenance or bi-temporal queries directly (DMR plus LongMemEval QA accuracy only). The knowledge-update category even regressed with gpt-4o-mini (76.9% to 74.4%). There is no published evidence of invalidation precision or recall to compare against, so ContextDB must build that measurement itself.

Spec 9.2 #5 ('graph backend / temporal graph adapter, same semantics') is impossible to match exactly with Graphiti's public API, because add_triplet and add_episode always invoke the LLM. The spec should explicitly allow a direct-driver structural adapter plus an oracle LLM client, and document that deviation.
papers.reported_results: Paper (arXiv 2501.13956v1). DMR (500 conversations, about 60 messages each): Zep 94.8% vs MemGPT 93.4% (reported) and full-context 94.4% with gpt-4-turbo; Zep 98.2% vs full-context 98.0% with gpt-4o-mini. The authors themselves call DMR inadequate. LongMemEval_s (about 115k tokens per conversation): gpt-4o-mini 63.8% vs 55.4% full-context (+15.2% relative), latency 3.20 s vs 31.3 s; gpt-4o 71.2% vs 60.2% (+18.5% relative as stated), 2.58 s vs 28.9 s; average context 1.6k vs 115k tokens. Per-type: large gains on single-session-preference, temporal-reasoning and multi-session. Regressions on single-session-assistant (-9.06% 4o-mini, -17.7% 4o) and on knowledge-update with 4o-mini (-3.36%). MemGPT could not be run on LongMemEval. No ingestion cost, throughput, invalidation accuracy or provenance experiments. Experiments ran Dec 2024 to Jan 2025 from a laptop against Zep on AWS us-west-2.

extra_related_work: Git Context Controller (GCC), Wu et al., arXiv:2508.00031 (v1/v2; abs confirmed via search, not fully read): https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00031. Agent context as a git-like workspace with COMMIT/BRANCH/MERGE/CONTEXT operations over a .GCC/ directory. Together with Letta, this is prior art for git-style branching and merging of agent memory, so ContextDB cannot claim branching or merging itself as novel (spec 1, 5.3).

Dongxu Yang, 'Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting' / ForgetEval, arXiv:2606.15903 (abstract read): https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15903. A 385-case adversarial suite for supersede/release/purge operations plus a six-method Adapter Protocol for heterogeneous memory stores. Directly relevant to building fair adapters (spec 9.2) and to measuring missed and false invalidation. A search snippet claimed it includes a Graphiti adapter that maps 'supersede' onto edge invalidation, but the abstract does not mention Graphiti and I did not verify this in the repo.

Graphiti source code, github.com/getzep/graphiti, v0.31.1, commit 6e3e3cb (read): https://github.com/getzep/graphiti. The authoritative definition of the invalidation rules (graphiti_core/utils/maintenance/edge_operations.py, temporal_edge_utils.py) and remove_episode provenance counting (graphiti_core/graphiti.py). The paper's description is coarser and partly superseded (e.g. a late-arriving older fact now expires itself).

letta-code source, github.com/letta-ai/letta-code, v0.34.18, commit e8073d4 (read): https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code. src/agent/memory-worktree.ts (worktree branch letta/<label>/<id>; plain git merge, abort and discard on conflict), src/agent/memory-conflict-repair.ts (LLM subagent conflict repair with lease tokens), and skills managing-shared-memory / syncing-memory-filesystem (cross-agent shared repos, pull --rebase and retry). This is the real behaviour a #7 baseline must reproduce.

Dolt (DoltHub), a SQL database with git semantics, cell-level three-way merge and conflict tables: https://github.com/dolthub/dolt (from prior knowledge, not fetched this session). The strongest 'versioned database with branch/merge' baseline: structured merge rather than text merge, so it is fairer than git files for spec 5.3 merge semantics and 9.2 #5.

Bitemporal databases: Snodgrass, 'Developing Time-Oriented Database Applications in SQL' (1999); SQL:2011 system-versioned and application-time period tables; XTDB (https://xtdb.com). From prior knowledge, not fetched. These are the formal grounding for Graphiti's T/T' split that ContextDB should cite if it adds valid time to Revision (spec 2.1/2.5).

Lin et al., 'Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time', arXiv:2504.13171 (Letta; from prior knowledge, not fetched). The research basis for Letta's background reflection subagent, which is the asynchronous writer pattern that produces concurrent memory branches in R14.

issues.problem: The spec never says whether base_e(r) stays true after r is superseded. 2.4 defines base_e(r) as 'explicitly adopted as a valid input in the current branch at epoch e', which reads as tied to the head. 4.1 step 1 builds the oracle DAG 'from the branch's final head set and base facts', which implies superseded revisions drop out. 2.3, though, says only REQUIRES_CURRENT edges are invalidated by a head change, which implies a superseded revision keeps supporting things through SUPPORTS edges. The two readings give opposite S_e values for every rule over a superseded premise.
issues.evidence: Counterexample, intro scenario. D1@v1 is base; J2: D1@v1 -SUPPORTS-> D2@v1; J3: D1@v1 -SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY-> D3@v1. Commit head(D1) := v2. Reading A (base follows head): base(D1@v1)=false, so S(D2)=S(D3)=false and D3 becomes UNSUPPORTED. That contradicts 4.2 ('do not automatically declare it FALSE') and the 6 example JSON (structural SUPPORTED + PENDING). Reading B (base persists): S(D2)=true, D2 is CURRENT (D2's own head was never revised) and VerifiedAgainstHeads is vacuous (no semantic dependency), so Certified(D2)=true. The stale MongoDB schema stays actionable, which is exactly the failure from section 0. Implementers of the oracle and of the incremental engine could pick different readings and both 'pass' their own tests.
issues.proposed_resolution: Define base_e as head-independent: base_e(r) = r was asserted as a premise/assumption/evidence in branch b at or before e and has not been explicitly retracted. Supersession must not change base. All currency effects then flow only through currency_e(j,p) and Current_e. Rewrite 4.1 step 1 so the oracle includes every revision ever asserted in the branch, not just heads. Add golden test G-base: after supersession, a SUPPORTS-only consumer stays SUPPORTED, and its Certified value is whatever the rule in the next issue makes it.

issues.problem: currency_e(j,p) is never defined for each edge type, and the four edge 'types' mix two independent axes: whether the edge is a premise for structural support, and how a version change is treated. It is unclear whether SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY and HISTORICAL_REFERENCE edges are premises of j at all (and so appear in the AND of S_e), and whether an edge can be both SUPPORTS and REQUIRES_CURRENT. REQUIRES_CURRENT is also described as invalidating 'this support / validation certificate' without saying which one.
issues.evidence: Counterexample: J: {D1@v1 [SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY], X@v1 [SUPPORTS]} -> D3@v1, then head(D1) := v2. (a) If semantic edges are premises and currency(j,D1@v1) = [head(D1)=v1], S(D3) becomes false, which contradicts 4.2. (b) If they are premises with currency=true, a semantic edge to a revoked revision silently removes support, so semantic edges carry hidden structural force. (c) If they are not premises, S(D3) depends only on X, and the D1 edge has to live in a separate index that 3.3 does not list. Each choice gives a different oracle output for the same event log.
issues.proposed_resolution: Model each edge as (role ∈ {PREMISE, REFERENCE}) × (currency ∈ {PINNED, EXACT_CURRENT, SEMANTIC_RECHECK}). Only PREMISE edges enter S_e. currency_e(j,p) = [head_b(logical(p)) = p] for EXACT_CURRENT (the old REQUIRES_CURRENT), and true for PINNED and SEMANTIC_RECHECK. SEMANTIC_RECHECK affects only the semantic-validation dimension. REFERENCE edges (the old HISTORICAL_REFERENCE) affect neither S_e nor validation and are not in rules_by_premise. Put this table in 2.3 and add a separate index logical_id -> {(j,p) : EXACT_CURRENT} for head-flip propagation.

issues.problem: VerifiedAgainstHeads_e(r) is not defined as transitive, and a PENDING state does not propagate structurally. A deterministic consumer of a PENDING revision can therefore be CERTIFIED. The spec also does not say how REJECTED affects S_e, enabled_e(j), or consumers.
issues.evidence: Counterexample: D2@v1 has J2: D1@v1 [SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY] -> D2@v1. D3@v1 has J3: D2@v1 [SUPPORTS] -> D3@v1 and no edge to D1. Revise D1 to v2. D2 becomes PENDING (T15). S(D2) is unchanged, so S(D3)=true. D3 is CURRENT and has no semantic dependency of its own, so VerifiedAgainstHeads(D3) is true and Certified(D3)=true. The deployment plan built on the unrevalidated schema is actionable, even though 4.5 says STRICT reads must detect 'transitive dependencies are dirty'. Second case: a validator returns REJECTED for D2. Nothing in 2.4 makes S(D2) or S(D3) false, so D3 stays SUPPORTED and Certified.
issues.proposed_resolution: Define Certified recursively: Certified_e(r) = Current_e(r) ∧ S_e(r) ∧ LocallyVerified_e(r) ∧ Authorized_e(r) ∧ for some active justification j of r (or base), every premise p of j satisfies Certified_e(p) or is base evidence. An alternative that also works: define a derived 'Actionable' fixpoint over active justifications only. Make REJECTED either disable the justifications that depend on it (enabled_e(j)=false) or block certification, and pick one explicitly. Add golden test T15b (transitive PENDING blocks D3) and T15c (REJECTED blocks D3 but leaves its structural state unchanged).

issues.problem: Several expected results are disjunctive or underspecified, so they cannot be deterministic oracle tests. T06 says 'stale/pending' without fixing the edge type. T15 says 'rule references changed head ... PENDING', but a rule with REQUIRES_CURRENT on the changed head loses structural support (UNSUPPORTED/STALE), not PENDING. T07 asserts 'not current actionable proof' without naming the revision that claim applies to.
issues.evidence: T06 with REQUIRES_CURRENT gives Plan structural UNSUPPORTED, semantic unchanged, summary STALE. T06 with SEMANTIC_DEPENDENCY gives structural SUPPORTED, semantic PENDING, summary PENDING (matching the 6 JSON). These are different states, and an implementation returning either one passes the test as written. T07: the historical note N has base support, is CURRENT, and has no semantic dependency, so under 2.4 Certified(N)=true and N itself is actionable. 'Not actionable' can only refer to DB@v1 (SUPERSEDED) or to the HISTORICAL_REFERENCE edge contributing nothing, and the test does not say which.
issues.proposed_resolution: Split T06 into T06a (EXACT_CURRENT: Plan becomes UNSUPPORTED, summary STALE, WHY_NOT lists the superseded premise) and T06b (SEMANTIC_RECHECK: SUPPORTED + PENDING, actionable=false). Make T06c have the Plan with an alternative justification that does not touch DB: under EXACT_CURRENT it stays SUPPORTED. Restate T15 as SEMANTIC_RECHECK only. Restate T07 as five assertions: N's state is identical before and after the head switch; DB@v1 is SUPERSEDED and readable under HISTORICAL; the reference edge is not in rules_by_premise; IMPACT(DB) excludes N (or lists it as reference-only, explicitly); CERTIFIED_CURRENT never returns DB@v1.

issues.problem: The pseudocode propagates only premise-node state flips (S(P)) through rules_by_premise. Per-incidence satisfaction, however, is S(p) ∧ currency_e(j,p), and per-rule activity also depends on enabled_e(j). Head switches and rule enable/disable are not S flips, so they are missed. If they are bolted on as extra events, a premise whose S and currency both change in one batch gets counted twice.
issues.evidence: J: D1@v1 [REQUIRES_CURRENT] -> D3; D1@v1 is base. Batch 1: head(D1) := v2. S(D1@v1) does not flip (under the head-independent base), so changed_premises is empty and J stays active. That is a missed invalidation; the oracle says S(D3)=false. With naive extra events instead: batch with both 'retract base D1@v1' and 'head(D1) := v2'. The S-flip event decrements J.unsatisfied, and the currency-flip event decrements again, giving 2 for a 1-premise rule. A later batch restores only the base, the count goes to 1, and J stays inactive forever, even though the oracle says inactive (head is still v2), so the drift is hidden. Reverting the head later then leaves count 1 against an oracle value of 0, and D3 is wrongly UNSUPPORTED.
issues.proposed_resolution: Track a per-incidence bit sat(j,p) = S(p) ∧ currency(j,p), plus a per-rule enabled bit. In a batch, collect the touched incidences from three sources: S flips via rules_by_premise, head flips via the EXACT_CURRENT index, and rule enable flips. Recompute each touched sat bit once against its pre-transaction value and adjust unsatisfied by the net difference only. Define unsatisfied_premise_count = |{p : ¬sat(j,p)}| over canonicalized premises, and active(j) = enabled(j) ∧ unsatisfied=0. Add proptest generators that mix base, head and enable flips in the same batch.

issues.problem: The pseudocode contradicts itself. The loop adjusts each J 'for P's final state' and schedules conclusions immediately, then separately says 'process scheduled nodes in topological order'. In arbitrary order, P's final state is not known when P is first visited, and a node can be scheduled twice with opposite flips. The spec names this trap but gives no discipline that avoids it.
issues.evidence: J1: A -> B, J3: X -> B, J2: B -> C. A and X are base. Batch: retract base A, assert base X (X was previously not base). Processing A first: active_support_count[B] goes 1->0, B flips to false, B is scheduled, and J2 is decremented, so C flips to false and is scheduled. Then X: B goes 0->1, flips to true, is scheduled again, and J2 is incremented. C's net state is correct only if every intermediate flip is applied and undone exactly once. Any 'dedupe the schedule' optimisation, which the first line suggests, drops one of the two opposite B events and leaves J2's count off by one.
issues.proposed_resolution: Define the discipline. Option (a): process changed nodes from a priority queue keyed by topological rank, and finalise each node's S only after all its in-incidences are final (Gupta's delta rules: new values for already processed premises, old values for the rest). Each J is then adjusted at most once per premise per batch, by the net change sat_new - sat_old. Option (b): BPS two-phase, all OUT propagation first, then IN. State which option the oracle comparison relies on, and add the counterexample above as golden test T08b, with an assertion on counter values as well as on states.

issues.problem: It is unclear whether base_e(r) contributes to active_support_count. 2.6 says the count is the number of currently valid rules. S_e is base ∨ (some rule). 4.2's flip test 'conclusion support status flips' only works if base is folded in. The oracle in 4.1 has to compare counters, not only booleans (Gupta Thm 4.1), so the definition must be exact.
issues.evidence: C is base and has J: A -> C. Retract A. If base counts, the count goes 2->1 with no flip. If it does not count, the count goes 1->0 and the code must still check base before scheduling C. An implementation that schedules on count==0 marks C UNSUPPORTED while the oracle (S = base ∨ ...) says SUPPORTED. The counter-equality check also gives 1 against 0, depending on which convention each side used.
issues.proposed_resolution: Specify active_support_count = |{j : head(j)=r, active(j)}| (base excluded), store base as a separate bit, define S = base ∨ count>0, and make the oracle return both. Rename head(j) in the 2.4 formula to concl(j), so it does not collide with head(logical_id) used by REQUIRES_CURRENT.

issues.problem: Support, rules and premises are keyed by RevisionId (RuleHeader.conclusion, premises), but CURRENT/WHY/IMPACT and examples like 2.6 'D' are phrased per logical id. Several consequences go unstated. A revised conclusion D3@v2 does not inherit D3@v1's justifications. An EXACT_CURRENT rule over D1@v1 can never be satisfied by D1@v2. A positive validator verdict against D1@v2 has no defined way to restore structural support.
issues.evidence: D3@v1 has J: D1@v1 [REQUIRES_CURRENT] -> D3@v1. D1 is revised to v2 (a typo fix) and the validator confirms D3 still applies. J is permanently inactive, and nothing in the spec says whether the validator's ValidationRecord creates J': D1@v2 -> D3@v1, re-enables J, or requires a new revision D3@v2. CURRENT('deployment.plan') returns the head D3@v1 with UNSUPPORTED, and the semantic dimension cannot fix that.
issues.proposed_resolution: State in 2.1/2.4 that S_e, Certified_e and all counters are per RevisionId, and that the logical-level status reported by CURRENT is the status of head_b(l). Define the revalidation transition: a successful validation of r against new head versions commits, as one atomic Transition, a new justification (or rebinds an EXACT_CURRENT incidence to the new revision). Pick one and test it, for example T06d: revise D1, validate OK, and the plan becomes CERTIFIED again without a new plan revision.

issues.problem: The spec does not say whether REVISE may point a head back to an earlier RevisionId. It also does not say whether VerifiedAgainstHeads is a stateless function of current heads plus ValidationRecords, or a sticky flag set by eager PENDING marking (dirty_since). The two give different results after a revert.
issues.evidence: D3 was validated against D1@v1 (ValidationRecord keyed {D1:v1}). Epoch e1: head(D1)=v2, and eager marking sets D3 to PENDING (dirty_since=e1). Epoch e2: REVISE(D1, expected=v2, new=v1). Under a stateless version-vector check, D3 is VERIFIED again. Under sticky eager marking, D3 stays PENDING until it is revalidated. The oracle and the incremental engine diverge, and T13/T16 do not cover the case. If revert is instead forbidden and a new revision v3 with identical content is required, the old certificate stays invalid, which is a third behaviour.
issues.proposed_resolution: Decide and state: (1) whether heads may move to any previously committed revision of the same logical id. (2) VerifiedAgainstHeads_e(r) := there exists a ValidationRecord for r whose dependency version vector equals the current heads of r's SEMANTIC_RECHECK dependencies. This is stateless, and dirty_since is only a cache hint. Add golden test T16b, head v1->v2->v1, with the expected result chosen explicitly.

issues.problem: currency_e(j,p) = [head(l)=p] makes S_e depend on head pointers becoming different, which is an outlist (non-monotonic) condition in Doyle's terms. The kernel is well defined and polynomial only while head pointers and policies are base inputs that are never derived from justifications. The spec presents V0 as purely positive and states no such invariant. The 2.7 cycle check is also not specified as running at revision level or at logical level.
issues.evidence: If a later feature auto-promotes a head ('head(D1) := D1@v2 when S(D1@v2) ∧ verified'), and D1@v2 is supported by J: X@v1 [REQUIRES_CURRENT on X] -> D1@v2 while X's head is itself derived from D1, the system gets Doyle type-2/3 circularity (stable-model semantics, NP-complete per Elkan 1990), with no positive cycle visible in the premise graph. A smaller case: revision-level rules A@v1 -> B@v1 and B@v1 -> A@v2 are acyclic over revisions but cyclic over logical ids. The spec does not say whether 2.7 must reject this.
issues.proposed_resolution: Add an invariant to 2.4: heads, base, enabled and policy are base inputs set only by committed Transitions and are never conclusions of justifications. Reject any API that derives them, and add a test for that. State that the V0 DAG check runs over the revision-level premise->conclusion graph, and that logical-level cycles through different revisions are allowed. Add a golden test for the A@v1 -> B@v1 -> A@v2 case.

issues.problem: Structural UNKNOWN is undefined: in an eager V0, every revision is SUPPORTED or UNSUPPORTED outside staging. The mapping from the five orthogonal dimensions to CERTIFIED/PENDING/STALE/CONFLICTED/UNAVAILABLE has no precedence, and STALE is not tied to SUPERSEDED or to UNSUPPORTED. Certified_e also omits the principal and the branch, although Authorized and BRANCH_ONLY depend on them.
issues.evidence: A revision that is SUPERSEDED + SUPPORTED + PENDING + CONFLICTED could be summarised as STALE, PENDING or CONFLICTED. A revision that is CURRENT + UNSUPPORTED + VERIFIED could be STALE or UNAVAILABLE. Different adapters will disagree, and the 9.3 metrics 'stale action acceptance' and 'false invalidation' depend on which summary counts as stale.
issues.proposed_resolution: Define UNKNOWN as 'dirty / not yet recomputed in lazy mode', unreachable in V0 eager mode, and require STRICT reads to map it to PENDING. Give a total precedence, for example UNAVAILABLE(denied) > CONFLICTED > STALE(superseded or unsupported) > PENDING(semantic pending/unknown) > CERTIFIED, and parameterise as Certified_{b,e,principal}(r). Add one golden test per row of the precedence.

issues.spec_section: 4.2 (pseudocode: 'deduplicated premise state flips' + 'process scheduled nodes in topological order')
issues.problem: The pseudocode propagates each flip as soon as it happens, inside the loop. It also deduplicates the changed-node set. The topological-order line sits outside the loop, so it does not say that a node is propagated only after all its premises are final. Deduplication is safe only under that topological discipline, or when the event is the net delta (pre-transaction status vs final status). With FIFO or arbitrary processing plus set-dedup, a node that flips OUT and then IN within one batch propagates only its first (transient) flip, and the counters downstream end up wrong.
issues.evidence: Counterexample. Rules J1: A->C, J2: B->C, J3: C->D. Base {A}, so C and D are SUPPORTED. One transaction retracts base A and adds base B. Process A first: J1 becomes inactive, C's count goes 1->0, C flips OUT and is scheduled. Process C: J3's unsatisfied count goes 0->1, D flips OUT. Process B: J2 becomes active, C's count goes 0->1, C flips IN, but C is 'already in the deduplicated changed set' and is skipped. Final: D=UNSUPPORTED, oracle: D=SUPPORTED. Without dedup, pure event-by-event counter propagation is correct on a DAG (counter updates commute) but can propagate a node many times (Doyle's churn). The Gupta et al. 1993 delta rules (R3, Def 4.1: new versions for j<i, old for j>i) and R4's batch normalisation exist to give each rule instance exactly one net adjustment.
issues.proposed_resolution: State the discipline precisely. (1) Normalise the batch to net deltas: E- := (E- ∩ E) \ E+, E+ := E+ \ E (R4 Alg 2, line 21). (2) Record each touched node's pre-transaction status. (3) Pop nodes from a priority queue keyed by topological rank, so a node is popped only after every premise that can change in this batch is final. (4) When a node is popped, compare final status with its pre-transaction status, and propagate to rules_by_premise only if they differ, exactly once. Add golden test T08b (the counterexample above) and a property test that compares per-J unsatisfied counts and per-node active_support_count with the oracle, not just the boolean states.

issues.problem: In S_e(r), each premise literal is S_e(p) ∧ currency_e(j,p). The pseudocode seeds propagation only from 'premise state flips', which are flips of S(p), and finds consumers through rules_by_premise keyed by revision. A head switch L: v1->v2 leaves S(v1) unchanged in general, yet it flips currency for every J that has a REQUIRES_CURRENT edge to v1 (and to v2). Those J are never seeded. Also, if one transaction changes both currency and S(p) for the same premise, and the code treats them as two separate events, J's unsatisfied counter is adjusted twice.
issues.evidence: Missed seed: J: {DB@v1 (REQUIRES_CURRENT)} -> Plan. Base keeps DB@v1 supported. REVISE switches the head to v2 and S(DB@v1) does not change, so the pseudocode never revisits J, and Plan stays SUPPORTED, which contradicts T06. Double count: in one transaction, head switches v1->v2 AND base(v1) is retracted. The 'currency lost' event and the 'support lost' event each increment J.unsatisfied, giving +2. A later restore of only one of them leaves J permanently inactive (counter drift). An unsigned u32 counter can also wrap on the reverse sequence.
issues.proposed_resolution: Define the counted unit as the per-(J,p) literal sat(j,p) = S(p) ∧ (kind != REQUIRES_CURRENT ∨ head(logical(p)) = p). On each J, adjust by (old_sat - new_sat), computed once from the pre-transaction and final states. Add an index requires_current_by_logical[L] -> J list, or filter rules_by_premise by edge kind, and seed every J on that list for both the old and the new revision whenever head(L) changes. Use checked or debug-asserted counter arithmetic. Add golden tests for a head switch without a support change, and for a head switch combined with retraction of the same revision.

issues.spec_section: 4.2 (rule insertion / enable / disable in a batch)
issues.problem: Rule insertion, deletion and enable/disable change whether J is active without any premise flip, so the pseudocode never seeds them. If a new rule's counter is initialised from the final staged state and the rule is also placed in rules_by_premise before premise-flip processing, every premise that flips in the same batch is counted twice. Disabled rules are also unspecified: if propagation skips them, their unsatisfied counters go stale and re-enabling them gives wrong activity.
issues.evidence: Batch {add base A; insert J: A->C}. J's counter is initialised from the final state (A satisfied), so unsatisfied=0 and active=1. A's flip is then processed over rules_by_premise[A], which now contains J, and decrements the counter to -1 (wraps as u32). Rule insertion on an already-supported conclusion (count 1->2) correctly causes no flip only if status is defined as base(c) ∨ count(c)>0, and the spec never states that formula. Disable case: J disabled while A is OUT, propagation skips disabled J, A comes back IN, J is re-enabled with a stale unsatisfied=1, and C is wrongly UNSUPPORTED. BPS ch.9 (LTMS) keeps counts current even on satisfied or inactive clauses for exactly this reason.
issues.proposed_resolution: Specify the following. (a) Structural rule changes are applied first, and a new rule's counter is computed against the pre-batch state, then flows through the same net-delta processing. Equivalently, compute it against the final state when its topological rank is reached, and exclude it from premise-flip processing. (b) enabled(j) is treated as a virtual premise literal of J (Gupta-style base fact), so enable and disable are ordinary seeds. (c) Counters of disabled rules are always maintained, or recomputed in O(|premises|) on re-enable. (d) Node status is base(c) ∨ active_support_count(c)>0, and base flips are seeds. Add golden tests: insert a rule plus its premise in one batch; insert an alternative rule for an already-supported conclusion (no downstream visits); disable, flip a premise, then re-enable.

issues.spec_section: 2.7 V0 / 4.2 (cycle check cost and topological order maintenance)
issues.problem: Three gaps. The spec never says how the topological order that 4.2 relies on is obtained or kept up to date as rules are added. Its cycle check ('c reaches p' per premise) costs O(V+E) per premise per insert. And it leaves open which edges belong to the cycle-check graph. If disabled rules or rules with failed currency are left out of that graph, an enable or head switch can create a cycle without any write being checked. Checking a batch rule by rule, in arbitrary order, can also wrongly reject a batch whose final graph has no cycle.
issues.evidence: (1) In a 1M-revision graph, an alternative justification E->D added to an existing old revision D runs a full DFS, and a k-premise rule run naively costs k DFSs. One DFS from c that stops on any premise is sufficient. (2) A batch {delete J: A->B; insert J': B->A}, checked insert-first, reports CYCLE_DETECTED although the final graph is acyclic. (3) A disabled J: B->A is excluded from the graph; A->B is then inserted and passes; enabling J now creates a cycle that is never checked, which breaks the V0 'no cycles' invariant behind counter correctness (2.7, T11). (4) Self-loop {C}->C needs explicit rejection if reachability is not reflexive.
issues.proposed_resolution: (a) The cycle-check graph contains every non-deleted rule, regardless of enabled or currency status, so enable and head switches can never create a cycle. (b) Within a batch, apply rule deletions before insertions, then check each inserted rule against the staged graph. (c) Maintain a dynamic topological order with Pearce-Kelly (JEA 2006); see also Haeupler et al. TALG 2012 and Bender-Fineman-Gilbert-Tarjan TALG 2016. Inserting edge p->c with ord[p] < ord[c] costs O(1). Otherwise, search only the affected region ord[c]..ord[p], forward from c and backward from p; a cycle exists if and only if the forward search reaches p. The same structure therefore gives both the cycle check and the rank used by the 4.2 priority queue. (d) Note the common case: a rule whose conclusion is a revision created after all its premises already respects creation-id order, so revision-id order is a good initial ord and most inserts cost O(1). Only rules that conclude pre-existing revisions trigger reordering. (e) Report cycle-check and reorder cost as a separate benchmark metric (9.3), and use the ord values after all structural changes of the batch.

issues.spec_section: 2.4 / 2.5 / 4.1 (definition of base_e(r) relative to head currency)
issues.problem: The spec does not define whether superseding a head removes base_e(old revision). That choice determines the seed set of a REVISE and whether SUPPORTS-only dependents of a superseded revision stay supported. The incremental algorithm and the oracle may resolve it differently, and all T06-style results depend on it.
issues.evidence: J: {DB@v1 (SUPPORTS)} -> Plan. REVISE DB v1->v2. If base is tied to head, S(DB@v1) flips OUT and Plan loses support. If it is not tied, Plan stays SUPPORTED, and only REQUIRES_CURRENT edges invalidate. 2.4 says only 'explicitly adopted as valid input in the current branch', which is ambiguous on this point.
issues.proposed_resolution: Make base_e(r) an explicit base input that is independent of heads: adoption, evidence, assumption enabled. Express currency only through REQUIRES_CURRENT literals. Or, if base implies head, state that and list REVISE's seeds as {base(v1) off, base(v2) on, currency flips}. Encode the choice identically in the oracle (4.1) and add a golden test for a SUPPORTS-only dependent of a superseded revision.

issues.problem: currency_e(j,p) holds only while no other revision is head of logical(p). That is an absence condition, i.e. an outlist in Doyle's terms. The V0 kernel stays positive (counter-maintainable, unique least model) only if heads, policies and enabled flags are base inputs that are never derived from justifications. The spec does not state this invariant.
issues.evidence: If a later feature derives heads, e.g. 'auto-promote revision when its support is SUPPORTED', a rule can make its own premise's head change, and you get Doyle (R1) type-2/3 circularities. NM-TMS labelling is NP-complete (Elkan 1990), and counters stop being sound.
issues.proposed_resolution: Add the invariant 'heads, enabled(j), policies and base are never conclusions of justifications', and treat these inputs as a lower stratum. Reject at write time any rule whose conclusion is a head pointer or flag, and add a test that expects that rejection.

issues.spec_section: T09 / 3.2 rule_arena (duplicate premise canonicalisation with typed edges)
issues.problem: 'Canonicalize or reject' leaves open how to merge a revision that appears twice with different edge kinds. It also leaves open how to handle two revisions of the same logical id that are both REQUIRES_CURRENT, and identical hyperedges submitted as different RuleIds. All three affect counter correctness or how the oracle compares counts.
issues.evidence: J lists DB@v1 as SUPPORTS and also as REQUIRES_CURRENT. Deduplicating by (rev, kind) keeps two entries in rules_by_premise[DB@v1], so one S flip decrements J twice. Deduplicating by rev while keeping the first kind silently drops the currency requirement. J requiring DB@v1 and DB@v2 both current can never be satisfied. Two identical {A}->C rules give count 2, which an oracle that deduplicates hyperedges reports as 1.
issues.proposed_resolution: Canonicalise at insert: sort premises by revision and deduplicate by revision, keeping the strongest kind (REQUIRES_CURRENT > SUPPORTS). Reject rules with two REQUIRES_CURRENT premises of the same logical id. Explicitly either deduplicate identical (premise set, conclusion) rules or define support_count as counting RuleIds, and make the oracle match.

issues.spec_section: 4.2 / 4.4 / 3.2 RuntimeState (V1 recursion needs more than one counter)
issues.problem: 4.4 plans a 'DRed/B/F/Counting hybrid' for V1, but RuntimeState has a single active_support_count. Under cycles, a single count reproduces the self-support bug of 2.7. R4's DRed^c needs two counters per node, C_nr and C_r, plus a per-justification recursive bit. In ContextDB those must be reclassified as SCCs merge and split dynamically, which R4 never handles because it assumes a static stratification.
issues.evidence: Motik et al. AIJ 2019, Example 5: after naive counting on R(x,y)->R(y,x) and deletion of R(a,b), R(a,b) and R(b,a) keep supporting each other. R4 Example 3 gives a ground golden test (counters a(1,0) b(1,0) c(0,2) d(1,1) e(0,1); delete A(a); final c(0,1) d(1,1) e(0,1)). Inserting a justification can merge SCCs and turn other justifications from nonrecursive to recursive.
issues.proposed_resolution: Reserve layout space now: cnr (base plus justifications whose premises all lie in earlier SCCs) and cr (justifications with a premise in the same SCC), plus a per-rule recursive flag. In DAG regions cr is always 0, so the algorithm is exactly the V0 counter algorithm (pay-as-you-go). For V1, list dynamic SCC/topological-order maintenance with counter reclassification as an open problem. A sound fallback is coarse conservative 'cycle regions'. Change the V1 oracle to least-fixpoint forward chaining from base only, emitting (cnr, cr) for property tests of R4's Theorem 1 invariant.

issues.spec_section: 4.2 batch-trap paragraph / 11 contribution 2 (prior art for the counter algorithm)
issues.problem: The spec presents exact batch delta counting as a later optimisation ('first staged + affected topological recomputation, then exact delta counters') and claims 'incremental maintenance algorithm with correct alternative-support handling' as a contribution. The V0 algorithm (per-rule unsatisfied counter, per-conclusion support counter, flip-only propagation in stratum order) is already published and proved.
issues.evidence: Gupta-Mumick-Subrahmanian 1993 (R3): Counting with the set-semantics Statement (2), Thm 4.1, RSN ordering. BPS (Forbus & de Kleer 1993), Exercise 7.5, and the LTMS pvs/sats counters. Dowling-Gallier 1984: linear-time Horn propagation with per-clause counters. Doyle 1979 (R1): forward and reverse justification indexes. The spec also never says support_count is the set-semantics count (number of active rule instances) rather than Gupta's duplicate-semantics derivation count, which grows exponentially on DAGs.
issues.proposed_resolution: Cite R3 Def 4.1 / Thm 4.1, BPS Ex 7.5 and Dowling-Gallier as the source of the V0 algorithm. State that support_count = number of active justifications (set semantics). Restrict contribution 2 to the versioned currency literals, dynamic topological order inside staged transactions, native layout and measured costs.

issues.problem: The novelty boundary says the publishable contribution is 'correct multi-support/recursive maintenance'. That algorithmic core is old prior art, so it cannot carry a systems paper. The paragraph also never names the closest 2026 competitors.
issues.evidence: (1) AND unsatisfied-counter, OR support-counter and flip-only propagation are Gupta et al. 1993 Counting with the set-semantics Statement (2) [R3]. The same scheme is BPS ch.7 Exercise 7.5 and the LTMS pvs/sats counters, and Dowling-Gallier 1984 Horn propagation. (2) Correct maintenance of recursive positive Datalog with alternative support and no self-support is DRed^c/B/F^c [R4], plus Motik et al. AIJ 2019 (recursive counting, FBF, optimality Def. 26). (3) DD [R5] maintains this exact S_e semantics (least fixpoint, OR support, deletions). The readers' prototype got 0 mismatches against the oracle over 2400 epochs, and DBSP did too after the #7284 fix. (4) Forward and reverse justification indexes are Doyle 1979's SL-JUSTIFICATIONS/CONSEQUENCES and the JTMS justs/consequences slots.
issues.proposed_resolution: Rewrite the boundary and §11 claim 2 so they explicitly concede counting, DRed/B/F and recursive IVM as prior art, citing R3, R4, Motik 2019, BPS ch.7 and Dowling-Gallier. Then name the deltas that can be defended: (a) versioned head-currency semantics (REQUIRES_CURRENT) layered into support maintenance; (b) multi-key, snapshot-consistent, dependency-scoped certificates combined with transitive derived state; (c) maintenance whose cost does not depend on depth, with a compact native layout, measured against tuned DD/DBSP; (d) V1 dynamic-SCC ground maintenance, which R4 does not cover because its stratification is static. Name MemTX, PACMI, PlanFence, Graphiti and Letta in the paragraph.

issues.problem: H2 frames its benefit as lower false invalidation from keeping OR-alternative support. Against any correct IVM baseline (DD, DBSP, DRed) the false-invalidation rate is identically 0. Against no-alternative baselines (MemTX BFS revoke, PACMI max-join) the advantage holds by construction. So the false-invalidation side of H2 is either trivial or unfalsifiable. Whether it matters in practice also depends on how common OR support is in real agent graphs, and the spec never measures that.
issues.evidence: MemTX code revokes every transitive descendant regardless of alternative parents. PACMI's Algorithm 1 uses 'stronger state wins' over paths with no counting, and its dataset has only fixed 2-hop single-path chains; the authors list confluence and branching as untested (App. J). DD and DBSP produce the oracle's outputs exactly, which the readers' randomized check confirmed.
issues.proposed_resolution: Split H2 into two parts. H2a, effectiveness: the false-invalidation rate and the avoided semantic-validator calls versus MemTX-style BFS-revoke and PACMI-style typed-BFS max-lattice, reported as a function of measured multi-support prevalence. H2b, efficiency: update cost versus correct IVM (DD, DBSP, JTMS two-phase), measured in rule evaluations beyond the optimal set instr[I] Δ instr[I'] plus latency. Add a workload-characterization step: measure the distribution of OR-alternative justifications per node in real traces (MemTrace DeepSWE receipts, MemTX/PACMI suites) before treating the 'multi-support' shape as representative.

issues.problem: H3, that pre-action version certificates reduce stale-plan execution with measurable overhead, has already been demonstrated. Exact-version, dependency-scoped action-time validation is PlanFence's main contribution. MemTX already ships action gating with five isolation levels, including causally-stable-read. S-Bus already does read-set validation for agents. As written, H3 does not separate ContextDB from these systems.
issues.evidence: PlanFence (R10 v2) defines observation versus derivation currency and proves frontier invariance and conditional soundness (Proposition 1). It reports 30/30 stale acts for owner-head freshness against 30/30 completions for PlanFence, and gives a cost model with crossover rho*. MemTX's gate is global and existential. Its 'supersede_old' does not cascade, and has_pending_invalidation checks only the revoked set. S-Bus (arXiv 2605.17076) does declared read-set OCC.
issues.proposed_resolution: Restate H3 against PlanFence, MemTX and S-Bus. The deltas: (a) a multi-key certificate taken from one epoch snapshot, which PlanFence explicitly does not provide; (b) the certificate covers transitively maintained derived state, so an OR alternative avoids the replan that PlanFence would force on any leaf-ID mismatch; (c) structural invalidation and semantic PENDING are separated, where PlanFence treats every mismatch as a replan; (d) supersession triggers currency invalidation, where MemTX cascades only on revocation. Adopt PlanFence's terminology and its recorded-input contract (Assumption 1). Add golden tests that only these deltas can pass: a plan that keeps an alternative justification after D1 is revised; D1@v1 superseded while D2/D3 are still committed under MemTX semantics; the same key reached at two versions through different branches, which must block.

issues.problem: The baseline list leaves out every closest competitor and pushes the strongest correct-IVM baseline to v1/v2. Without these baselines, H2 and H3 cannot be evaluated credibly.
issues.evidence: Missing: PACMI typed-BFS max-lattice (R9), MemTX BFS revoke-all-descendants with its global action gate (R8), PlanFence leaf frontier validation (R10), S-Bus read-set validation, JTMS support-pointer with two-phase retraction (BPS ch.7, the classic cycle-safe competitor), and an ATMS/minimal-support-set label variant (R2). The readers already built a DD baseline on the local Rust 1.95 toolchain, so treating DD as v1/v2 work is not justified by effort.
issues.proposed_resolution: Make these kernel baselines mandatory for v0: full recompute; naive BFS plus recompute; MemTX-style revoke-all (named instance of #4); PACMI-style max-lattice BFS; JTMS two-phase support-pointer; DD (both encodings, tuned workers/batch, arrangement reuse); native counters. Make these certification baselines mandatory: PlanFence frontier check, MemTX gate, S-Bus read-set OCC, and Git blob-OID depends_on frontmatter. Add an explicit rule that every external baseline must pass the same per-epoch oracle harness. The harness found dbsp 0.349.0 wrong on 117-118/2400 epochs because of Feldera bug #7284.

issues.problem: 'Faithful reproduction according to available libraries' is too vague, and specific library and version traps already apply.
issues.evidence: differential-dataflow 0.25.1 and timely 0.31 build on Rust 1.95. Every dbsp release newer than 0.349.0 needs rustc ≥1.96.1, and 0.349.0 has the recursive-join bug fixed upstream in PR #7284 (merged 2026-09-29). DDlog has been archived since 2023. ascent, crepe and datafrog are not incremental.
issues.proposed_resolution: Pin the baselines in the spec: DD 0.25.1 with both encoding A (prefix chain, pure positive Datalog) and encoding B (count inside iterate). For DBSP, either bump the toolchain to a release that contains #7284 or backport the fix, and document which. Use ascent or crepe only as 'full recompute in Datalog'. List DDlog as unmaintained.

issues.problem: The research question compares only against 'record-, graph-, or replay-oriented baselines' and leaves out general IVM engines, the strongest class. H1 compares against a 'generic object pointer graph', which is not in §9.2 and is a weak comparison point. Its framing (forward and reverse indexes) is 1979 prior art.
issues.evidence: Doyle 1979 and BPS jtms.lsp store the forward and reverse dependency indexes natively. Measured DD costs scale with the number of fixpoint rounds a change crosses: about 35-70 µs per round, a 100K-deep chain root flip taking about 3.6-7.6 s, while a leaf flip stays at about 0.1-0.5 ms. DBSP latency grows with maximum DAG depth even for leaf updates. The advantage is therefore expected on deep and hub shapes and to be weak on shallow, modular ones.
issues.proposed_resolution: Add 'general incremental view maintenance (DD/DBSP)' to the research question. Recast H1 as: the same counter algorithm on (a) a HashMap/petgraph pointer graph, (b) DD arrangements, and (c) the native packed layout, isolating layout effects in bytes per premise incidence, cache misses and latency. Report results per shape statistic (depth, fanout, alternative-proof count), and state ahead of time that gains are expected only on deep or hub shapes, to avoid charges of cherry-picking (spec §9.4).

issues.problem: The metrics are not defined precisely enough to compare with prior work, and several standard measures are missing.
issues.evidence: PACMI App. B defines OI, UI, AR and Recall@Depth formally. R4 and Motik 2019 Def. 26 define optimality as instr[I] Δ instr[I']. Doyle §9 names 'churn', meaning nodes that are reset and then restored. MemTX scores trap-and-control pairs so that blanket refusal cannot score. PlanFence counts 'Gap', the input change between validation and the effect, as a TOCTOU measure. CoMemBench defines VHS and ICS. Graphiti invalidation is contradiction-driven, not dependency-driven, so a single 'false invalidation rate' conflates two different failure modes.
issues.proposed_resolution: Define false and missed invalidation using PACMI's OI/UI/AR formulas, with separate definitions for dependency-driven and contradiction-driven systems. Add: excess rule evaluations over the optimal set; churn (transient resets with unchanged final status); stale-action acceptance reported together with the legitimate-action allow rate; the TOCTOU Gap count; Remat, Remat-1C and Remat-2C counter-overhead baselines; and for end-to-end runs, VHS, ICS and tokens per verified node.

issues.problem: The claim that the data model 'separates structural support from semantic currency' overlaps prior work, and the spec gives no example that competitors cannot express.
issues.evidence: PlanFence formalizes observation versus derivation currency. MemTX distinguishes revocation from quarantine-for-rebuild through typed repair. R7 GEM/MemState splits EXTENSION from ASSOCIATION edges and uses flag_for_revision instead of marking dependents false, which is the same idea as PENDING. PACMI keeps needs-verification separate from superseded and historical-only, though in one lattice. Graphiti keeps valid time T separate from transaction time T'.
issues.proposed_resolution: Argue orthogonality with concrete states that competitors' single enums or lattices cannot represent, for example CURRENT + SUPPORTED + PENDING, or SUPERSEDED head with SUPPORTED derived state. Turn each into a golden test. Decide explicitly whether Revision carries valid time (Graphiti, SQL:2011) or whether the system is transaction-time only, and state it.

issues.problem: ContextDB is a centralized lineage store. PlanFence evaluates exactly this architecture as a losing baseline, and the spec does not respond.
issues.evidence: In PlanFence's replay at rho=4 over an AT&T LTE trace, centralized lineage stalled 508.6 ms per action against PlanFence's 230.8 ms, and used 15.6 KiB against 8.1 KiB.
issues.proposed_resolution: Either limit claims to co-located or single-site deployments where the store is in-process, or report certification latency under PlanFence's emulated-link setting with the same rho sweep {0.25, 1, 4, 16}. Note that PlanFence excludes local processing from its stall numbers, so an in-memory Rust result cannot be compared directly.

issues.problem: V1 plans 'least fixed point + SCC / DRed or B/F', but RuntimeState has a single active_support_count, which cannot express the correct hybrid. The spec also misses the one technically new problem in this area: SCCs that change dynamically under justification inserts and deletes.
issues.evidence: R4 DRed^c needs two counters per fact (C_nr and C_r) and a recursive/nonrecursive classification per rule. A single count reproduces the self-support bug (Motik 2019 Example 5). R4 assumes a static program stratification. In ContextDB's ground graph, adding a justification can merge SCCs and reclassify rules. The M0 per-insert reachability check is also O(V+E) worst case.
issues.proposed_resolution: Specify cnr and cr per node plus a 'recursive' bit per justification, so that DAG regions reduce exactly to the v0 counters. Name dynamic SCC and topological-order maintenance with counter reclassification as a candidate novelty, citing Pearce-Kelly 2006 and Bender-Fineman-Gilbert-Tarjan 2016. Add the golden test: base X, X→A, A→B, B→A, revoke X, expecting A and B both UNSUPPORTED. Use DD as the V1 cycle baseline.

issues.problem: The correctness bar of 10,000 random seeds compared on booleans is weaker than what the closest competitor already reports, and boolean comparison can hide counter drift.
issues.evidence: MemTX ran bounded exhaustive enumeration over 5,530,160 canonical states and 10,537,260 transitions with 0 violations, plus 10k random traces. Gupta Theorem 4.1 and R4 Theorem 1 state counter-compatibility invariants that booleans may not reveal for many epochs.
issues.proposed_resolution: Have the oracle emit exact counters (unsatisfied_premise_count, active_support_count, and later cnr/cr) and compare them every epoch. Add bounded exhaustive checking of small graphs (for example ≤5 revisions, ≤3 rules, depth ≤10 commits) with symmetry reduction, alongside proptest.

issues.problem: Failure modes that competitors found empirically, and that apply directly to ContextDB's design, are absent.
issues.evidence: MemTX reports retry escape: a correctly aborted stale write passes when retried in a fresh transaction. It also reports that undeclared transcription provenance defeats every method. Letta's textual git merge silently produces a stale D2 when the branch depended on D1@v1 and main revised D1. MemTX allows partial commit and does not prevent cross-record write skew.
issues.proposed_resolution: Add these risks: retry escape (CAS prevents lost updates but not an informed overwrite), undeclared dependencies (the guarantees depend on declared justifications), and semantic merge skew. Add golden tests T19 (write skew: two plans each read A and B and write different keys), T20 (merge skew must return CONFLICT or PENDING), and T21 (certificate frontier with an ambiguous version must block).

issues.problem: The v0 kernel is presented as purely positive, but REQUIRES_CURRENT depends on the absence of a superseding head, which is an outlist (non-monotonic) condition. It stays safe only if heads are never derived.
issues.evidence: Doyle 1979 SL justifications treat this as an outlist condition. Elkan 1990 shows NM-TMS labeling is NP-complete, and Doyle's type-2/3 circularities arise once outlists exist.
issues.proposed_resolution: State the stratification invariant that heads and policies are base inputs and are never derivable from justifications. Add a test that tries to create a derived head (for example 'auto-promote if verified') and expects rejection.

issues.problem: The spec says ATMS-style environments 'avoid exhaustive environment explosion' and groups them with negation and defaults. Both statements are inaccurate.
issues.evidence: McAllester AAAI-90 shows ATMS labels can need exponential time and space even for acyclic Horn clauses. The basic ATMS (de Kleer 1986) is monotone Horn plus nogoods, the same logic class as V0. Defaults come from the separate 'Extending the ATMS' paper.
issues.proposed_resolution: Rewrite as: 'labels can be exponential (McAllester 1990); WHAT_IF and branch labels need focusing or bounds (Forbus & de Kleer AAAI-88)'. Move the ATMS out of the negation group, and add a minimal-support-set label variant as an H2 ablation.

issues.problem: Eager/lazy hybrid maintenance is presented without prior art, even though both extremes and the conflict-must-be-eager invariant already exist in the literature.
issues.evidence: de Kleer 1986 §6 suggests lazy label update with backward 'update' messages while keeping contradiction labels eager. 'Focusing the ATMS' (AAAI-88) bounds work through focus environments. MemTrace is the lazy, read-time-validation extreme in practice.
issues.proposed_resolution: Cite these works. Use MemTrace-style read-time validation as the lazy baseline for H4. Add the invariant that conflict detection stays eager even when support maintenance is lazy.

issues.problem: The benchmark claim overlaps existing suites. Its novel part should be stated as the live-revision cascades at scale that existing suites do not cover.
issues.evidence: PlanFence provides stale-plan race workloads (rho, keyspace, scope d, updates during replanning). MemTX publishes 90- and 56-case JSON suites with 24 downstream episodes. CoMemBench injects a single static polluted artifact, has no live mid-workflow revision cascades, and works at small scale (MemTX cases have 1-4 turns; MemTrace has about 100 traces per task).
issues.proposed_resolution: Scope contribution 4 to live revision cascades with OR support at 10K-1M revisions, calibrated on MemTrace statistics (about 34 revisions per task, about 5.6 invalidations per revision, 57% exposure). Reuse the PlanFence, MemTX and CoMemBench suites as external conformance checks instead of claiming a benchmark built from scratch.

issues.problem: The reading list has outdated or incomplete citations and is missing prior art the novelty claims rely on.
issues.evidence: R10's v2 title is 'Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Derivation Currency for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory'. R15 should cite arXiv:2501.13956 (Rasmussen et al.) and pin Graphiti v0.31.1. R6 should also cite open-access PVLDB 16(7) 2023. R14 is dated 2026-02-12, and cross-agent sharing appears only in letta-code source. Missing entirely: Forbus & de Kleer, Building Problem Solvers (1993); McAllester AAAI-90; Motik et al. AIJ 2019; Shared Arrangements PVLDB 2020; GCC arXiv 2508.00031; S-Bus 2605.17076; Dowling-Gallier 1984.
issues.proposed_resolution: Update the citations and add the missing works to §1 and §12, so the related-work comparison covers the closest prior work.

scores.angle: Design 1: correctness first (pure-function InputState->DerivedState, Jacobi oracle, three-layer L0/L1/L2 fixpoints)
scores.notes: Strongest semantics. Every blocker gets one decision: head-independent base (SD1), role x currency edges (SD2), per-incidence sat bits that make refresh idempotent (SD3), disabled rules kept in the cycle graph and still maintained (SD4/SD5). The three positive fixpoints L0 ⊆ L1 ⊆ L2 make transitive PENDING and REJECTED exact, and the oracle can check them, which is the cleanest fix for T15b/T15c. The oracle uses a different algorithm (Jacobi from all-false) over an independent InputModel, and the two are compared on exact counters plus a canonical witness. Flaws: (1) sem(j) and ValidationRecord are keyed per rule, not per revision. Two rules concluding the same revision each need their own validation, and it is unclear how a validator verdict on a revision maps onto rules. (2) The 'author-attested vector A(j) = Sem premise revisions' means a freshly added rule over a non-head Sem premise starts PENDING. That is probably intended but should be stated. (3) Certified checks Current only at the top revision, so a Pin edge to a superseded decision still certifies, which recreates the section-0 failure if agents misuse Pin. The design only documents this. (4) NaiveTopo does a full Kahn recompute per batch in M0, which is acceptable only because M0 reads come from the oracle. (5) cur_by_logical seeds every Cur incidence on any revision of l. That is correct but over-seeds. (6) The exhaustive alphabet (about 20 ops at depth 8) is feasible only with state dedup, and the plan assumes it works. (7) cargo-mutants with 'every mutant killed' is an expensive gate for M1. Research weakness: no baselines, no DD, no H1/H2 measurement anywhere in M0-M3, and benchmarks are pushed to M5. It is an excellent kernel spec but does not yet support a paper.

scores.angle: Design 2: performance first, native layout (SoA, CSR + delta postings, stamped shadow arrays, Pearce-Kelly from M0b)
scores.notes: The core propagation is sound: rank heap keyed by PK ord, FRESH-rule initialisation from final premises, compare against the pre-batch published S. Head-flip seeding through exact_by_rev covers both the old and new revision. Concrete flaws: (1) Moving DeleteRule ops to the front of a batch breaks ops that refer to rule ids allocated earlier in the same batch, and it changes op semantics in ways the oracle has to copy exactly (common-mode risk). (2) Physical deletion removes edges from the cycle graph while tombstoned rules remain in postings, so every iteration needs a deleted check. That is fine, but it adds compaction and tombstone state for little gain in V0. (3) SD11/SD12 semantics are underspecified. The ValidationRecord dep vector covers 'exactly those logicals', but which rule's Sem logicals, when a revision has several active rules? Semantic(r)=NOT_REQUIRED as soon as any active rule lacks Sem premises can hide a REJECTED path, so the REJECTED and NOT_REQUIRED precedence is ambiguous. (4) Actionable is computed only on read and has no oracle-level equality. (5) KernelSnapshot omits the per-incidence sat bits even though the design claims exact counter comparison. (6) Pin to a superseded premise certifies, the same risk as Design 1. Implementability: StampedVec shadows, a chunked delta-tier CSR with compaction, a 64-bit dedup hash index, and a 14 B/incidence target, all within 'days 1-10', is premature optimisation before correctness is established. The stamp-wrap and compaction tail-latency risks are self-inflicted. Research: good H1 isolation (pointer_graph and vecvec_layout run the same algorithm), MemFootprint, a rich CommitReport (excess over optimal = reevaluated - flipped), PK cost counters, a DD baseline in M1.5, and faithful MemTX/PACMI-style baselines. H3 and certification baselines are only sketched.

scores.angle: Design 3: paper first (one front-end, swappable Maintainer modes incl. faithful RevokeAll/TypedMaxLattice ablations, policy-eval harness)
scores.notes: The best fit for H1-H3. All modes share one transaction front-end (canonicalisation, CAS, cycle check, net-delta), so results differ only in propagation policy. Ablations are traceable to MemTX dependency_graph.py and PACMI Algorithm 1, include a 'fixed' variant, and are evaluated with warm-start policy-eval, which answers the strawman critique. Metrics include PACMI OI/UI/AR, excess over optimal, JTMS churn, and FI vs p_alt; the H2a/H2b split and D1-D4 differentiation tests are well done. The semantics are mostly sound, and the counting algorithm matches Designs 1 and 2. Flaws: (1) It is internally inconsistent: a new rule is 'unsat = n+1' while flags=ENABLED, and the virtual enabled literal should give n. (2) The idempotent dedup in SD3 returns an existing RuleId even when that rule is disabled, so the AddRule silently has no effect. It should either re-enable the rule or return DuplicateRule. (3) SD13 makes a PINNED edge to any superseded non-Evidence revision block certification. That is safer than Designs 1 and 2, but PINNED then differs from EXACT_CURRENT only structurally, and CertOK for SEMANTIC_RECHECK requires Certified(head(logical(p))), a cross-revision dependency the oracle has to mirror exactly. (4) Certification is computed on read through a memo, with only a 'cert_bruteforce' oracle and no layered fixpoint definition like Design 1's L1/L2, so T15b/T15c rest on a recursive definition that is harder to check by property tests. (5) ValidationRecord is keyed by (rev, vector restricted to j's Sem logicals), which mixes rule-scoped and revision-scoped keys. (6) Witness-closure certificates make certification cost depend on depth (acknowledged). Implementability: six maintainers, three ReverseIndex impls, a harness, a checker, and generators in a 4-week M1 is heavy. The generic Maintainer::apply<impl ReverseIndex> plus Mode-enum dispatch needs care in Rust. M2 chunked MVCC means redesigning the undo-log engine (acknowledged).

best_ideas_to_graft: Take Design 1's three positive fixpoint layers (L0=S, L1 gate sem!=Rejected, L2 gate sem in {Verified, NotRequired} plus a conflict node gate) as the normative definition of transitive PENDING/REJECTED. Have the Jacobi oracle emit all three layers so certification is oracle-checked, instead of Design 3's recursive on-read CertOK.

Take Design 1's independent InputModel (BTreeMap op application that shares no code with txn.rs) together with exact comparison of sat/unsat/active/support/witness every epoch. Also take its proptest coverage counters with hard thresholds (head+base flips on the same revision, alternative-support saves, cycle rejections, CAS conflicts), so the generators cannot silently test nothing.

Take Design 1's append-only rules (disable rather than delete) plus a cycle graph that includes disabled rules. This removes Design 2's deletion-hoisting and tombstone complexity, and PK insert-only maintenance is enough.

Take Design 3's Maintainer trait and shared front-end, with Counting/FullRecompute/NaiveBfs/JtmsTwoPhase as correct modes and RevokeAll{cascade_on_supersede}/TypedMaxLattice as faithful ablations run under warm-start policy-eval, plus FI/MI/OI/UI/AR, excess over optimal, churn and FI vs p_alt.

Take Design 2's layout-isolation baselines (the same counter algorithm on a HashMap pointer graph and on Vec<Vec>), its exact MemFootprint in bytes per incidence, its CommitReport fields (incidences_visited, rules_reevaluated - rules_flipped, PK fast inserts / edges scanned / reorders), and its 'paranoid' feature that cross-checks against naive recompute every commit.

Resolve the ValidationRecord keying explicitly: key by (conclusion revision, the sorted vector of current heads over the union of Sem logicals in its rules), or per rule as in Design 1, and choose one. Make AddRule on a duplicate of a disabled rule return DuplicateRule{existing, enabled:false} rather than silently reusing it.

Decide the Pin-to-superseded certification question deliberately. Design 3's stricter choice (block unless the premise is immutable Evidence) is safer against the section-0 failure. Encode it as an L2 gate (Current(p) required for non-Evidence Pin premises) so it stays inside the oracle-checked fixpoint.

Freeze a versioned EventLog with client-local RevRef::New(u16) ids (Design 3) early, so DD 0.25.1 (encodings A/B) and later DBSP with the #7284 fix replay identical logs through the same per-epoch oracle harness.

Postpone Design 2's StampedVec shadows and CSR+delta postings until after M1 correctness. Introduce them as ReverseIndex/staging implementations behind Design 3's layout knob and measure them as an H1 ablation.
judgements.winner: Design 3 (paper first) as the skeleton, with Design 1's semantics core grafted in: L0/L1/L2 layered fixpoints, the independent InputModel oracle, append-only rules and coverage-gated property tests. Design 1 is the most correct, but it cannot answer H1-H3 by itself. Design 2's layout work should become a later H1 ablation, not the M0 foundation.

scores.angle: Correctness-first (SD1-SD17, Jacobi oracle, exact-counter differential testing, M0 oracle-backed store)
scores.notes: This design resolves every critique blocker cleanly. Base is head-independent; edges are typed role x currency; there is one stored sat bit per incidence; net-delta propagation pops in rank order; disabled rules stay in the cycle graph, which grows monotonically, so sequential checking is valid; and semantic checks are stateless with ABA chosen explicitly. The L0/L1/L2 three-gate fixpoint is the most rigorous answer to transitive PENDING/REJECTED, and because the oracle is cyclic-safe it can serve as the V1 reference. Concrete flaws: (1) SD11 lets a Pin premise that has been superseded still certify the consumer. That reproduces the section-0 stale-MongoDB failure whenever an agent picks Pin, and the only mitigation is 'no default kind' plus a README warning. Design 3's SD13, which blocks certification while leaving S unchanged, is safer. (2) In M1, L1/L2 are computed on demand by ancestor DFS, so T15b/T15c are only checked lazily until M3.
