(3) Every external or ablation baseline (DD, RevokeAll, PACMI, JTMS) is put off past M1, so H1/H2 get no evidence for months, and the design says almost nothing about workloads. (4) NaiveTopo recomputes the whole graph with Kahn after every AddRule batch in M0. That is fine at test scale, but it means the rank discipline isn't exercised until Pearce-Kelly lands. (5) 'Two non-Pin premises on different revisions of one logical id are rejected' also rejects Sem+Sem across versions, which may be legitimate. Implementability is strong: the scope is small, core depends only on thiserror, the API shape is fixed early by an oracle-backed store, and coverage thresholds plus cargo-mutants make the proptest results believable.

scores.angle: Performance-first native layout (CSR+delta postings, stamped shadow arrays, PK rank heap, baselines from M1b)
scores.notes: The kernel semantics (SD1-SD5) match the other designs and the FRESH-rule initialisation works. The weaknesses are elsewhere. (1) KernelSnapshot carries only per-revision (base, S, count) and per-rule (enabled, deleted, unsat, active). Per-incidence sat bits are missing even though SD5 says they are compared, and witnesses are never compared at all. (2) Physical DeleteRule plus 'hoist deletions to the front' breaks a batch that adds a rule and deletes it in the same transaction (UnknownId), and deleted rules leave counters stale. Tombstones also complicate compaction and Pearce-Kelly. (3) The semantic layer (SD11/SD12) attaches ValidationRecords to the subject revision instead of to the rule plus dependency vector, the definition of 'clear(j,r)' is muddled, and Actionable is computed on read only. Pin to a superseded premise still certifies, as in Design 1. (4) Too much engineering is front-loaded: CSR plus a chunked delta tier, StampedVec shadows with u32 stamp wrap, and a 14 B/incidence target, all before the incremental algorithm is proven. The estimates (M0a in 4 days, seven baselines plus a 6x3 bench matrix in two weeks) are unrealistic, and the 'paranoid' cross-check is the only thing guarding the risk that an edge bypasses Pearce-Kelly. (5) H3 and certification are only a sketch, so the PlanFence/MemTX differentiation, which is the most defensible novelty, has no near-term plan. The research value is good for H1 layout isolation (pointer_graph and vecvec ablations on the same algorithm) and for honest DD tuning, but the design optimises the part the critiques say is least novel.

scores.angle: Paper-first (Maintainer trait with correct modes + MemTX/PACMI ablations, harness metrics FI/MI/OI/UI/AR, D1-D4 differentiation)
scores.notes: The semantics are sound and complete (SD1-SD20). Folding enabled in as a virtual literal and the T27 head+retract-same-revision test are good choices. SD13 is the best answer to the 'Pin superseded' trap: S stays SUPPORTED, but certification is blocked with SUPERSEDED_PREMISE, and evidence is exempt. Having two oracles (naive and Kahn) cross-checked is also good. Concrete flaws: (1) Rule dedup is keyed on (RevId, u64 hash) with no full compare, so a hash collision silently merges different rules. Idempotent AddRule that returns an existing disabled RuleId has no defined meaning. (2) The CertOK rule for SEMANTIC_RECHECK requires Certified(head(logical(p))), which couples the plan's certification to the new revision's own support. That is defensible, but nothing in the critiques demands it, and it needs its own test. (3) The certificate fast path (max last_changed <= cert.epoch) does not account for ValidationRecord or enable changes unless last_changed is bumped for those too. (4) The undo-log in-place mutation of M1 has to be rebuilt as chunked MVCC in M2, which the design itself admits. (5) The dirty Map<RuleId,...> ordering needs to be deterministic for CommitStats to reproduce. (6) M1 is far too big for 4 weeks: six modes, the harness, seven generators, an exhaustive checker, three index layouts and first figures. The oracle also emits counters but no witness. On the research side it is the strongest. The H2a/H2b split is plotted against measured OR-prevalence. The ablations are traceable to MemTX dependency_graph.py and PACMI Algorithm 1, each with a 'fixed' variant. Policy-eval mode is separated from cumulative mode. D1-D4 are tests that only ContextDB's deltas can pass. Certification baselines (PlanFence, MemTX gate, S-Bus, Git OID) are run in a rho sweep, and the design admits it cannot beat PlanFence's centralised-lineage critique. This is the only design that answers the novelty-eval lens directly.

best_ideas_to_graft: From Design 1: an M0 store whose queries are answered by the oracle over an independent BTreeMap InputModel that shares no code with txn/engine. This fixes the API before the engine exists and avoids common-mode bugs.

From Design 1: the L0/L1/L2 three-gate positive fixpoint for transitive certification (gate = true / sem != Rejected / sem in {Verified, NotRequired}) as the normative definition. Combine it with Design 3's SD13 rule that a Pin premise to a superseded non-Evidence revision blocks certification but never changes S.

From Design 1: coverage counters with hard thresholds (mixed head+base flips, alternative-support saves, cycle rejects, CAS conflicts), cargo-mutants over propagate.rs/txn.rs, and P7 permutation and P4 rebuild-equals-incremental properties.

From Design 1 SD10: semantic state keyed by (rule, current version vector restricted to its Sem logicals), with an implicit author-attested vector, rather than keyed by the subject revision as in Design 2.

From Design 3: a single Maintainer trait shared by the transaction front-end, with correct modes (FullRecompute, NaiveBfs, JtmsTwoPhase) asserted against the oracle and RevokeAll{cascade_on_supersede}/TypedMaxLattice scored with PACMI OI/UI/AR in both policy-eval and cumulative mode.

From Design 3: the H2a/H2b split plotted against measured OR-prevalence (p_alt knob), the D1-D4 differentiation goldens, and the M3 certification baselines (PlanFence frontier, MemTX gate, S-Bus OCC) with a rho sweep and trap/control pairs.
From Design 3: enabled(j) as a virtual premise literal (unsat includes !enabled), plus two independent oracles (naive fixpoint and Kahn) cross-checked in CI.

From Design 2: a CommitReport where excess_over_optimal = rules_reevaluated - rules_flipped, with Pearce-Kelly fast-insert, search and reorder counters and MemFootprint bytes per incidence. Keep timers behind a feature flag so the counters stay deterministic.

From Design 2: H1 layout isolation that runs the identical counter algorithm on pointer_graph (HashMap<u64, Box<Node>>), Vec<Vec>, and CSR+delta over the same EventLog. Defer the CSR delta tier and stamped shadows until after M1 correctness.
Compare per-incidence sat bits and canonical witnesses in the oracle snapshot (Design 2 omits both; Design 3 omits the witness). Reject exact-duplicate rules with a full compare, never by hash alone.

Avoid physical DeleteRule in V0. Use disable-only, append-only rules as in Designs 1 and 3, so the cycle graph only grows and sequential within-batch checks are equivalent to checking the final graph.
judgements.winner: Paper-first (Design 3), cut down in scope. Use Design 1's M0 (oracle-backed store, independent InputModel, the L0/L1/L2 definitions, coverage and mutation gates) as its correctness foundation, and limit M1 to the counting kernel plus FullRecompute, JTMS, RevokeAll and TypedMaxLattice. Defer the extra index layouts and the full bench matrix to M1b.

scores.angle: Correctness-first (pure-function InputState->DerivedState, Jacobi oracle, exact-counter differential testing)
scores.notes: Strongest on the critique blockers. SD1/SD2/SD3/SD8/SD10/SD11 resolve every semantic blocker. The oracle applies ops to an independent BTreeMap InputModel and shares no canonicalization or arena code with the engine, so it is the only design that guards against common-mode bugs in validation as well as in derivation. Each cached value is a stored bit compared with recomputed truth, so the propagation invariant is simple and sound. Three-layer L0/L1/L2 positive fixpoints handle transitive PENDING and REJECTED (T15b/c) cleanly. Flaws: (1) SD11 lets a Pin premise to a superseded Decision still certify, which reproduces the section-0 failure mode whenever agents misuse Pin. It is only documented, not prevented. (2) SD10 keys ValidationRecords by (rule, curvec) rather than by revision. A conclusion with two Sem rules then needs two validations, which diverges from the spec's per-revision record and from PlanFence's model. (3) Canonicalize rejects any two non-Pin revisions of one logical id, including Sem v1 + Sem v2, which is stricter than needed. (4) M1 computes L1/L2 by an on-demand ancestor DFS, so CURRENT costs as much as the closure on deep graphs. (5) Biggest weakness: no baseline, workload or benchmark harness before M5. H1/H2a/H2b/H3 cannot be measured in early iterations, DD, MemTX and PACMI comparisons are deferred, and the paper story lags. Scope and dependencies (thiserror only) are very realistic on 1.95.

scores.angle: Performance-first native layout (CSR+delta postings, stamped shadow arrays, Pearce-Kelly from M0, rich CommitReport)
scores.notes: Semantics SD1-SD15 mostly match design 1. Concrete correctness flaws: (1) Heap-key staleness bug. Phase 1 pushes nodes with key (ord<<32|rev) during SetBase, SetHead and SetRuleEnabled ops, but a later AddRule in the same batch can reorder ord through Pearce-Kelly. Queued keys then go stale and the 'premise final before conclusion pops' invariant breaks. The text claims seeds are pushed 'after PK fixed the final order', which contradicts the phase-1 loop as written. Seeds must be deferred until all structural ops finish. (2) KernelSnapshot omits per-incidence sat bits and witnesses, so the oracle comparison is weaker than the critique asked for. (3) DeleteRule with deletion hoisting changes op order relative to CAS and other ops, adding semantic surface: if a delete is hoisted ahead of an enable of the same rule, it is unclear which wins. (4) The FRESH path initializes from final premises, which works, but it is a second code path next to the delta path and needs its own tests. (5) SD11 matches a per-revision ValidationRecord against a per-rule Sem-logical set, so two rules with different Sem logicals are ambiguous. (6) The <=14 B/incidence target is implausible: prem_rev(4) + mode(1) + inc_rule(4) + posting(4) + sat bit, plus a stamped shadow (bool + u32 stamp), already exceeds it. Implementability risk: StampedVec staging, a CSR delta tier with compaction, PK, and a 7-crate split all land in 'days 1-10'. That is premature optimization before semantics are locked, and the bench-dd crate depends on a scratchpad path. Research value is high: layout-isolated ablations (pointer_graph, vecvec vs CSR), exact versus inexact baselines with OI/UI/AR, MemFootprint, excess-over-optimal, PK cost, error-equivalence checking, and a paranoid cross-check mode. H3 and certification are only sketched.

scores.angle: Paper-first (one front-end, swappable Maintainer modes incl. MemTX/PACMI-faithful ablations, harness with policy-eval metrics from M1)
scores.notes: This is the best research framing. H2 is split into H2a (effectiveness against faithful MemTX/PACMI ablations, plotted against OR-prevalence p_alt) and H2b (efficiency: excess over optimal, churn, against correct IVM). Differentiation tests D1-D4 target PlanFence, MemTX and PACMI directly, policy-eval is warm-started from the oracle so the ablations are not strawmen, all modes share one front-end so only propagation policy differs, DD is admitted only through the oracle harness, and the stats/no-stats runs are monomorphized. SD13 is the most defensible choice on Pin: a Pin edge to a superseded non-Evidence premise blocks certification with SUPERSEDED_PREMISE, which avoids the section-0 failure that designs 1 and 2 accept. The cost is that PINNED is effectively Evidence-only for certification, which should be stated. Concrete flaws: (1) The oracle reads the graph through a GraphView backed by core's arenas and canonicalization. Bugs in canonicalize, dedup or CAS are therefore common-mode and invisible to the oracle (design 1's independent InputModel fixes this). (2) The text sets unsat=n+1 for new enabled rules, then the algorithm recomputes unsat from sat_count + enabled. This is an inconsistent spec, harmless only because the value is overwritten. (3) Idempotent AddRule dedup returns the existing RuleId even when that rule is disabled, which silently yields an inactive rule. It should reject or report it. (4) The commit pipeline runs all CAS checks before appending revisions and rules, so op ordering inside a transaction is underspecified compared with design 1's sequential staging. (5) Certification is computed on read with a per-call memo, so cost depends on closure size on hub graphs, which the design acknowledges. (6) M1 in about 4 weeks is ambitious: 6 modes, harness, 7 generators, exhaustive checker and benches. The modes are small, though, and the M0 scope is sane. The M2 chunked Arc MVCC plan is realistic.

best_ideas_to_graft: From design 1: an oracle that applies ops to its own BTreeMap InputModel with its own validation (canonicalize, CAS, cycle, duplicate), sharing no code with txn or arena. Compare inputs as well as derived state after every commit or reject, so design 3's GraphView common-mode gap goes away.

From design 1: the three-layer L0/L1/L2 positive-fixpoint formulation (gate g_k per layer, conflict as an L2 node gate), computed by the oracle from M0. It is the cleanest oracle-checkable definition of transitive PENDING and REJECTED, and M3 can make it incremental by reusing propagate with the gate as a virtual premise.

From design 1: proptest coverage counters with hard thresholds (head+base flips on the same revision, alternative-support saves, cycle rejects, CAS conflicts), cargo-mutants on propagate.rs and txn.rs, digest-unchanged-on-reject (T29), and exact witness comparison.

From design 3: the Maintainer trait over a shared transaction front-end, with Counting/Full/NaiveBfs/JTMS plus MemTX-faithful RevokeAll{cascade_on_supersede} and PACMI-faithful TypedMaxLattice. Use warm-started policy-eval for the FI/MI/OI/UI/AR metrics, and plot H2a against measured p_alt.

From design 3: the SD13 rule that a Pin edge to a superseded non-Evidence premise blocks certification (SUPERSEDED_PREMISE) while leaving S unchanged, plus a REBIND helper. This closes the section-0 hole that designs 1 and 2 only document.

From design 3: differentiation golden tests D1-D4 and T06c as the PlanFence-differentiating case, plus pre-registered expectations (wins only on deep/hub/OR-heavy shapes) and env.json/ShapeStats attached to every result row.

From design 2: error-equivalence checking between oracle and engine (same error class on the same op), a 'paranoid' feature that cross-checks incremental against naive recompute after every commit, MemFootprint bytes/incidence, and a posting-layout ablation (Vec<Vec> vs CSR+delta vs HashMap pointer graph) with the same algorithm and the same log for H1.

From design 2 (with a fix): defer every heap push until all structural ops in the batch are done and Pearce-Kelly ord is final. Collect seeds as dirty sets during phase 1 and push afterwards, so heap keys never go stale.

Common to all three: no physical rule deletion in V0, with a cycle graph over all rules ever added including disabled ones. Keep design 1's/3's append-only approach and do not adopt design 2's DeleteRule hoisting yet.
Keep stamped shadow arrays and the CSR delta tier as post-M1 optimizations behind the differential harness. Do not build them in M0.
judgements.winner: Design 3 (paper-first) as the overall skeleton, because only it makes H1, H2a/H2b and H3 measurable from M1 against faithful competitor ablations. Graft design 1's independent InputModel oracle, its L0/L1/L2 layered fixpoints and its coverage/mutation gates to fix design 3's common-mode oracle weakness. Design 1 is the strongest on pure correctness but too weak on research value to win alone. Design 2 has a concrete heap-key staleness bug and too much early complexity.
